vr.e: Claiming only an extra hour rather than changing the world keeps her claims small and unexaggerated, which is what modest means here; boastful and grand describe exactly the big claims she avoids, and her careful wording is the opposite of reckless.

y.A: Reckless means charging ahead without thinking what could go wrong, and the inventor is doing the careful opposite — claiming only what she is sure of.
y.B: Boastful means talking up how good you are, and the inventor does the reverse — she deliberately keeps her claim small.
y.C: A grand claim is a huge, sweeping one, and hers was deliberately small — one extra hour, not changing the world.

vr.q: When the rest of the team stopped speaking to Priya after the missed penalty, Dana walked home with her as she always had; nobody who knew Dana was surprised at how ______ she was.
vr.e: Standing by a friend when everyone else turns away is faithfulness, which is what loyal means; the sentence is not about bragging, about being liked by the crowd, or about running out of patience.

y.A: Popular means liked by a great many people, and the sentence is not about how many people like Dana — it is about her standing by the one friend everyone else dropped.
y.C: Boastful means going on about how good you are, and Dana says nothing about herself; she just keeps walking Priya home.
y.D: Impatient means quickly annoyed at having to wait; nobody is waiting for anything here, and walking Priya home is faithfulness, not irritation.

vr.q: His advice was accurate but so ______ that it stung: “Your essay is dull, and you never checked the spelling.”
vr.e: “Stung” rules out gentle and tactful, and the quoted remark names two specific faults, which rules out vague; blunt means honest in a way that spares no feelings.

y.A: Gentle means soft and careful of people's feelings, and his advice stung, so it was anything but gentle; blunt means saying the truth without softening it.
y.B: Vague means unclear and short on detail, and he named two exact faults — the dull writing and the unchecked spelling — so his advice was the opposite of vague.
y.C: Tactful means telling the truth in a way that spares the other person's feelings, and his remark spared none, which is what made it sting.

vr.q: Nobody had asked Mr. Odile to drive two hours with the costumes the cast had forgotten, and the cast was so ______ that they made him a card and clapped when he walked in.
vr.e: Making a card and clapping for someone who drove two hours unasked is a show of thanks, which is what grateful means; annoyance and indifference would show no thanks at all, and nothing about the drive puzzles them.

y.A: Puzzled means confused and unable to work something out; nothing confuses the cast here — they know exactly what Mr. Odile did and are thanking him for it.
y.B: Indifferent means not caring one way or the other, and a card and applause are what people do when they care very much.
y.D: Annoyed means mildly cross, and the cast has nothing to be cross about — the forgotten costumes were their own fault and he put it right.

vr.q: The assembly opened with a ______ minute of silence for the school's founder, and even the youngest students stopped fidgeting.
vr.e: A minute of silence that makes small children go still is grave and dignified, which rules out festive, playful, and casual.

y.A: Playful means full of fun and games, and this is the moment even the fidgeters go still; solemn means grave and serious.
y.C: Casual means easy-going and informal, the way you are with friends, and a minute of silence for the school's founder is as formal as an assembly gets.
y.D: Festive means cheerful in the way a party or a holiday is, and this silence is a mark of respect, which is grave rather than merry.

vr.q: Ms. Ortiz did not excuse the late homework, but her voice was so ______ that Danny came away feeling understood rather than scolded.
vr.e: “Feeling understood rather than scolded” rules out severe and mocking, and indifference would leave him feeling nothing; sympathetic means sharing in how someone else feels.

y.A: Indifferent means not caring either way, and an indifferent voice would have left Danny feeling nothing at all rather than understood.
y.B: Severe means harsh and stern; Ms. Ortiz did hold him to the rule, but she did it in a kind voice, and severe describes a voice that is not kind.
y.C: Mocking means making fun of someone, and nobody is laughing at Danny — he comes away feeling understood.

vr.q: The box of old camp photographs left Grandma smiling and ______, saying again and again how much she missed those summers by the lake.
vr.e: She is smiling and speaking fondly of what she misses, which rules out bitter and anxious; nothing is being waited for, so not impatient. Nostalgic is exactly this fond longing for the past.

y.B: Impatient means fed up with waiting, and Grandma is not waiting for anything; she is looking back at summers that are already over.
y.C: Anxious means worried about what might happen, and her feeling points backwards to the lake summers she misses, not forwards to anything to fear.
y.D: Bitter means sour and angry over something that went wrong, and she is smiling as she remembers, so her feeling is fond rather than sour.

vr.q: By the last mile of the hike Ana had stopped chattering altogether, and her answers came out in a ______ mumble.
vr.e: Falling silent and mumbling at the end of a long hike shows worn-out tiredness, which is what weary means; a cheerful or playful hiker would still be talking, and nothing on the trail has alarmed her.

y.A: Cheerful means bright and in good spirits, and Ana has gone quiet and is mumbling, which is what being worn out looks like at the end of a long walk.
y.C: Playful means in the mood for fun and games, and someone in that mood would still be chattering; Ana has stopped altogether.
y.D: Alarmed means suddenly frightened by something, and nothing on the trail has frightened Ana — she is simply worn out.

vr.q: BOASTFUL most nearly means:
vr.e: A boastful person keeps announcing how good he is; complaining, fear, and generosity are unrelated traits.

y.B: Always complaining about others is grumbling and faultfinding, and a boastful person's subject is not other people at all — it is himself.
y.C: Being very generous with money means giving it away freely, and boastful says nothing about money; it is about how a person talks about himself.
y.D: Being easily frightened by noise is being jumpy or timid, and a boastful person is not shrinking from anything — he is announcing how good he is.

vr.q: GRACIOUS most nearly means:
vr.e: Gracious describes warm good manners, the direct opposite of coldly rude, and it has nothing to do with confusion or humor.

y.A: Wildly funny is about making people laugh, which is humor rather than manners, and gracious is about how warmly and politely you treat people.
y.B: Being confused by simple things means struggling to understand, and gracious has nothing to do with how quickly you understand — it is about kind good manners.
y.D: Coldly rude is meeting someone with no warmth at all, and gracious is its exact opposite — warmth and good manners.

vr.q: RESENTFUL most nearly means:
vr.e: Resentful is the sour anger left behind by treatment you think was unfair; gratitude is its opposite, and eagerness and puzzlement are not anger.

y.B: Being eager to begin a task is keenness, wanting to get started, while resentful is a sour, angry feeling that looks back at something already done to you.
y.C: Grateful means thankful for a kindness, and resentful is its opposite — the bitterness left behind when you feel you were treated unfairly.
y.D: Being puzzled by a new rule means not understanding it, and a resentful person understands the rule perfectly well — she just feels she was treated unfairly and stays angry about it.

vr.q: MELANCHOLY most nearly means:
vr.e: Melancholy is a low, lingering sadness, so humor, energy, and alertness all miss it.

y.A: Extremely funny is about making people laugh, and melancholy is a low, lingering sadness — the furthest thing from laughter.
y.C: Wide awake is about being alert rather than sleepy, and melancholy describes a mood; you can feel melancholy wide awake or half asleep.
y.D: Full of energy describes someone bursting to get going, and melancholy is a quiet, heavy sadness that slows a person down.

vr.q: GRIM most nearly means:
vr.e: Grim describes something stern and cheerless; hopeful, silly, and welcoming are all the opposite in feeling.

y.A: Warm and welcoming is how a friend greets you at the door, and grim is the opposite — hard, cheerless and forbidding.
y.B: Silly and light means playful and not serious, while grim is heavy and severe, the look on a face when the news is bad.
y.C: Bright and hopeful means expecting things to turn out well, and grim is the opposite in feeling — hard, cheerless and gloomy to look at.

vr.q: APOLOGETIC most nearly means:
vr.e: Apologetic means showing that you regret something you did; pride, anger, and curiosity carry no regret.

y.B: Being proud of a win is pleasure in something you did well, and apologetic is the opposite feeling — regret for something you did badly.
y.C: Being curious about a plan means wanting to know more about it, and apologetic carries no question in it at all, only sorriness for a fault.
y.D: Being angry at a rule is temper aimed at the rule, and an apologetic person is not angry; she is admitting she was in the wrong.

vr.q: SCORNFUL most nearly means:
vr.e: Scorn is contempt, so scornful means treating something as beneath you — the opposite of admiring, and unrelated to helpfulness or uncertainty.

y.B: Eager to help describes someone quick to pitch in, which says nothing about scorn — scorn is the cold feeling that a thing is beneath you.
y.C: Admiration is looking up to someone and thinking well of them, which is the exact opposite of scorn — a scornful person looks down.
y.D: Being unsure of the answer is doubt, which is about not knowing something; scorn is about looking down on a thing as not worth your respect.

vr.q: DEFIANT most nearly means:
vr.e: Defiant means openly standing against an order, the opposite of obedient; amusement and gratitude are different feelings entirely.

y.A: Easily amused means quick to find things funny, which is about laughing, not about standing up to an order.
y.B: Grateful means full of thanks for something you have been given, and someone defiant is refusing rather than thanking.
y.D: Quietly obedient means doing as you are told without any fuss, which is the very opposite of defiant — defiance is refusing out loud.

vr.q: Though the whole town praised her invention, Maya stayed ______, insisting that her science teacher deserved as much credit as she did.
vr.e: She insists on sharing the credit, which rules out smug, and insisting aloud is not timid; she plainly cares, so not indifferent. Humble means not thinking too highly of yourself.

y.A: Timid means shy and easily frightened, but Maya insists out loud that her teacher deserves the credit, and insisting takes nerve rather than shyness.
y.C: Indifferent means not caring one way or the other, and Maya plainly cares a great deal — she insists her teacher be given credit.
y.B: Smug means pleased with yourself and showing it, and Maya does the reverse — she hands the credit to her teacher.

vr.q: After the win, Trent's grin was ______, and he reminded everyone yet again that he had predicted the score exactly.
vr.e: Reminding everyone “yet again” of his own correct prediction is self-satisfied, not gracious; he is neither sorry (apologetic) nor worried (anxious) after winning.

y.A: Gracious means being kind and generous about other people, especially when you have won, and Trent does the opposite by reminding everyone of his own cleverness.
y.D: Apologetic means looking sorry, as though you wished you had not done something, and Trent is enjoying himself far too much for that.
y.C: Anxious means worried, and Trent has just won and is reminding everyone that he called the score.

vr.q: The kitten's ______ streak showed the moment she batted every pencil off the desk and darted away with her tail high.
vr.e: Knocking pencils down harms nobody, so vicious (cruel) is far too strong; she is causing trouble, so not obedient, and darting off tail-high is not timid. Mischievous means playfully naughty.

y.A: Obedient means doing what you are told, and a kitten who sweeps every pencil off the desk is doing the opposite of what she is told.
y.B: Vicious means cruel and meaning to cause harm, which is far too strong for a kitten knocking pencils about for fun.
y.D: Timid means shy and easily scared, but this kitten darts off with her tail high, which is the swagger of a confident cat.

vr.q: Two goals behind at half time, Coach stayed ______, telling the players the comeback was still theirs for the taking.
vr.e: He encourages the team, which rules out gloomy and furious, and “still theirs for the taking” shows he is sure rather than uncertain; optimistic means expecting things to turn out well.

y.A: Gloomy means low-spirited and expecting the worst, and the coach tells his players the comeback is still theirs, which is expecting the best.
y.B: Furious means extremely angry, and the coach is encouraging his players rather than raging at them.
y.D: Uncertain means not knowing which way things will go, but "still theirs for the taking" is said with confidence, not with doubt.

vr.q: Ravi had been certain he had failed the audition, so when the cast list went up with his name on it, he sat down on the steps looking utterly ______.
vr.e: Seeing his name after expecting the worst lifts a weight off him, which is what relieved means; alarm, annoyance, and disappointment would all follow bad news, not good.

y.B: Disappointed is what you feel when something you hoped for does not happen, and Ravi's name is on the list, so the hoped-for thing did happen.
y.C: Alarmed means suddenly frightened by something bad, and finding out you have been cast is good news, not a fright.
y.D: Annoyed means mildly cross at something irritating, and there is nothing to be cross about when you have been cast after expecting to fail.

vr.q: Rather than saying the painting was ugly, Nina gave a ______ reply, praising its colors before suggesting one change.
vr.e: “Rather than saying it was ugly” and the praise that comes first rule out blunt and rude, and she says nothing about herself, so not boastful; tactful means honest without wounding.

y.A: Blunt means saying exactly what you think without softening it, which is precisely what Nina avoided by praising the colors first.
y.B: Boastful means showing off about yourself, and Nina says nothing about herself at all — she is talking about the painting.
y.C: Rude means openly disrespectful, and Nina goes out of her way to be kind about the painting before she suggests a change.

vr.q: The old dog was ______, nudging Nora's hand until she petted him and then settling his head in her lap.
vr.e: He seeks Nora out for petting, so he is not indifferent, and resting his head in her lap shows trust, which rules out hostile and fearful; affectionate means showing fondness.

y.B: Hostile means unfriendly and ready for a fight, and a dog who settles his head in your lap is doing the opposite of picking one.
y.C: Indifferent means not caring either way, but this dog nudges Nora's hand until she pets him, so he cares very much.
y.D: Fearful means frightened and expecting to be hurt, and a dog who feels that way shrinks back rather than pushing his head into someone's hands.

vr.q: With the results due any minute, Dev chewed his sleeve and kept checking the clock; he was plainly ______, certain the news would be bad.
vr.e: Being “certain the news would be bad” is worry, not boredom, and the sleeve-chewing and clock-watching rule out relaxed and delighted; anxious means uneasy about what is coming.

y.B: Relaxed means calm and free of worry, and someone chewing his sleeve and watching the clock is the opposite of calm.
y.C: Bored means having nothing interesting to occupy you, but Dev is not short of something on his mind — he is certain the news will be bad.
y.D: Delighted means filled with joy, and Dev expects bad news, which is nobody's idea of a delight.

vr.q: The review was sharply ______, listing every flaw in the play and praising almost nothing.
vr.e: Listing every flaw and praising almost nothing rules out admiring and cheerful, and the word “sharply” rules out neutral; critical here means fault-finding.

y.A: Neutral means taking neither side, but a review that lists every flaw and praises almost nothing has plainly taken a side.
y.B: Cheerful means bright and good-humoured, which is not how a review reads when it finds fault with everything in the play.
y.D: Admiring means full of praise for something, and this review praises almost nothing.

vr.q: DISCRETION most nearly means:
c: the power to decide for yourself
a rule that must always be followed
vr.e: When a trip is “left to the principal's discretion,” she has the power to decide; a rule that must be followed is the opposite of leaving a choice to someone.

y.B: A loud and public complaint is an outcry or a protest; discretion points the other way, at quietly being trusted to make the choice yourself.
y.C: A rule that must always be followed leaves nobody any choice, and discretion is exactly the opposite — it is what you have when the choice is left up to you.
y.D: A careful written record is a log or a register, but discretion is not something written down; it is the freedom to decide.

vr.q: UNANIMOUS most nearly means:
c: agreed to by every single member
decided by one person in charge
put off until a later meeting
vr.e: A unanimous vote is one in which everyone agrees. The look-alike word is anonymous, which means the name is not known.

y.B: A decision made by one person in charge is a decree, an order given from the top; unanimous means every single member agreed, not just the one in charge.
y.C: Putting something off until a later meeting is postponing it, which is about when the decision is made, not about how many people agreed.
y.D: Kept secret from every member is not what unanimous means — that word, with a u, means every single member agreed. You may be thinking of anonymous, which does not mean secret either: there the thing is out in the open and only the name behind it is unknown.

vr.q: CONSPICUOUS most nearly means:
c: acting in a sneaky, guilty way
vr.e: A conspicuous stain is one everyone sees at once. Suspicious (sneaky) and conscientious (careful) are the two look-alike words that do not mean the same thing.

y.A: Someone extremely careful about details in their work, because they want it done properly, is conscientious — the word that looks and sounds like this one; conspicuous is about being easy to see.
y.B: Something kept carefully out of sight is hidden, which is the opposite of conspicuous — a conspicuous thing is right there where you cannot miss it.
y.D: Acting in a sneaky, guilty way is suspicious, another look-alike word; something conspicuous simply stands out where everyone notices it, with no guilt about it at all.

vr.q: BENIGN most nearly means:
vr.e: A benign remark or a benign old dog does no harm; none of the other choices carries the idea of harmlessness.

y.B: Large and very heavy is massive or bulky, and size has nothing to do with benign — a huge old dog can be perfectly benign.
y.C: Quick and noisy describes how something moves and sounds, while benign describes whether it can do you any harm.
y.D: Sharply critical of others means finding fault with people, which is the opposite of benign — a benign remark hurts nobody.

vr.q: PREDICAMENT most nearly means:
c: a hard spot to get out of
a promise made in front of a crowd
a guess about what will happen next
a long delay before an event
vr.e: Being locked out in the rain with no phone is a predicament — a situation you cannot easily escape. The look-alike word is prediction, a guess about the future.

y.B: A promise made in front of a crowd is a pledge or a vow, but a predicament is trouble you are stuck in, not something you promised.
y.C: A guess about what will happen next is a prediction, the look-alike word; a predicament is the fix you are already in.
y.D: A long delay before an event is a wait or a postponement, which is about time passing, while a predicament is a difficulty you cannot easily get out of.

vr.q: REMINISCE most nearly means:
c: to remind someone of a chore
to plan carefully for next year
to talk fondly about times gone by
vr.e: To reminisce is to look back and share memories, the way grandparents do about their childhood; reminding, apologizing, and planning all point at the present or future.

y.A: To remind someone is to make them think of something they still have to do, while to reminisce, which looks similar, is to look back at the past for pleasure.
y.B: To apologize is to say sorry for something you did wrong, and reminiscing is simply sharing stories about the past, with no fault in it.
y.C: To plan carefully for next year looks forward to what has not happened yet, and reminiscing looks the other way, back at what already has.

vr.q: WANE most nearly means:
c: to get smaller little by little
vr.e: Interest that wanes fades bit by bit, the way a waning moon shrinks each night; its partner word wax means to grow.

y.B: To break apart suddenly is to shatter, but waning is slow and gradual, the way the moon loses a sliver each night.
y.C: To stay exactly the same is to remain constant, but something that wanes is changing all the while by growing less.
y.D: To grow larger and brighter is to wax, wane's partner word; wane is the shrinking half of the pair.

vr.q: LITERAL most nearly means:
c: spoken in a very loud voice
having to do with books and authors
taking words in their exact meaning
vr.e: The literal meaning of “raining cats and dogs” would be actual animals falling from the sky. Literary, the look-alike word, is about books.

y.A: Spoken in a very loud voice is about how something is said, not about what the words mean, and literal is entirely about meaning.
y.B: Having to do with books and authors is literary, the look-alike word with two r's; literal has one r and means taking words exactly as they stand.
y.D: Full of colorful comparisons describes figurative language, which is the opposite of literal — the literal meaning is the plain one, with no comparison in it.

vr.q: SUBORDINATE most nearly means:
vr.e: In “cost was a subordinate concern,” cost mattered less than the main issue; something subordinate ranks below, never above or equal.

y.B: Being in charge of everyone else makes you superior, and a subordinate is the one ranked below, not above.
y.C: Exactly equal in rank means neither one stands above the other, but subordinate always means lower than something else.
y.D: Needed more than anything else is essential, and subordinate says the opposite — that this concern matters less than the main one.

vr.q: COMPACT most nearly means:
c: spread out over a wide area
vr.e: A compact kitchen fits everything into a small area; compact says nothing about softness, single use, or wide spread.

y.A: Used only one time is disposable, which is about how often you use a thing, not about how much room it takes up.
y.C: Made of very soft material is about what a thing is made of, while compact is about how tightly it is packed into a small space — a compact kitchen can be full of soft things.
y.D: Spread out over a wide area is the opposite of compact, which means everything gathered neatly into a small space.

vr.q: Starting a bakery takes more ______ than most people expect: ovens, rent, and flour must all be paid for before the first loaf is sold.
vr.e: Capital is the money and resources needed to start or run a business, which is exactly what the ovens, rent, and flour require.

y.A: A trace is a tiny amount of something, or a mark it leaves behind, which is the opposite of the large sum ovens and rent cost.
y.B: A sanctuary is a safe place where something is protected, like a wildlife sanctuary, and a new bakery needs money rather than shelter.
y.D: A conflict is a fight or a disagreement, and this sentence is about what must be paid for before the first loaf is sold, not about anyone quarrelling.

vr.q: Mr. Alvarez graded the ______ of each essay — the ideas and the evidence — rather than the neatness of the handwriting.
vr.e: Here content means what is inside the essay — the ideas and the evidence — rather than how much was written (volume); this is a different meaning from “content with her meal,” which means satisfied.

y.A: Volume can mean how much there is of something — how many pages an essay runs to — and Mr. Alvarez is grading the ideas inside it, not the amount.
y.B: Discipline is training yourself to keep at something and behave well, which is a habit a person has, not something written inside an essay.
y.C: Stock is the supply of goods a shop keeps ready to sell, so it has nothing to do with the ideas and evidence in an essay.

vr.q: Our science teacher wrote the ______ “habitat” on the board and asked us to explain what it names.
vr.e: A term is a word or expression used for something — a different meaning from a school term or the terms of a contract.

y.A: A riddle is a puzzling question meant to be guessed at, but "habitat" is not a puzzle — it is a word with a settled meaning.
y.B: A rumor is a story passed from person to person that may well not be true, and "habitat" is a word from science, not gossip.
y.D: A custom is something a group has long been in the habit of doing, like a holiday tradition, and "habitat" is a word, not a practice.

vr.q: Grandma keeps the first ______ of the old encyclopedia, the one covering A through C, beside her chair.
vr.e: A volume is one book of a set; “the one covering A through C” rules out the loudness and the amount meanings.

y.B: A verdict is the decision reached at the end of a trial, which has nothing to do with a book beside Grandma's chair.
y.C: A sanctuary is a safe place where something is protected, such as a bird sanctuary, and an encyclopedia is a set of books, not a refuge.
y.D: Stock is the supply of goods a shop keeps to sell, so a shop might hold a stock of encyclopedias, but one book of the set is a volume.

vr.q: When the storm knocked out the power, the fire department ______ assistance to every family on the block, delivering water and blankets before midnight.
vr.e: To render assistance is to give it, which is exactly what delivering water and blankets describes; refusing or suspending help would mean the opposite, and to eradicate something is to wipe it out completely.

y.A: Suspended means stopped for a while with the idea of starting again later, but the fire department did not pause its help — it carried water and blankets out that same night.
y.B: Eradicated means wiped out completely, the way a disease can be eradicated; help given to families is handed over, not destroyed.
y.C: Refused means said no and would not do it, which is the opposite of a crew delivering water and blankets to every family before midnight.

vr.q: The museum applied for a ______ from the city and used the money to repair its leaking roof.
vr.e: A grant is a sum of money given for a purpose; “used the money” shows this is the noun, not the verb “to grant permission.”

y.A: A warning tells you trouble may be coming so you can get ready for it; a warning from the city would not have paid for a new roof.
y.B: A custom is a way of doing something that people have kept up for years, like a birthday custom — it is a habit, not money a museum can apply for.
y.C: A verdict is the decision a jury or a judge reaches at the end of a trial, and nobody is being judged here; the museum was given money.

vr.q: Because no ferry ran on Sundays, the team had to ______ a boat to reach the island for the tournament.
vr.e: To charter a boat or a bus is to hire it for private use — the verb sense, not the city charter that is a founding document.

y.B: Stifle means to smother something or hold it back, the way you stifle a yawn in class; you can stifle a laugh, but you cannot stifle a boat.
y.C: Eradicate means to get rid of something completely, like eradicating the weeds from a garden — the team needed to hire a boat, not destroy one.
y.D: Suspect means to think something may be true before you have proof; the team's problem is not a doubt about the boat, it is having no boat at all.

vr.q: Ticket sales began to ______ in the third week, dropping from four hundred a night to barely fifty.
vr.e: The numbers fall from 400 to 50, so decline here means to go steadily down, not to turn down an invitation.

y.A: Retaliate means to strike back at someone who has hurt you first, but ticket numbers are not paying anybody back — they are simply falling.
y.B: Cultivate means to tend something so that it grows, the way a gardener tends a row of beans; sales going from four hundred to fifty are shrinking, not growing.
y.C: Strive means to try hard at something, which says nothing about numbers falling from four hundred to fifty.

vr.q: The vet spoke in a ______ voice and moved slowly, and the frightened kitten stopped shaking.
vr.e: Tender here means gentle and kind, which is what calms the kitten; the sore-to-the-touch meaning of tender would not describe a voice.

y.A: Domestic means having to do with the home — domestic chores, a domestic cat — so it can describe a household, but not the sound of someone's voice.
y.C: Tangible means solid enough to touch, like a receipt you can hold in your hand; a voice can be heard but never touched, and it is the vet's kindness that calms the kitten.
y.D: Restless means unable to keep still or settle down, which is how the frightened kitten was — the vet is the opposite, moving slowly and speaking gently.

vr.q: The old radio crackled with so much ______ that we could not make out a single word of the weather report.
vr.e: Static is the crackling noise that blocks a radio signal — a noun, and a different meaning from static as “not changing.”

y.A: A trace is a tiny bit of something left behind, like a trace of mud on the floor; what fills this radio is a loud crackling, which is the opposite of a tiny bit.
y.C: Conflict means a fight or a clash between people or ideas, and a radio crackling on a shelf is making a noise, not having an argument.
y.D: Rust is the reddish-brown flaking that grows on old iron when it gets wet; rust can ruin a radio, but it is something you see, not the crackle you hear.

vr.q: EXPLOIT most nearly means:
c: to take unfair advantage of someone
vr.e: An employer who exploits workers profits from them by paying unfairly; praising, repairing, and handing over involve no unfair use.

y.A: Repairing something with care is mending or restoring it, which leaves a thing better than you found it; someone who exploits people is using them for his own gain instead.
y.C: Praising someone in public is complimenting or commending them, which is treating them well; exploiting them is treating them unfairly.
y.D: Handing something over willingly is surrendering or giving it up, and the giving is your own choice; exploiting is taking advantage of someone who has no such choice.

vr.q: STRIVE most nearly means:
c: to wait for someone else to act
to try hard over a long time
vr.e: To strive for a goal is to keep making real effort toward it; each of the other choices describes not making that effort.

y.A: Waiting for someone else to act is being passive and leaving the work to others, while striving is effort you make yourself.
y.B: Wandering with no plan is roaming or drifting, going wherever you happen to end up; someone who strives is heading somewhere on purpose.
y.D: Giving up quickly is quitting, which is exactly what striving is not — you strive by keeping at something even when it is hard.

vr.q: DISCIPLINE most nearly means:
c: a talent a person is born with
a piece of unexpected good luck
vr.e: The discipline to practice every day is trained control over your own behavior, not a mood, a natural gift, or luck.

y.A: A sudden burst of anger is an outburst, or losing your temper — a feeling that takes hold of you; discipline is the steady self-control that stops feelings taking hold.
y.B: A talent a person is born with is a gift, something you have without working for it; discipline is trained, which is the whole point of the word.
y.D: A piece of unexpected good luck is a stroke of fortune that arrives by chance; discipline is built on purpose, a little at a time, and chance has nothing to do with it.

vr.q: FEISTY most nearly means:
c: polite and quiet in a crowd
vr.e: A feisty puppy barks boldly at a much larger dog — full of spirit and unwilling to back down.

y.B: Shy and easily frightened is timid, and a timid puppy backs away from a bigger dog rather than barking boldly at it, which is what a feisty one does.
y.C: Polite and quiet in a crowd is reserved or well-mannered; feisty describes someone spirited and ready to stand up for herself, which is rarely quiet.
y.D: Slow and always sleepy is sluggish, and it takes energy to square up to a much larger dog; feisty is full of that energy.

vr.q: PROMPT most nearly means:
vr.e: A prompt reply arrives right away, so prompt is about speed; care, repetition, and group size are different ideas.

y.A: Done by a large group is collective work, everybody's effort together; prompt tells you how soon something happened, not how many people did it.
y.B: Done again from the start is repeated; a prompt reply is a quick one, and a reply can be quick the very first time it is sent.
y.C: Done very carefully is meticulous; prompt is about being quick, and you can be prompt and sloppy, or slow and careful.

vr.q: CULTIVATE most nearly means:
c: to grow and care for over time
to cut down and clear away
vr.e: Farmers cultivate crops and people cultivate friendships — both mean tending something so it develops; cutting down is closer to the opposite.

y.B: Cutting down and clearing away is clearing or felling, which takes a growing thing away; cultivating is the opposite, keeping it growing.
y.C: Copying exactly is imitating or duplicating; cultivating a friendship or a garden means building it up over time, with nothing copied from anybody.
y.D: Buying in large amounts is stocking up; a farmer who cultivates a field works the soil and raises the crop rather than buying it ready-made.

vr.q: DOMESTIC most nearly means:
c: built a very long time ago
having to do with the home
vr.e: Domestic chores are household chores and a domestic animal is one kept at home; the other choices all point away from the home.

y.A: Coming from somewhere outside your own country is what foreign means, and foreign is domestic's opposite — domestic points at home, whether that is your house or your own country.
y.B: Living wild in the forest is being wild or feral; a domestic animal is the tame one kept at home, which is the other end of the same scale.
y.C: Built a very long time ago is ancient; domestic tells you something belongs to the home and says nothing at all about its age.

vr.q: RETALIATE most nearly means:
c: to strike back after being harmed
to go back and fetch something
to say sorry and make peace
vr.e: A team that trips a player after being tripped retaliates. Retrieve (fetch) and retreat (pull back) are the look-alike words.

y.B: Moving away from danger is retreating, and retreat looks a lot like retaliate at the start; retaliating means hitting back rather than backing off.
y.C: Going back to fetch something is retrieving it — a dog retrieves a ball — and retrieve is the look-alike word; retaliating is something you do back to a person, not something you go and get.
y.D: Saying sorry and making peace is apologizing and forgiving, the gentlest way a quarrel can end; retaliating is the harshest, striking back at whoever harmed you.

vr.q: Two coaches told Nadia the record was out of reach, but she remained ______ and trained every morning anyway.
vr.e: “Trained every morning anyway” shows she held firmly to her purpose, which is what resolute means; the other three say nothing about determination.

y.A: Whimsical means playful and full of odd little fancies that change from moment to moment; Nadia training every single morning is steady, which is the opposite of whimsical.
y.B: Literal means sticking to the plain, exact meaning of words rather than picture-language; it describes how a person reads or speaks, not how firmly she holds to a goal.
y.C: Subordinate means lower in rank, placed under somebody else's authority; the sentence is not about Nadia's rank, it is about her refusing to give up on the record.

vr.q: The class had plenty of theories about the missing mascot but no ______ proof — no photograph, no footprint, nothing they could point to.
vr.e: Tangible proof is solid evidence you can touch or point to, which is exactly what the missing photograph and footprint would have been.

y.A: Unanimous means agreed on by everybody, with nobody against it; the class could all agree on a theory and still have no photograph and no footprint.
y.C: Remote means far away — a remote farmhouse, or a remote chance, meaning a very slight one — but what the class lacks is proof solid enough to point to, not proof from somewhere distant.
y.D: Benign means harmless and kindly, the way a benign smile does nobody any damage; proof is either there or missing, and that is not a question of harm.

vr.q: A classroom rule that punishes every mistake can ______ the very curiosity the teacher hopes to build.
vr.e: To stifle something is to smother or hold it back, and a rule that punishes every mistake crushes the curiosity the teacher wants; cultivating curiosity would grow it instead, exploiting means using something unfairly for your own gain, and nothing here is being measured.

y.A: Exploit means to use someone or something unfairly for your own gain; the rule in the sentence is crushing curiosity, not making a profit from it.
y.B: Measure means to find out how much or how big something is; a rule that punishes every mistake is not measuring curiosity, it is snuffing it out.
y.C: Cultivate means to tend something so that it keeps growing, which is what the teacher hopes to do with curiosity — the rule does the reverse.

vr.q: The general finally learned that his most trusted messenger had been ______ all along, quietly carrying the battle plans to the enemy.
vr.e: Treacherous here means disloyal — betraying the trust placed in him — a different sense from a treacherous mountain road. Conspicuous is ruled out by “quietly.”

y.B: Compact here means packed neatly into a small space, like a compact kitchen — a size or a shape, which says nothing about whether a person can be trusted.
y.C: Conspicuous means easy to notice, standing out so that everyone sees you; this messenger worked quietly, which is why nobody caught him for so long.
y.D: Literal means taking words at their exact, plain meaning; a messenger can be literal-minded and still be perfectly loyal, so it says nothing about carrying plans to the enemy.

vr.q: The offer sounded ______ to Mom: a free bicycle for anyone who simply forwarded the message to ten friends.
vr.e: Something dubious is doubtful and not to be trusted, which is how an offer that seems too good to be true sounds; the other three say nothing about doubt.

y.A: Static means staying the same without changing, and as a noun it is the crackle that spoils a radio; neither one describes an offer that sounds too good to be true.
y.B: Unanimous means agreed on by everyone, with nobody disagreeing; only Mom is judging this offer, and what she feels about it is doubt.
y.D: Compact means packed tightly into a small space; the sentence is about how believable the offer is, not about how much room it takes up.

vr.q: The umpires had to ______ the game in the fourth inning, and both teams waited under the bleachers until the lightning had passed.
vr.e: To suspend something is to stop it for a while, which is what umpires do when lightning arrives; extending, announcing, or repeating the game would all keep it going. Suspend can also mean to hang something up.

y.A: Extend means to make something longer or stretch it out, so extending the game would add to it; the lightning made the umpires stop it instead.
y.C: Announce means to tell everybody something openly; the umpires probably did announce their decision, but the word for halting the game while the storm passes is not announce.
y.D: Repeat means to do something over again from the beginning; the teams are waiting under the bleachers for the same game to carry on, not to start afresh.

vr.q: The injured owl was carried to a bird ______ outside town, where volunteers fed it by hand until it was strong enough to hunt again.
vr.e: A sanctuary is a safe place where something is protected, which is what a refuge for hurt birds is; a laboratory is for experiments, a boundary is a line, and a predicament is a situation rather than a place.

y.A: A boundary is the line where one piece of land ends and the next begins; an owl cannot be carried to a line and fed by hand there.
y.B: A laboratory is a room fitted out for experiments and testing; the volunteers are feeding the owl until it can hunt again, which is looking after it, not experimenting on it.
y.C: A predicament is a difficult spot you are stuck in, and the injured owl was certainly in one — but a predicament is a situation, not a place anyone can carry a bird to.

vr.q: By noon there was not a ______ of snow left on the field; the grass was green and dry from one end to the other.
vr.e: A trace is the tiny amount left behind, so “not a trace” means none at all, which fits grass that is green and dry from end to end. Trace can also mean to copy a drawing through thin paper.

y.A: A verdict is the decision reached at the end of a trial; snow melting off a field is weather, and there is nothing for anyone to decide.
y.C: Volume means how much of something there is — it can also mean loudness, or one book of a set; here the word needed is for the tiniest bit left behind, which is what a trace is.
y.D: A custom is something people have done the same way for years, like a family custom at Christmas; snow on a field is weather, not a habit.

vr.q: After the third sandwich went missing from the counter, Dad began to ______ that the new puppy was not as innocent as she looked.
vr.e: To suspect is to start believing something is true before you have proof, which is what the missing sandwiches lead Dad to think about the puppy; he is not telling anyone, he is far from certain, and he plainly has not forgotten.

y.A: Forget means to let something slip out of your mind, and Dad has done the opposite — three missing sandwiches are very much on it.
y.B: Announce means to tell people something openly; Dad is only beginning to think the puppy is guilty, and he has not declared it to anyone.
y.C: Guarantee means to promise something for certain, and Dad is nowhere near certain — he has a hunch, a puppy, and three missing sandwiches.

qr.q: A garden club plants 28 bulbs, and 3/4 of them bloom. How many bulbs bloom?
qr.e: Find 3/4 of 28: 28÷4=7, and 7×3=21 bulbs.

y.A: 24 is 28 − 4, taking off the 4 from the bottom of the fraction rather than a quarter of the bulbs. A quarter of 28 is 7, so three quarters is 7 × 3 = 21.
y.B: 18 is three short of the answer. A quarter of 28 is 7, and three of those quarters is 7 × 3 = 21.
y.D: 25 is 28 − 3, three bulbs taken off the total. Three quarters means 7 × 3 = 21.

qr.q: Two runners complete 5/6 and 7/9 of a relay. Which runner completed more?
qr.e: Use eighteenths: 5/6=15/18 and 7/9=14/18, so the 5/6 runner completed more.

y.A: Equal would mean the same share, but over eighteenths 5/6 is 15/18 and 7/9 is 14/18 — one eighteenth apart.
y.C: There is enough here: give both fractions the same bottom number. 5/6 becomes 15/18 and 7/9 becomes 14/18, so the 5/6 runner did more.
y.D: 7/9 has the bigger numbers, but bigger numbers do not mean a bigger share. In eighteenths it is 14/18, just under 5/6 at 15/18.

qr.q: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for 8 muffins. At the same rate, how many cups are needed for 20 muffins?

y.A: 7 is half a cup short — the 7 1/2 rounded down to a whole cup. 20 muffins is 2 1/2 lots of 8, and 3 × 2 1/2 = 7 1/2 cups.
y.B: 8 is the number of muffins in the recipe, not a number of cups. 20 muffins is 2 1/2 times as many, so it takes 3 × 2 1/2 = 7 1/2 cups.
y.C: 6 is 3 × 2, enough flour for 16 muffins. Twenty muffins is 2 1/2 lots of 8, so 3 × 2 1/2 = 7 1/2 cups.

qr.q: Four notebooks cost $10. What is the cost per notebook?

y.C: 4 is 10 ÷ 2.5, the number of notebooks rather than the price of one. Divide the money by the notebooks instead: 10 ÷ 4 = $2.50.
y.A: 2.25 would make four notebooks $9.00; $10 ÷ 4 is $2.50.
y.D: 2.0 would make four notebooks $8.00, leaving $2 unaccounted for.

qr.q: 3/5 of a class is 18 students. How many students are in the whole class?
qr.e: 18 is 3 parts, so 1 part is 6; 5 parts = 30.

y.D: 36 is 18 × 2, the eighteen students doubled. Those 18 make up three of the five parts, so one part is 6 and all five parts come to 30.
y.A: 45 would make 3/5 of the class 27 students, not 18.
y.B: 24 would make 3/5 of the class 14.4, which is not a whole number of students.

qr.q: The ratio of red to blue marbles is 2:3. If there are 25 marbles total, how many are red?
qr.e: There are 5 equal parts; 25 ÷ 5 = 5, and 2 parts = 10.

y.A: 8 is 2 × 4. The ratio makes 5 parts, each 25 ÷ 5 = 5 marbles, so red is 2 × 5 = 10.
y.B: 12 is 3 × 4, using the blue number. Red is 2 parts of 5 marbles: 10.
y.C: 15 is the blue share, 3 parts of 5. Red is the other 2 parts: 10.

qr.q: Mia read 2/3 of a 60-page book, then read half of the pages that remained. How many pages are still unread?
qr.e: She read 40 pages, then 10 more of the 20 remaining, leaving 10.

y.A: 20 is 60 ÷ 3, the pages left over after the first two thirds were read. Half of those 20 were then read as well, so 10 are still unread.
y.B: 30 is 60 ÷ 2, half of the whole book. The halving only applies to the 20 pages left after the first two thirds: half of 20 leaves 10 unread.
y.D: 15 is what half of 60, halved again, would leave. She read 2/3 first, which is 40 pages, and half of the 20 remaining is 10.

qr.q: A car travels 180 miles in 3 hours at a constant speed. What is its speed?

y.B: 90 is 180 ÷ 2, the miles shared over two hours rather than the three hours the car took. Divide by 3 instead: 180 ÷ 3 = 60 miles per hour.
y.C: 50 mph over 3 hours covers 150 miles, not 180.
y.D: 45 mph over 3 hours covers 135 miles.

qr.q: A trail is 2/3 paved and 1/4 gravel, with no overlap. What fraction of the trail is paved or gravel?

y.A: 3/7 is what you get by adding the tops and the bottoms straight across: 2 + 1 on top, 3 + 4 underneath. The bottoms have to match before you add — 2/3 is 8/12 and 1/4 is 3/12, so together they make 11/12.
y.C: 7/12 is 4/12 + 3/12, and 2/3 is not 4/12 — the 4 is what you multiply by, not the new top number. Multiply both parts by 4: 2/3 is 8/12, so 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.
y.D: 3/4 is what is left when the 1/4 of gravel is taken off the whole trail. Here the two parts are added instead: 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.

qr.q: A 5 1/2-yard ribbon loses 2 3/4 yards. How much ribbon remains?
qr.e: Rename 5 1/2 as 5 2/4, regroup, and subtract 2 3/4 to get 2 3/4 yards.

y.B: 2 1/4 comes from 5 − 2 = 3 and then taking the whole 3/4 off, with the half yard dropped on the way. Borrow instead: 5 1/2 is 4 and 6/4, and 6/4 − 3/4 = 3/4, so 2 3/4 yards.
y.C: 2 1/2 comes from 5 1/2 − 3, with the 2 3/4 rounded up to 3. Keep the quarters: 5 1/2 is 4 and 6/4, and 6/4 − 3/4 = 3/4, leaving 2 3/4 yards.
y.D: 3 1/4 turns the fraction round, taking 1/2 from 3/4 because the half looked too small to take from. Borrow instead: 5 1/2 is 4 and 6/4, and 6/4 − 3/4 = 3/4, so 2 3/4 yards.

qr.q: How many 1/8-cup servings are in 3/4 cup?
qr.e: 3/4 = 6/8, so there are six 1/8-cup servings.

y.B: 8 is the 8 out of one-eighth, not a count of servings. Written as eighths, 3/4 is 6/8 — six of them.
y.C: 4 is the 4 out of three-quarters. Rename it in eighths: 6/8, so six servings.
y.D: 5 is 8 − 3, the two bottom numbers subtracted. Rename 3/4 as 6/8 and count: six.

qr.q: A paint recipe mixes yellow and blue in a 4:5 ratio. Which batch keeps the same ratio?
qr.e: Multiply both parts of 4:5 by 3 to get the equivalent ratio 12:15.

y.A: 16:25 times each part by itself, 4 × 4 and 5 × 5. An equal ratio needs both parts times the same number: 4 × 3 = 12 and 5 × 3 = 15.
y.C: 10:12 halves down to 5:6, which keeps the gap of one but not the mix. Both parts of 4:5 times 3 gives 12:15.
y.B: 8:12 reduces to 2:3, not 4:5; doubling 4:5 gives 8:10.

qr.q: Museum tickets cost $6 each. A family spends $24 on x tickets. How many tickets does the family buy?
qr.e: The equation is 6x=24. Divide both sides by 6 to get x=4 tickets.

y.A: 6 is the price of one ticket, not how many were bought. Divide instead: 24 ÷ 6 = 4.
y.B: 3 is 6 ÷ 2. The spend divides by the price: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 tickets.
y.D: 18 is 24 − 6, one ticket taken off the money. Each ticket costs 6, so 24 ÷ 6 = 4.

qr.q: A baker needs the fraction of a pie that is closest to one whole pie. Which amount is closest to 1?
qr.e: Compare each gap from 1. The gap for 9/10 is only 1/10, smaller than the other gaps.

y.A: 2/3 is a whole third away from one, the biggest gap of the four. 9/10 is short by only 1/10.
y.B: 3/4 is 1/4 away from a whole pie, and a quarter is bigger than a tenth. 9/10 misses by just 1/10.
y.D: 7/10 is 3/10 away from a whole pie — three times as far as 9/10, which misses by 1/10.

qr.q: Five pens cost $7.50. At the same rate, how much do 8 pens cost?

y.A: 10.5 is $7.50 with $3 put on because there are 3 more pens — but a pen costs $1.50, not $1. Three more pens add 3 × $1.50 = $4.50, so eight pens come to $12.
y.C: 4.5 is what the three extra pens cost, not what all eight cost. A pen is $7.50 ÷ 5 = $1.50, so eight of them come to 8 × $1.50 = $12.
y.D: 10 is 8 × 1.25, and $1.25 is $7.50 shared six ways rather than five. Share it five ways: 7.50 ÷ 5 = $1.50, so eight pens cost $12.

qr.q: 2/5 of the students are boys. If 18 students are girls, how many students are in the class?
qr.e: Girls are 3/5 of the class. If 3/5 = 18, then the whole is 30.

y.C: 36 is 18 × 2, the eighteen girls doubled. The girls make up three of the five parts, so one part is 6 and the whole class comes to 30.
y.A: 45 would make the 18 girls 2/5 of the class, and the girls are the other 3/5.
y.D: 24 would make 3/5 of the class 14.4, not 18.

qr.q: A 48-seat bus has 25% of its seats reserved. How many seats are reserved?
qr.e: Twenty-five percent is one fourth, and 48÷4=12 reserved seats.

y.B: 16 is 48 ÷ 3, a third of the seats instead of a quarter. 25% is one quarter, and 48 ÷ 4 = 12.
y.C: 36 is how many seats are not reserved — the other three quarters of the bus. The question asks for the quarter that is reserved: 48 ÷ 4 = 12.
y.D: 10 is a quarter of 40, with the 48 rounded down first. A quarter of 48 itself is 48 ÷ 4 = 12.

qr.q: A 6/8-mile route is shortened to an equivalent fraction on a map label. Which label matches the route?
qr.e: Divide numerator and denominator by 2: 6/8=3/4 mile.

y.A: 3/8 mile halves the top of the fraction and leaves the bottom as it was. Both parts have to be halved: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so 6/8 is 3/4.
y.B: 6/4 mile halves the bottom of the fraction and leaves the top as it was. Both parts have to be halved: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so 6/8 is 3/4.
y.C: 2/3 is 4/6, which is 2 taken off the top and the bottom instead of both being halved. Halving gives 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so 3/4.

qr.q: A school has 18 violins and 12 cellos. What is the ratio of violins to cellos in simplest form?
qr.e: 18:12 simplifies by dividing both numbers by 6 to 3:2.

y.A: 6:4 is 18:12 with both parts divided by 3, and it will still simplify — 6 and 4 both halve. Dividing by 6 in one go gives 3:2.
y.B: 2:3 is cellos to violins, the right pair the wrong way round. Violins come first here, so 18:12 becomes 3:2.
y.D: 3:4 divides 18 by 6 but 12 by 3. Both parts have to be divided by the same number: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 12 ÷ 6 = 2, so 3:2.

qr.q: A tank is 3/4 full and contains 18 gallons. How many gallons does it hold when full?
qr.e: 18 ÷ 3 × 4 = 24 gallons.

y.B: 21 is 18 + 3. One quarter of the tank is 18 ÷ 3 = 6 gallons, so the full tank is 6 × 4 = 24.
y.C: 22 is 18 + 4. Three quarters is 18 gallons, so a quarter is 6 and the whole tank is 24.
y.D: 27 is 24 + 3, the answer with three more added on. The tank holds 24.

qr.q: Store A sells 6 markers for $9. Store B sells 10 markers for $14. Which store has the lower cost per marker?
qr.e: Store A is $1.50 each; Store B is $1.40 each.

y.A: The two are not the same once you price one marker: 9 ÷ 6 = $1.50 at the first store and 14 ÷ 10 = $1.40 at the second.
y.B: There is enough here — divide each price by the number of markers it buys: 9 ÷ 6 = $1.50 and 14 ÷ 10 = $1.40.
y.D: Store A has the smaller bill, but it also hands over fewer markers. Per marker it is 9 ÷ 6 = $1.50, against 14 ÷ 10 = $1.40 at Store B.

qr.q: A tile pattern has 2, 6, 18, and 54 tiles, tripling each time. How many tiles are in the next design?
qr.e: The rule is multiply by 3, so 54×3=162 tiles.

y.B: 216 is 54 × 4, the last design multiplied by 4 rather than by 3. The pattern triples each time: 54 × 3 = 162.
y.C: 108 is 54 × 2, the last design doubled. Each design is three times the one before, so 54 × 3 = 162.
y.D: 126 is not 54 × 3; tripling 54 gives 162.

qr.q: Three quiz scores are 8, 10, and 15. What is their average?
qr.e: Add the scores to get 33, then divide by 3: 33÷3=11.

y.B: 11 1/2 is halfway between the lowest and highest scores, 8 and 15 — the middle score left out altogether. An average uses all three: 8 + 10 + 15 = 33, and 33 ÷ 3 = 11.
y.C: 11 1/3 comes from dividing 34 by 3, one too many in the total. The three scores come to 8 + 10 + 15 = 33, and 33 ÷ 3 = 11 exactly.
y.D: 10 is the middle score, not the average of all three. Add them first: 8 + 10 + 15 = 33, and 33 ÷ 3 = 11.

qr.q: The ratio of cats to dogs is 7:3. If there are 50 animals total, how many are cats?
qr.e: There are 10 equal parts; 50 ÷ 10 = 5, so cats = 7 × 5 = 35.

y.A: 21 is 7 × 3, the two ratio numbers multiplied together. Those numbers count parts, not animals: 50 animals make 10 parts of 5, and the cats have 7 parts, so 7 × 5 = 35.
y.C: 15 is 50 − 35, the animals left once the cats are counted — the dogs rather than the cats. The cats are 7 of the 10 parts: 7 × 5 = 35.
y.B: 30 is not 7 parts of 5; 50 ÷ 10 = 5, so the cats are 7 × 5 = 35.

qr.q: A recipe uses 4/5 cup of milk and 1/2 cup less water. How much water does it use?

y.A: 1/2 is how much less the water is, not how much water there is. Take it off the milk: 8/10 − 5/10 = 3/10 cup.
y.B: 1/10 comes from writing 4/5 as 4/10, doubling only the bottom — that leaves just a tenth between 4/10 and 5/10. 4/5 is really 8/10, and 8/10 − 5/10 = 3/10 cup.
y.C: 2/5 is half of 4/5, as if the water were half as much. It is half a cup less, not half as much: 8/10 − 5/10 = 3/10 cup.

qr.q: A 2 1/4-liter jug is used to fill 3/4-liter bottles. How many full bottles can it fill?
qr.e: Rename 2 1/4 as 9/4. Then (9/4)÷(3/4)=3 full bottles.

y.A: 3 1/4 counts the last quarter as left over, but nothing is left over — that quarter goes into the third bottle. 2 1/4 is 9/4, and 9/4 ÷ 3/4 = 3 exactly.
y.C: 2 is the whole-number part of 2 1/4, not how many 3/4s fit inside it. Three fit: 3/4 + 3/4 + 3/4 = 2 1/4.
y.D: 9 counts the quarter-liters in the jug, not the bottles. 2 1/4 liters is 9 quarters, and each bottle takes three of them, so the jug fills 9 ÷ 3 = 3 bottles.

qr.q: On a map, 1 inch represents 6 miles. Two towns are 3.5 inches apart. How far apart are they?

y.A: 20 is 21 − 1, one mile short of the full distance. Each inch on the map stands for 6 miles, so 3.5 × 6 = 21 miles.
y.C: 24 is 6 × 4, four inches' worth of map rather than three and a half inches' worth. The towns are 3.5 inches apart, so 3.5 × 6 = 21 miles.
y.D: 18 is 3 × 6, dropping the half inch; 3.5 × 6 = 21.

qr.q: A 7-by-7 photo display uses one tile per space. How many tiles are needed?
qr.e: A photo display has 7 rows of 7 tiles, so 7×7=49.

y.A: 56 is 49 + 7, the display with one more row added. Seven rows of seven is 7 × 7 = 49.
y.C: 28 is 7 × 4, four rows. There are seven: 7 × 7 = 49.
y.D: 14 is 7 + 7, two rows added rather than seven rows multiplied: 7 × 7 = 49.

qr.q: An 81-square-inch mosaic is a square. How long is one side?
qr.e: A square with area 81 has side √81=9.

y.A: 10 would need 10 × 10 = 100 square inches, more than the mosaic has. 9 × 9 = 81, so the side is 9 in.
y.B: 8 gives 8 × 8 = 64 square inches, short of 81. The side that fills 81 is 9, because 9 × 9 = 81.
y.D: 7 gives 7 × 7 = 49 square inches, far short of 81. 9 × 9 = 81, so each side is 9 in.

qr.q: A square game board uses 64 small tiles. How many tiles are in each row?
qr.e: The side length is √64=8 tiles.

y.D: 16 is 8 × 2, two rows of tiles rather than one. A row is the number that multiplies by itself to make 64: 8 × 8 = 64.
y.B: 7 rows of 7 make 49 tiles, not 64.
y.C: 6 rows of 6 make 36 tiles.

qr.q: A square flower bed covers 50 square feet. Between which whole-number side lengths is its side?
qr.e: 7²=49 and 8²=64, so √50 lies between 7 and 8.

y.A: 6 and 7 square to 36 and 49, and 49 is still under 50 — so the side is more than 7, not less.
y.C: 8 and 9 square to 64 and 81, both past 50. The pair that traps 50 is 7 and 8, since 49 is under it and 64 is over it.
y.D: 5 and 6 square to 25 and 36, and 25 is only half of 50 — the side is not half the area. 7 × 7 = 49 sits just under 50, so the side is between 7 and 8.

qr.q: Which patio tile count can be arranged as a perfect square array?
qr.e: 36 makes a 6-by-6 array; the other counts do not make equal rows and columns.

y.A: 32 makes rows like 4 by 8, never the same number each way. 36 does it, because 6 × 6 = 36.
y.B: 40 makes 5 by 8 or 4 by 10, but never equal rows and columns. 6 × 6 = 36 is the square one.
y.C: 30 makes 5 by 6, one row short of a square. The count that works is 36, since 6 × 6 = 36.

qr.q: A square has side length 12 cm. What is its area?
qr.e: Area of a square is side × side: 12×12=144 cm².

y.C: 48 is 12 × 4, the distance all the way round the square, not the space inside it. Area is side times side: 12 × 12 = 144 cm².
y.D: 24 is 12 × 2, two of the sides added together. Area comes from multiplying a side by a side: 12 × 12 = 144 cm².
y.A: 124 is not 12 × 12, which comes to 144.

qr.q: A square has area 81 square inches. What is its perimeter?
qr.e: The side is √81=9; perimeter =4×9=36 in.

y.B: 27 is 81 ÷ 3. The side is the number that multiplies by ITSELF to make 81, which is 9.
y.C: 32 is 4 × 8, so the side was taken as 8 — but 8 × 8 is 64, not 81.
y.D: 18 is two sides. A square has four.

qr.q: Corner tiles in a growing display number 1, 4, 9, 16, ... . What is the next count?
qr.e: The counts are square arrays 1²,2²,3²,4²; next is 5²=25.

y.A: 24 is 25 − 1, one short. The counts are square arrays, and after 4 × 4 = 16 comes 5 × 5 = 25.
y.B: 20 is 4 + 16, two of the earlier counts added. Each count is a square number: next is 5 × 5 = 25.
y.C: 36 is 6 × 6, one square too far. The one straight after 16 is 5 × 5 = 25.

qr.q: Choosing one odd bead and one even bead gives a total that is always:
qr.e: Odd + even is always odd.

y.A: Even totals come from two odd beads or two even ones. One of each always leaves a single bead over, so the total is odd: 3 + 4 = 7.
y.B: Primes do turn up, as 3 + 4 = 7, but 3 + 6 = 9 is not prime. The part that is always true is that odd + even is odd.
y.D: Multiples of 4 are all even, and one odd bead with one even bead always leaves a single bead over — 3 + 4 = 7, 5 + 2 = 7. The total is odd every time.

qr.q: A theater sells 234 tickets. Is that number divisible by 3?
c: No; it does not end in 3
qr.e: A number is divisible by 3 when its digit sum is divisible by 3. 2+3+4=9.

y.A: 3 does not have to be the last digit — 234 ÷ 3 = 78 with nothing left over. The test for 3 is the digit sum: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9.
y.B: Being even is the test for dividing by 2, not by 3. For 3 you add the digits: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9, and 9 divides by 3.
y.C: 2 + 3 + 4 comes to 9, not 8. Nine divides by 3, so 234 does too.

qr.q: 53 supplies are packed in boxes of 6. How many supplies are left over?
qr.e: 6×8=48, leaving 5 supplies.

y.B: 3 is 6 ÷ 2, half of a box rather than what is left after the full boxes. Take the full boxes off the total: 6 × 8 = 48, and 53 − 48 = 5.
y.A: 4 is one short; 6 × 8 = 48, and 53 − 48 = 5.
y.D: 6 cannot be left over when packing in sixes — another full box would fit.

qr.q: 42 flags are placed in equal rows. Which row size works with no flags left over?
qr.e: 42÷6=7, so rows of 6 work exactly.

y.B: 8 leaves 2 flags over: 8 × 5 = 40, and there are 42. Rows of 6 fit exactly, since 6 × 7 = 42.
y.C: 9 leaves 6 over: 9 × 4 = 36, six short of 42. Rows of 6 work, because 6 × 7 = 42.
y.D: 5 leaves 2 over: 5 × 8 = 40, not 42. Six goes in exactly — 6 × 7 = 42.

qr.q: A 100-square mural is arranged in a square. How many squares are on one side?
qr.e: √100=10, so a 10-by-10 mural has 100 squares.

y.D: 20 is 10 × 2, two sides' worth of squares rather than one side. One side is the number that multiplies by itself to make 100: 10 × 10 = 100.
y.A: 9 rows of 9 make 81 squares, not 100.
y.B: 8 rows of 8 make 64 squares.

qr.q: A square seating section holds 121 seats in equal rows. How many seats are in each row?

y.D: 22 is 11 × 2, two rows of seats rather than one. A row is the number that multiplies by itself to make 121: 11 × 11 = 121.
y.A: 144 is 12 × 12, the seats a 12-row section would hold; this one holds 121.
y.B: 111 is not a row length here; 11 × 11 = 121.

qr.q: An 8-by-8 mural and a 2-to-the-6th grid both cover how many cells?
qr.e: 8²=64 and 2⁶=64, so both cover 64 cells.

y.A: 16 is 8 + 8, two rows added. The mural is 8 rows of 8: 8 × 8 = 64.
y.C: 128 is 64 × 2, the grid counted twice. Both cover 64.
y.D: 32 is 64 ÷ 2, half of it. The mural is 8 × 8 = 64, and 2⁶ is six 2s multiplied together, which is 64 as well.

qr.q: A shelf holds 40 books. Which square numbers is that count between?
qr.e: 6²=36 and 7²=49, so 40 lies between them.

y.B: 50 and 64 are both bigger than 40, and 50 is not a square number at all. The squares either side of 40 are 36 and 49.
y.C: 36 is a square number, but 38 is not. The next square after 6 × 6 = 36 is 7 × 7 = 49.
y.D: 34 and 36 both sit below 40, so 40 is not between them. It falls between 6 × 6 = 36 and 7 × 7 = 49.

qr.q: Lanterns are arranged in rows of 5, 9, 17, 33, ... . What is the next row size?
qr.e: Each term is double the previous term minus 1: 33×2−1=65.

y.D: 66 is 33 × 2, the last row doubled. Each row is double the one before with 1 taken off: 33 × 2 − 1 = 65.
y.A: 57 is not 33 × 2 − 1, which comes to 65.
y.C: 49 is 33 + 16, repeating the last difference; the differences double each time, so the next is 32.

qr.q: Bells ring every 6 and 8 minutes. After ringing together now, when do they first ring together again?
qr.e: The least common multiple of 6 and 8 is 24.

y.B: 12 is 6 × 2, when only the six-minute bell rings. The eight-minute bell is not there until 24.
y.C: 48 is 6 × 8, multiplying the two gaps. They do meet at 48, but 24 comes first.
y.D: 18 is 6 × 3, another six-minute ring. The first time both ring is 24.

qr.q: 18 red and 24 blue ribbons are cut into the largest equal bundles with no ribbon left. How many ribbons are in each bundle?
qr.e: The greatest common factor of 18 and 24 is 6.

y.A: 12 is 24 ÷ 2, which does not divide 18. The largest number that divides both is 6.
y.B: 9 is 18 ÷ 2, which does not divide 24. The bundles must split both: 6.
y.D: 3 divides both, but it is not the largest that does. 6 divides 18 and 24 as well.

qr.q: A 42-card code is factored into primes. What is its greatest prime factor?
qr.e: 42=2×3×7, so the greatest prime factor is 7.

y.C: 6 is 42 ÷ 7, what is left of the 42 once the 7 is taken out. It splits again into 2 × 3, so it is not a prime at all: the primes here are 2, 3 and 7, and the greatest is 7.
y.B: 5 does not divide 42 at all; 42 is 2 × 3 × 7.
y.D: 3 is a prime factor of 42 but not the greatest, since 7 is larger.

qr.q: If n is odd, which expression must be even?
qr.e: An odd number plus 3 (an odd number) is even.

y.A: n² is an odd number times itself — 3 × 3 = 9, 5 × 5 = 25 — and that stays odd.
y.C: 2n is even, but adding 1 tips it back to odd: with n = 3 it comes to 7. It takes another odd number added on to make it even.
y.D: 2 added to an odd number keeps it odd — 5 + 2 = 7. It takes an odd number added on, like 3, to tip it to even.

qr.q: Three consecutive locker numbers total 36. What is the middle locker number?
qr.e: The three numbers are 11,12,13; the middle is 12.

y.B: 18 is 36 ÷ 2, the total halved — "the middle" taken as the middle of 36 itself rather than the middle locker. The three lockers share the total out: 36 ÷ 3 = 12, and they are 11, 12 and 13.
y.C: 13 is the largest of the three lockers, not the middle one. They are 11, 12 and 13, so the middle is 12.
y.D: 11 is the smallest of the three lockers. They are 11, 12 and 13, so the one in the middle is 12.

qr.q: A museum expects about 198 visitors in each of 6 groups. About how many visitors is that?

y.A: 600 is 1200 ÷ 2, half of the full total. All six groups count: 198 is close to 200, and 200 × 6 = 1,200.
y.B: 1,800 would need nine groups of about 200, and there are six.
y.D: 900 works out at about 150 a group, and each group is close to 200.

qr.q: A rectangular screen is 4 units by 3 units. The expression 4²+3² equals:

y.B: 7 is 4 + 3, the two side lengths added together. Each one is squared first: 4 × 4 = 16 and 3 × 3 = 9, which come to 25.
y.A: 14 is 2 × (4 + 3), doubling the sides instead of squaring them; 4² + 3² is 16 + 9.
y.C: 49 is (4 + 3)², squaring the sum; the expression squares each side and then adds.

qr.q: A point starts at (2,3). It moves 4 units right and 2 units down. Where does it end?
qr.e: 2+4=6 and 3−2=1, so the point is (6,1).

y.A: (4,1) uses the 4 steps as the new across number instead of adding them to the 2 it started on: 2 + 4 = 6, so (6,1).
y.C: (6,5) is a move of 2 up rather than 2 down. Down makes the second number smaller: 3 − 2 = 1, so (6,1).
y.D: (-2,1) is 4 steps to the left instead of the right. Right makes the first number bigger: 2 + 4 = 6, so (6,1).

qr.q: A display uses factor tags 1, 2, 4, and 8—and no others. What is the display number?
qr.e: Those are exactly the positive factors of 8.

y.A: 16 has 1, 2, 4, 8 among its factors but 16 as well, so the tags would not stop at 8.
y.B: 6 is 2 + 4. Its factors are 1, 2, 3 and 6, which is not the list on the tags.
y.C: 4 has only 1, 2 and 4 as factors — the 8 would have no tag.

qr.q: Which square display count is greater than 70 but less than 90?

y.A: 72 sits between 8 × 8 = 64 and 9 × 9 = 81, so no whole number times itself lands on it. The count that does is 9 × 9 = 81.
y.B: 88 sits between 9 × 9 = 81 and 10 × 10 = 100, so nothing times itself makes 88. Between 70 and 90 the square count is 9 × 9 = 81.
y.C: 75 also sits between 8 × 8 = 64 and 9 × 9 = 81, with no whole number times itself landing on it. The one that works is 9 × 9 = 81.

qr.q: What is the volume of a rectangular prism that is 5 cm long, 4 cm wide, and 3 cm high?
qr.e: Volume = length × width × height = 5×4×3 = 60.

y.A: 20 is 5 × 4, one layer. Volume needs the height as well: 5 × 4 × 3.
y.B: 12 is 4 × 3, one face. Volume uses all three measurements: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.
y.D: 120 is 60 × 2, the volume counted twice. 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 already.

qr.q: A rectangular prism has volume 96 cm³. Its length is 8 cm and width is 4 cm. What is its height?

y.A: 4 is the width, not the height. Divide the volume by the floor: 96 ÷ 32 = 3.
y.B: 6 is 3 × 2, the height doubled. 96 ÷ 32 = 3.
y.C: 2 is 8 ÷ 4, the length over the width. The height is the volume over the floor: 96 ÷ 32 = 3.

qr.q: A cube has edge length 4 inches. What is its volume?

y.B: 16 is 4 × 4, one square face of the cube. A cube has a third direction as well: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cubic inches.
y.D: 32 is 64 ÷ 2, half the volume of the cube. All three edges multiply together: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cubic inches.
y.C: 48 is 4 × 4 × 3, which takes three as the third edge; every edge of a cube is 4.

qr.q: A rectangle is 7 m long and 5 m wide. What is its perimeter?
qr.e: Perimeter = 2(7+5)=24.

y.B: 12 m is 7 + 5 — two sides out of four.
y.C: 49 m is 7 × 7, using the long side twice and the short side not at all.
y.D: 35 m is 7 × 5, the area. Perimeter is the walk around the outside.

qr.q: A triangle has base 10 cm and height 6 cm. What is its area?

y.A: 60 is 10 × 6, the whole rectangle round the triangle. The triangle is half of it: 30.
y.C: 120 is 60 × 2 — the rectangle doubled. Halve it instead: half of 10 × 6 is 30.
y.D: 16 is 10 + 6. Area multiplies the base and the height.

qr.q: Two angles form a straight line. One angle is 125°. What is the other angle?
qr.e: Angles on a straight line total 180°; 180−125=55.

y.A: 65° is what you get if 120 comes off 180 to make 60 and then the last 5 is added on instead of taken off. All of the 125 has to come off: 180 − 125 = 55°.
y.B: 75° is 200 − 125, which happens when 180 is rounded up to 200 to make the take-away easy and the extra 20 is never taken back off. Angles on a straight line make 180°: 180 − 125 = 55°.
y.C: 35° is 125 − 90, the two angles treated as though they made a right angle. On a straight line they make 180°, so the other one is 180 − 125 = 55°.

qr.q: A square window is tested for reflection symmetry. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
qr.e: A square matches across its vertical, horizontal, and two diagonal folds, for 4 lines.

y.A: 2 counts the fold down the middle and the fold across, and stops there. A square also matches along both of its diagonals, making 4 lines.
y.C: 3 is one fold short: the two straight folds and one diagonal. The other diagonal folds neatly too, so a square has 4.
y.D: 1 is the single fold down the middle. A square also folds across and along both diagonals, so there are 4 lines in all.

qr.q: If only the height of a rectangular prism is doubled, its volume becomes:
qr.e: Volume is proportional to height, so doubling height doubles volume.

y.A: The same would mean the box did not change, but it is now twice as tall. Twice the height holds twice as much.
y.B: Half as large is what halving the height would do. The height here is doubled, so the volume doubles too.
y.D: Four times as large is what happens when two of the measurements double. Only the height changed, so the volume simply doubles.

qr.q: A rectangle has vertices (1,1), (5,1), (5,4), and (1,4). What is its area?
qr.e: Width = 4 and height = 3, so area = 12.

y.A: 7 is 14 ÷ 2, half of the distance all the way round the rectangle. The area comes from the width times the height: 4 × 3 = 12.
y.C: 20 is not 4 × 3; the width runs from 1 to 5 and the height from 1 to 4.
y.D: 15 is 5 × 3, using the x-coordinate 5 as the width; the width is 5 − 1 = 4.

qr.q: Five daily readings are 6, 8, 9, 12, and 15. What is the mean reading?
qr.e: The readings total 50; 50÷5=10.

y.A: 12 is 6 × 2, double the first reading — and one of the readings itself, not their mean. The mean adds all five and shares them out: 50 ÷ 5 = 10.
y.B: 9 is 15 − 6, the largest reading take away the smallest. The mean comes from adding all five and sharing: the total is 50, and 50 ÷ 5 = 10.
y.D: 11 would need the five readings to total 55, and they total 50.

qr.q: The ordered locker numbers are 3, 4, 8, 10, and 14. What is the median locker number?
qr.e: With five ordered values, the third value is the median: 8.

y.B: 9 is halfway between 4 and 14, not a value in the list. With five in order the median is the third: 8.
y.C: 4 is the second locker number. The middle of five is the third: 8.
y.D: 10 is the fourth locker number, one past the middle. The third is 8.

qr.q: Recorded temperatures range from a low of 11° to a high of 20°. What is the temperature range?
qr.e: Range is high minus low: 20−11=9°.

y.A: 31° is 20 + 11, the two temperatures added instead of one taken from the other. Range is the gap between them: 20 − 11 = 9°.
y.B: 8° is 19 − 11, one degree lost off the top. The high really is 20, so the range is 20 − 11 = 9°.
y.C: 20° is the highest reading on its own, with the low never taken off it. Range means the distance from lowest to highest: 20 − 11 = 9°.

qr.q: What is the volume of a rectangular prism measuring 9 by 2 by 5?

y.A: 45 is 9 × 5, two of the three measurements multiplied together — the 2 has not been used. Volume uses all three: 9 × 2 × 5 = 90.
y.B: 180 is 90 × 2, twice the volume of the prism. Each measurement is used once only: 9 × 2 × 5 = 90.
y.D: 72 is not 9 × 2 × 5, which comes to 90.

qr.q: A cube has volume 125 cubic units. What is the length of one edge?

y.A: 25 is 5 × 5, two edges multiplied — the area of one face, not the length of an edge. The edge is 5, because 5 × 5 × 5 = 125.
y.C: 10 is 5 × 2, double the length of an edge. Multiplying it back gives 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000, far past 125; the edge that works is 5.

qr.q: A rectangle has area 48 square units and width 6. What is its length?

y.B: 9 is one too many: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48 — that is eight sixes.
y.C: 10 would make the area 60, not 48.
y.D: 7 is one short. Seven sixes is 42, and there are six more to reach 48.

qr.q: A rectangle has perimeter 30 units and length 9 units. What is its width?

y.B: 12 is 30 − 9 − 9, which is BOTH widths together. One width is half of it.
y.C: 5 would make the perimeter 2(9 + 5) = 28.
y.D: 7 would make the perimeter 2(9 + 7) = 32.

qr.q: A triangle has angles 50° and 60°. What is the third angle?
qr.e: Triangle angles total 180°; 180−110=70.

y.A: 60° is one of the angles already given, written down again. Add the two you have and take them off 180: 180 − 110 = 70°.
y.C: 90° is the size of a right angle, but this triangle has none. The three angles make 180°, so the third is 180 − 50 − 60 = 70°.
y.D: 80° is 180 − 100, with 50 and 60 added up as 100. They make 110, so the third angle is 70°.

qr.q: The mean of four numbers is 18. Three of the numbers total 50. What is the fourth number?
qr.e: The total of all four is 72; 72−50=22.

y.A: 24 is 72 ÷ 3, the whole total shared out again instead of the missing number being found. Take the 50 away: 72 − 50 = 22.
y.C: 18 is the mean itself, copied down as the missing number. Four numbers averaging 18 total 4 × 18 = 72, so the fourth is 72 − 50 = 22.
y.D: 20 is 70 − 50, which is what you get if 4 × 18 slips to 70. It is really 72, so the fourth number is 72 − 50 = 22.

qr.q: Seven ordered scores are 2, 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, and 20. What is the median score?
qr.e: The fourth of seven ordered values is the median, so the median is 9.

y.A: 8 is halfway between 7 and 9, and is not one of the scores. With seven in order the median is the fourth: 9.
y.B: 7 is the third score. The middle of seven values is the fourth: 9.
y.D: 12 is the fifth score, one past the middle. The fourth is 9.

qr.q: A color poll records 4 red, 6 blue, 8 green, and 5 yellow votes. The most chosen color received how many votes?
qr.e: Green has the greatest frequency with 8 votes, so the modal response count is 8.

y.A: 10 is 4 + 6, the red votes and the blue votes added together. No single color got 10 — the question wants the biggest count on its own.
y.B: 6 is the blue count, and green has more with 8.
y.C: 7 is none of the four counts, which are 4, 6, 8 and 5.

qr.q: A bag has 3 red, 2 blue, and 5 green marbles. What is the probability of choosing a blue marble?
qr.e: There are 10 marbles total and 2 are blue: 2/10=1/5.

y.B: 1/2 would mean half of the marbles are blue. Only 2 of the 10 are blue, and 2 out of 10 is 1/5.
y.C: 1/4 sets the 2 blue against the 8 that are not blue. A probability counts them against every marble: 2 out of 10, which is 1/5.
y.D: 1/10 is one marble out of the ten, but there are 2 blue ones. Two out of ten is 1/5.

qr.q: Using the same bag, what is the probability of choosing a marble that is NOT red?
qr.e: 7 of the 10 marbles are not red.

y.A: 1/2 is the 5 green marbles out of 10. Not red means blue and green together: 2 + 5 = 7, so 7/10.
y.C: 3/10 is the chance of picking a red one, the opposite of what was asked. The other 7 marbles are not red: 7/10.
y.D: 4/5 is 8 out of 10, the 2 blue marbles taken away instead of the 3 red. Taking the red away leaves 7, so 7/10.

qr.q: If both the length and width of a rectangle are doubled, its area becomes:
qr.e: Doubling both dimensions multiplies area by 2×2=4.

y.A: Twice as large is what one doubled side would do. Both sides doubled here, so the area grows by 2 × 2 = 4.
y.B: Eight times as large is 2 × 2 × 2, a doubling counted three times. A rectangle has only length and width: 2 × 2 = 4.
y.C: Three times as large leaves out the corner. Doubling the length doubles the area and doubling the width doubles it again, so it grows by 2 × 2 = 4.

qr.q: If the length of a rectangular prism is doubled while width and height stay the same, its volume becomes:
qr.e: Volume is proportional to length.

y.A: Four times is what happens when two of the measurements double. Only the length changed, so the volume doubles.
y.B: Half is the result of halving the length rather than doubling it. Twice as long holds twice as much.
y.D: The same would mean nothing changed, but the box is now twice as long. Twice the length means twice the volume.

qr.q: A map point at (3,−2) is reflected across a vertical mirror on the y-axis. What is the reflected point?
qr.e: Reflection across the y-axis changes the sign of x and keeps y, giving (−3,−2).

y.B: (−3,2) has both numbers flipped. A mirror on the y-axis only flips the across number, so the −2 stays as it is: (−3,−2).
y.C: (3,2) flips the up-and-down number instead of the across one. The mirror turns 3 into −3 and leaves −2 alone: (−3,−2).
y.D: (−2,3) swaps the two numbers over, which mirrors the point in the slanted diagonal line rather than in the y-axis. The y-axis mirror keeps them in their order and only changes the sign of the first: (3,−2) becomes (−3,−2).

qr.q: The numbers 4, 5, 5, 6 have mean 5. If 20 is added to the data set, what happens to the mean?
qr.e: Adding a value much larger than the old mean raises the mean.

y.A: It stays 5 only if the number added is 5 itself. 20 is far above the others, so the total grows faster than the count and the mean rises.
y.B: It decreases is what a number below 5 would do. 20 is well above the old mean, so it pulls the mean up, to 40 ÷ 5 = 8.
y.C: Cannot tell would be right if the new number were a mystery, but we know it is 20 — bigger than every value there, so the mean goes up.

qr.q: Which measure is usually affected more by one extremely large outlier?
qr.e: The mean uses every value and is pulled toward an extreme outlier.

y.A: All measures equally sounds fair, but they are worked out in different ways. Only the mean adds every value in, so an outlier moves it most.
y.B: Mode is whichever value turns up most often, and one new number rarely changes that. The mean adds the value itself in, so it shifts most.
