y.A: 0.32 is a tenth of half of 6.4, which is 3.2.
y.B: 32 is ten times too long; half of 6.4 meters is 3.2.

ma.q: What is 25% of 64?

y.C: 39 is 64 − 25, the 25 taken away as a plain number rather than used as a percent. Twenty-five percent means a quarter: 64 ÷ 4 = 16.
y.B: 21 is about a third of 64, and a quarter is 16.
y.D: 12 is under a fifth of 64; 64 ÷ 4 = 16.

ma.q: A square has side length 5 units. What is its area?
ma.e: Area = 5² = 25.

y.B: 20 is 5 × 4, the perimeter — the way round the edge, not the space inside.
y.C: 10 is 5 × 2, two sides. Area is 5 × 5.
y.D: 30 is 25 + 5, the area with a side added on. 5 × 5 = 25 is the answer.

ma.q: What is the volume of a 7 × 5 × 3 rectangular prism?

y.A: 15 is 5 × 3, two of the three sides multiplied — one face of the box, not the space inside it. The 7 still has to come in: 15 × 7 = 105.
y.B: 38 is not 7 × 5 × 3, which comes to 105.
y.C: 142 is not the product; 7 × 5 = 35, and 35 × 3 = 105.

ma.q: What is the mean of 84, 88, and 92?
ma.e: The sum is 264; divide by 3 to get 88.

y.A: 264 is 84 + 88 + 92, the total before it is shared out. Divide by the three numbers: 264 ÷ 3 = 88.
y.C: 86 is the average of just 84 and 88, with the 92 left out. All three numbers count: 84 + 88 + 92 = 264, and 264 ÷ 3 = 88.
y.D: 90 is the average of just 88 and 92, with the 84 left out. All three numbers count: 84 + 88 + 92 = 264, and 264 ÷ 3 = 88.

ma.q: If 4x + 6 = 26, what is x?
ma.e: Subtract 6, then divide by 4: x = 5.

y.B: 22 is 26 − 4, the total with the 4 taken off instead of the 6. The 6 comes off first: 26 − 6 = 20, then 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
y.A: 4 does not check: 4 × 4 + 6 = 22, not 26.

ma.q: Which locker code has digits that add to 6 and is even?
ma.e: 24 is even and 2+4=6.

y.A: 184 is even, but that is only half of what the code needs: its digits add to 1 + 8 + 4 = 13, not 6. Only 24 does both — even, with 2 + 4 = 6.
y.C: 182 is even, but its digits add to 1 + 8 + 2 = 11. The code has to pass both tests, and 24 is even with 2 + 4 = 6.
y.D: 188 is even, but its digits add to 1 + 8 + 8 = 17, well past 6. Only 24 is even and has digits adding to 6.

ma.q: What is 7 + 6 × 9?
ma.e: Multiply first, then add, to get 61.

y.C: 67 is 61 + 6, the total with the 6 counted a second time. The 6 is only multiplied: 6 × 9 = 54, then 54 + 7 = 61.
y.D: 52 is 61 − 9, the total one nine short. There are six nines to add on: 6 × 9 = 54, then 54 + 7 = 61.
y.B: 117 adds first and then multiplies, (7 + 6) × 9; multiplication comes before addition.

ma.q: If 3x + 9 = 33, what is x?
ma.e: Subtract 9, then divide by 3: x = 8.

y.A: 30 is 33 − 3, the total with the 3 taken off instead of the 9. The 9 comes off first: 33 − 9 = 24, then 24 ÷ 3 = 8.

ma.q: Five sixths of a path is paved. One third of the whole path is closed for repairs, and all of the closed stretch lies within the paved part. What fraction of the path is paved and open?

y.B: 2/3 is 4/6, which comes from taking the 1 off the 5 and keeping the sixths. One third is really 2/6, so 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6, which is 1/2.
y.C: 1/3 is the closed part of the path, not the part that is paved and open. Take it off the paved part: 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6, which is 1/2.
y.D: 4/3 takes the tops away from each other, 5 − 1 = 4, and the bottoms too, 6 − 3 = 3. Bottoms never subtract: match them first and 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6, which is 1/2.

ma.q: What is 2.4 × 0.3?
ma.e: 24 × 3 = 72, then place two decimal digits.

y.B: 8 is 2.4 ÷ 0.3, the two numbers divided rather than multiplied. Multiplying gives 24 × 3 = 72, then two decimal places: 0.72.
y.C: 0.072 has three decimal places; 2.4 and 0.3 carry two between them, so 72 becomes 0.72.
y.D: 7.2 has only one decimal place, and the two factors carry two.

ma.q: Forty percent of 70 seedlings sprout. How many seedlings sprout?

y.A: 30 is 70 − 40, the forty taken off the seventy rather than used as a percentage. Forty percent means four tenths: 70 ÷ 10 = 7, then 7 × 4 = 28.
y.C: 7 is one tenth of 70, the first step done and then left there. Forty percent is four of those tenths: 7 × 4 = 28.
y.D: 42 is 70 − 28, the seedlings that did not sprout rather than the ones that did. Forty percent is four tenths: 70 ÷ 10 = 7, and 7 × 4 = 28.

ma.q: A square has side length 8 units. What is its area?
ma.e: Area = 8² = 64.

y.A: 16 is 8 × 2, two sides. Area is 8 × 8.
y.B: 32 is 8 × 4, the perimeter — round the edge, not the space inside.
y.D: 72 is 64 + 8, the area with one more side added on.

ma.q: What is the volume of a 7 × 3 × 4 rectangular prism?

y.A: 25 is 7 × 3 + 4, two of the sides multiplied and the third one added on. Volume multiplies all three: 7 × 3 = 21, then 21 × 4 = 84.
y.B: 122 is how much paper would cover all six faces, not the space inside the box. Volume multiplies the three sides: 7 × 3 = 21, then 21 × 4 = 84.
y.D: 14 is 7 + 3 + 4, the three sides added rather than multiplied. Volume multiplies them: 7 × 3 = 21, then 21 × 4 = 84.

ma.q: How many inches are in 9 feet?
ma.e: 9 × 12 = 108 inches.

y.A: 27 is 9 × 3, as if a foot were 3 inches — 3 is the number of feet in a yard. A foot is 12 inches, so 9 × 12 = 108.
y.B: 90 is 9 × 10, as if a foot were ten inches. A foot is twelve, so 9 × 12 = 108.
y.C: 21 is 9 + 12, the feet and the twelve added rather than multiplied. Each of the 9 feet holds 12 inches: 9 × 12 = 108.

ma.q: What is the mode of 95, 98, 98, 100, 103?
ma.e: 98 occurs most often.

y.B: 95 is the lowest number on the list. The mode is the one that turns up most often, and 98 is there twice.
y.C: 103 is the highest number on the list. The mode is the one that turns up most often, and only 98 appears twice.
y.A: 100 appears once, and 98 appears twice.

ma.q: A bag has 2 red and 5 blue marbles. What is the probability of red?
ma.e: There are 7 marbles and 2 are red: 2/7.

y.B: 1/7 is one marble out of the seven, but 2 of them are red. Two out of seven is 2/7.
y.C: 5/7 is the chance of a blue marble, the other color in the bag. Two of the 7 marbles are red, so 2/7.
y.D: 2/5 sets the 2 red marbles against the 5 blue ones. A chance counts them against every marble in the bag: 2 + 5 = 7, so 2/7.

ma.q: Which number is divisible by 6?
ma.e: 204 is even and its digits sum to 6, so it is divisible by 6.

y.A: 215 is odd, and every multiple of 6 is even. The 6s land on 210 and then 216, stepping straight over 215.
y.C: 211 is odd, so no number of 6s can land on it. They go 204, 210, 216 — and 211 is not among them.
y.D: 206 is even, but a multiple of 6 also has to be in the 3 times table, and its digits add to 8, which is not. 6 × 34 = 204, two short of 206.

ma.q: A price is written as 8+5×10. What is its value?
ma.e: Multiply first, then add, to get 58.

y.A: 48 is 58 − 10, the value with ten taken off it — one ten short of the whole. All five tens count: 5 × 10 = 50, then 50 + 8 = 58.
y.C: 63 is 58 + 5, the value with the 5 counted a second time. The 5 only multiplies the 10: 5 × 10 = 50, then 50 + 8 = 58.
y.B: 130 adds first and then multiplies, (8 + 5) × 10; multiplication comes first.

ma.q: What is the mean of 99, 103, and 107?
ma.e: The sum is 309; divide by 3 to get 103.

y.A: 101 is the average of just 99 and 103, with the 107 left out. All three numbers count: 99 + 103 + 107 = 309, and 309 ÷ 3 = 103.
y.C: 105 is the average of just 103 and 107, with the 99 left out. All three numbers count: 99 + 103 + 107 = 309, and 309 ÷ 3 = 103.
y.D: 309 is 99 + 103 + 107, the total before it is shared out. Divide by the three numbers: 309 ÷ 3 = 103.

ma.q: Which improper fraction is equal to 3 2/5?
ma.e: A mixed number converts as (3 × 5) + 2 = 17 fifths, so 3 2/5 = 17/5.

y.A: 32/5 writes the 3 and the 2 side by side on the top. The 3 wholes are 3 × 5 = 15 fifths, and 15 + 2 = 17, so 17/5.
y.C: 11/5 gets its 11 from 3 × 2 = 6 and then + 5, the right steps done on the wrong two numbers. The whole multiplies the bottom: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 2 = 17, so 17/5.
y.D: 13/5 is 2 3/5, the 3 and the 2 swapped round. The 3 is the whole part here: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 2 = 17, so 17/5.

ma.q: What is 2/3 + 1/4?
ma.e: Rewrite both with denominator 12: 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.

y.A: 5/12 is 2/12 + 3/12, with 2/3 turned into 2/12 by multiplying only the bottom. Both numbers multiply by 4, so 2/3 is 8/12 and 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.
y.C: 7/12 is 4/12 + 3/12, and 2/3 is not 4/12 — the 4 is what you multiply by, not the new top number. Multiply both parts by 4: 2/3 is 8/12, so 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.
y.D: 3/7 adds the tops, 2 + 1 = 3, and the bottoms, 3 + 4 = 7. Bottoms never add: put both fractions in twelfths first, then 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.

ma.q: What is 7/8 − 2/3?
ma.e: Rewrite with denominator 24: 21/24 − 16/24 = 5/24.

y.A: 5/11 takes 7 − 2 = 5 on the top, then adds the bottoms out of habit, 8 + 3 = 11. The bottoms are made to match, not added: 21/24 − 16/24 = 5/24.
y.B: 13/24 is what adding gives: 21/24 + 16/24 = 37/24, which is 1 and 13/24. This one takes away: 21/24 − 16/24 = 5/24.
y.D: 1/6 is 4/24, one twenty-fourth under the difference; 21/24 − 16/24 = 5/24.

ma.q: What is 3/4 × 2/5?
ma.e: Multiply across: (3 × 2)/(4 × 5) = 6/20, which simplifies to 3/10.

y.A: 6/9 multiplies the tops, 3 × 2 = 6, but adds the bottoms, 4 + 5 = 9. The bottoms multiply too: 4 × 5 = 20, and 6/20 is 3/10.
y.B: 1 7/8 is 3/4 ÷ 2/5, the second fraction flipped over — that is how you divide, not how you multiply. Multiplying needs no flip: 6 over 20, which is 3/10.
y.C: 5/9 adds where it should multiply: 3 + 2 = 5 on the top and 4 + 5 = 9 underneath. Multiply straight across instead: 6 over 20, which is 3/10.

ma.q: What is 5/8 ÷ 1/4?
ma.e: Dividing by 1/4 means multiplying by 4: 5/8 × 4 = 20/8 = 2 1/2.

y.B: 2 is the whole-number part of 20/8, the leftover thrown away. Eight goes into 20 twice with 4 over, and those 4 eighths are half of one more: 5/8 ÷ 1/4 = 2 1/2.
y.C: 2/5 is 8/5 × 1/4, the flip landing on the wrong fraction. It is the second fraction, the one you are dividing by, that turns over: 5/8 × 4 = 20/8 = 2 1/2.
y.D: 5/32 is 5/8 × 1/4, the two fractions multiplied instead of divided. Dividing by 1/4 asks how many quarters fit inside 5/8: 5/8 × 4 = 20/8, which is 2 1/2.

ma.e: Change to improper fractions: 5/2 × 8/5 = 40/10 = 4.

y.A: 2 3/10 multiplies the wholes on their own, 2 × 1 = 2, and the fractions on their own, 1/2 × 3/5 = 3/10. Turn both into improper fractions instead: 5/2 × 8/5 = 40/10 = 4.
y.B: 3 1/5 is 2 × 1 3/5, the half of the 2 1/2 left out of the multiplying. Both parts of it have to be used: 5/2 × 8/5 = 40/10 = 4.
y.C: 4 1/10 is 2 1/2 + 1 3/5, the two mixed numbers added instead of multiplied — 1/2 + 3/5 = 11/10, which is 1 1/10 on top of the 3. Multiplying wants improper fractions: 5/2 × 8/5 = 40/10 = 4.

ma.q: What is 0.6 × 0.07?
ma.e: 6 × 7 = 42, and the factors have 1 + 2 = 3 decimal places, so the answer is 0.042.

y.A: 4.2 is 0.6 × 7, with the 0.07 read as a whole 7. Count the places: 0.6 has one and 0.07 has two, so 6 × 7 = 42 becomes 0.042.
y.B: 0.42 is 0.6 × 0.7, one decimal place short, because 0.07 is much smaller than 0.7. There are three places in all, so the answer is 0.042.
y.C: 0.0042 counts four decimal places instead of three. There are three, one in the 0.6 and two in the 0.07, so 6 × 7 = 42 becomes 0.042.

ma.q: What is 4.05 ÷ 0.9?
ma.e: Multiply both numbers by 10: 40.5 ÷ 9 = 4.5. Check: 0.9 × 4.5 = 4.05.

y.B: 45 is 40.5 ÷ 0.9, the point moved in the 4.05 but not in the 0.9. Move it in both: 40.5 ÷ 9 = 4.5.
y.C: 0.45 is 4.05 ÷ 9, the point moved in the 0.9 but not in the 4.05. Move it in both: 40.5 ÷ 9 = 4.5.
y.D: 5.4 has the digits swapped: 0.9 × 4.5 = 4.05, while 0.9 × 5.4 = 4.86.

ma.q: What is 7.3 − 2.85?
ma.e: Line up the points and write 7.3 as 7.30: 7.30 − 2.85 = 4.45.

y.A: 4.5 is 7.3 − 2.8, with the last digit of the 2.85 dropped. Write 7.3 as 7.30 and take all of it: 7.30 − 2.85 = 4.45.
y.B: 5.45 borrows a ten for the tenths but leaves the 7 untouched. Borrowing turns that 7 into a 6, so 7.30 − 2.85 = 4.45.
y.D: 4.55 reads the last column backwards, doing 5 − 0 instead of taking 5 from 0. Borrow for that column instead: 7.30 − 2.85 = 4.45.

ma.q: Which decimal is equal to 3/8?

y.A: 0.125 is 1/8, one eighth where the question asks for three. The 3 on top counts how many eighths there are: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.
y.B: 0.625 is 5/8, the five eighths left over rather than the three you were asked for. Divide the 3 by the 8: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.
y.D: 0.83 puts the 8 before the 3, the bottom number of the fraction written first. The line in 3/8 means divide, and it is the 3 being shared out: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.

ma.q: Written as a percent, 0.045 is equal to which of the following?
ma.e: Move the decimal point two places right: 0.045 = 4.5%.

y.A: 450% is the point moved four places instead of two, which is × 100 done twice. Percent is exactly two places: 0.045 becomes 4.5%.
y.C: 0.45% moves the point one place, not two. Two places from 0.045 gives 4.5%.
y.D: 45% is what 0.45 would be as a percent, and 0.045 is ten times smaller than that. Two places from 0.045 gives 4.5%.

ma.q: What is 12.5% of 96?

y.A: 8 is 96 ÷ 12, the 96 split into twelve parts instead. Twelve and a half percent means an eighth of it: 96 ÷ 8 = 12.
y.B: 16 is 96 ÷ 6; 12.5% is an eighth, so it is 96 ÷ 8.
y.C: 10.5 is not 96 ÷ 8, which comes to 12.

ma.q: A muffin recipe uses 2 3/4 cups of flour for one batch. How many cups of flour are needed for 2 batches?

y.A: 4 3/4 comes from adding the 2 batches on rather than doubling: 2 3/4 + 2 = 4 3/4. Two batches means twice as much: 2 3/4 + 2 3/4 = 5 1/2 cups.
y.B: 5 3/4 turns the 6/4 into 1 3/4 by keeping the 3 you started with. Six quarters is one whole and 2/4, so 4 + 1 1/2 = 5 1/2 cups.
y.C: 3 1/2 is 2 + 1 1/2, the 3/4 doubled but the 2 whole cups left as one batch's worth. Both parts double: 2 3/4 + 2 3/4 = 4 + 1 1/2 = 5 1/2 cups.

ma.q: A pancake recipe calls for 2/3 cup of milk. To make only half of the recipe, how many cups of milk are needed?
ma.e: Half of 2/3 is 1/2 × 2/3 = 2/6, and 2/6 simplifies to 1/3 cup.

y.A: 1/6 halves the 2 on top and doubles the 3 underneath, which halves it twice over. Either one on its own is enough: half of 2/3 is 1/3 cup.
y.B: 1/2 is the half from the question, not half of the milk. Half of the 2/3 cup is 1/3 cup.
y.D: 1 1/3 is 2/3 × 2, the recipe doubled rather than halved. Half of 2/3 is 2/6, which is 1/3 cup.

ma.q: A pitcher holds 3 1/3 cups of juice. If 5/6 cup is poured out, how many cups of juice remain?

y.B: 2 1/3 is 3 1/3 − 1, the 5/6 rounded up to a whole cup. Five sixths is a little less than one: 20/6 − 5/6 = 15/6, which is 2 1/2 cups.
y.C: 3 1/6 is 3 1/3 − 1/6, the sixth left in the cup taken off rather than the 5/6 poured out. Take all five sixths: 20/6 − 5/6 = 15/6, which is 2 1/2 cups.
y.D: 2 5/6 takes 1/2 away rather than 5/6; over sixths, 20/6 − 5/6 = 15/6.

ma.q: A ribbon 4 1/2 feet long is cut into pieces that are each 3/4 foot long. How many pieces are there?

y.A: 3 3/8 comes from multiplying by 3/4 instead of dividing by it: 4 1/2 × 3/4 = 3 3/8. Asking how many 3/4-foot pieces fit is a division: 9/2 ÷ 3/4 = 9/2 × 4/3 = 6.
y.C: 1 1/2 comes from dividing by the 3 alone and leaving its quarters out: 4 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1 1/2. The pieces are 3/4 of a foot, not 3 feet: 9/2 ÷ 3/4 = 9/2 × 4/3 = 6.
y.D: 18 is the number of quarter-feet in the ribbon, since 4 1/2 feet is 18/4 — but each piece takes three of those quarters. One more step finishes it: 18 ÷ 3 = 6 pieces.

ma.q: Apples cost $1.35 per pound. What is the cost of 2.4 pounds of apples?

y.B: $2.70 is 1.35 × 2, the 0.4 of a pound never paid for. That last 0.4 pound costs 1.35 × 0.4 = 0.54, and 2.70 + 0.54 = $3.24.
y.C: $32.40 is the right digits with the point one place too far over. 1.35 and 2.4 have three decimal places between them, so 135 × 24 = 3240 becomes 3.240, which is $3.24.
y.D: $3.42 is the answer with its last two digits swapped round. 1.35 × 2 = 2.70 and 1.35 × 0.4 = 0.54, and 2.70 + 0.54 = 3.24.

ma.q: Ben buys 3 notebooks that cost $2.45 each and pays with a $10 bill. How much change should he receive?

y.D: 7.35 is 3 × 2.45, what the three notebooks cost, not the change. The change is what is left of the $10: 10 − 7.35 = 2.65.
y.A: 2.55 would follow if the notebooks came to $7.45, and 3 × $2.45 is $7.35.
y.B: 3.65 would follow if they came to $6.35; three at $2.45 is $7.35.

ma.q: A coat is on sale for 30% off its regular price. Rosa pays the sale price of $42. What was the regular price of the coat?
ma.e: The sale price is 100% − 30% = 70% of the regular price, so 10% of the regular price is $42 ÷ 7 = $6, and the whole price is 10 × $6 = $60.

y.D: 72 is 42 + 30, the sale price with the 30 added on as dollars rather than counted as a percent. Taking 30 percent off leaves seven tenths of the price, so 42 ÷ 7 = 6 and 6 × 10 = 60.
y.B: 140 divides $42 by 0.3 instead of 0.7; the $42 is the 70% Rosa actually paid.
y.C: 54.60 adds 30% to the $42, but the discount came off a larger price, so it is $42 ÷ 0.7.

ma.q: A store raises the price of a $28 board game by 25%. What is the new price?

y.B: 53 is 28 + 25, the 25 added on as dollars rather than counted as a percent. A quarter of the 28 goes on top: 28 ÷ 4 = 7, then 28 + 7 = 35.
y.A: 21 takes 25% off instead of adding it on.
y.D: 32 adds about 14%; 25% of $28 is $7, which gives $35.

ma.q: A choir has 40 members, and 15 of them play an instrument. What percent of the choir members play an instrument?

y.A: 15% is the 15 who play read straight off as a percent, as if the choir had 100 people in it. Out of 40 it is 15/40 = 0.375, which is 37.5%.
y.C: 62.5% is the share who do not play an instrument — the other 25 of the 40. The 15 who do play are 15 out of 40, and 15/40 = 0.375, or 37.5%.
y.D: 75% is 15 + 60, the 40 pushed up to 100 by adding 60 and that same 60 added to the 15. Scaling to 100 multiplies instead: 40 × 2.5 = 100, so 15 × 2.5 = 37.5, which is 37.5%.

ma.q: A bicycle is marked down from $200 to $150. What is the percent decrease in the price?
ma.e: The drop is $50, and 50/200 = 1/4, so the price decreased by 25%.

y.C: 50 is 200 − 150, the dollars the price fell by, not the percent it fell by. The drop is measured against the starting price: 50 ÷ 200 gives a quarter, or 25 percent.
y.B: 75% is what remains of the price, not how far it fell.
y.D: 33 1/3% compares the $50 drop with the new $150; percent decrease measures against the original $200.

ma.q: Which of these values is the greatest?
ma.e: Written as decimals, 3/5 = 0.6, 5/8 = 0.625 and 58% = 0.58, and 0.625 is more than 0.61, so 5/8 is the greatest value.

y.A: 3/5 works out at 0.6, a hundredth under 0.61 and less than 5/8. Dividing 5 by 8 gives 0.625, the biggest of the four.
y.C: 58% looks like the biggest number here, but a percent counts hundredths: 58% is 0.58, the smallest of the four. 5/8 is 0.625.
y.D: 0.61 beats 0.6 and 0.58, so it wins if 5/8 is left as a fraction. As a decimal, 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625, which is bigger still.

ma.q: A tank holds 12.5 liters of water. If 3/5 of the water is used, how many liters remain?
ma.e: The part left is 2/5 of 12.5, and 12.5 ÷ 5 = 2.5, so 2 × 2.5 = 5 liters.

y.A: 6.25 is 12.5 ÷ 2, half of the tank. Two fifths of it is what remains: 12.5 ÷ 5 = 2.5, then 2 × 2.5 = 5.
y.B: 7.5 is 12.5 − 5, the water that was used. The question asks for what is left in the tank: 12.5 − 7.5 = 5 liters.
y.C: 4.5 is not two fifths of 12.5; a fifth of 12.5 is 2.5, so two fifths is 5.

ma.q: In triangle ABC, angle A measures 34° and angle B is twice as large as angle A. What is the measure of angle C?

y.B: 68 is 34 × 2, the size of angle B, not angle C. All three angles make 180°: 180 − 34 − 68 = 78.
y.A: 82 would need angles A and B to total 98; they are 34 and 68, which total 102.
y.C: 112 is 180 − 68, which leaves angle A out; both known angles come off.

ma.q: Three angles of a quadrilateral measure 100°, 85°, and 65°. What is the measure of the fourth angle?

y.A: 100° is one of the angles you were already given, copied down again. The four angles make 360°, so the missing one is 360 − 100 − 85 − 65 = 110.
y.B: 120° comes from the three angles you have adding to 240, which happens when the carry goes missing in 85 + 65. That pair makes 150, so the three make 250 and 360 − 250 = 110.
y.D: 70° is 250 − 180, the three angles measured against 180° — and 180° is a triangle's total. Four angles make 360°, so 360 − 250 = 110.

ma.q: One acute angle of a right triangle measures 27°. What is the measure of the other acute angle?
ma.e: The two acute angles of a right triangle add to 90°, and 90° − 27° = 63°.

y.B: 73° is 100 − 27, the 27 taken off a hundred rather than off the right angle. The two acute angles share 90°, so 90 − 27 = 63.
y.C: 27° is the angle you were given, handed back. The other acute angle is what is left of the 90°: 90 − 27 = 63.
y.D: 153° is 180 − 27, the 27 taken off all 180° with the right angle forgotten. The right angle uses up 90, leaving 90 − 27 = 63.

ma.q: An isosceles triangle has a vertex angle of 40°, and its two base angles are equal. What is the measure of each base angle?
ma.e: The two base angles share 180° − 40° = 140°, so each one is 140° ÷ 2 = 70°.

y.A: 140 is 70 × 2, the two base angles added together rather than one of them on its own. They share 180 − 40 = 140, so each base angle comes to 140 ÷ 2 = 70.
y.B: 40 is the vertex angle, not a base angle.
y.C: 50 each would make the three angles total 140; the two base angles share 140, so each is 70.

ma.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 34 cm and a width of 6 cm. What is its length?
ma.e: One length plus one width is 34 ÷ 2 = 17 cm, so the length is 17 − 6 = 11 cm.

y.A: 17 is 34 ÷ 2, one length and one width together. Take the width off it: 17 − 6 = 11.
y.B: 28 is 34 − 6, the whole way round minus one width. Halve the perimeter first, then subtract.
y.C: 22 is 11 × 2, two lengths. The question asks for one.

ma.q: A rectangle has an area of 72 square inches and a length of 9 inches. What is its perimeter?
ma.e: The width is 72 ÷ 9 = 8 in, so the perimeter is 2 × (9 + 8) = 34 in.

y.B: 36 is 9 × 4, as if all four sides were 9. The width is 72 ÷ 9 = 8, not 9.
y.C: 81 is 9 × 9, as if it were a square. The width is 72 ÷ 9 = 8.
y.D: 17 is 34 ÷ 2, one length and one width. The perimeter is both pairs: 2 × 17 = 34.

ma.q: A large rectangle measures 8 cm along the bottom and 5 cm along each side. A small rectangle 3 cm by 2 cm is cut away from one corner of it, leaving an L-shaped tile. What is the area of the L-shaped tile?
ma.e: The whole rectangle covers 8 × 5 = 40 sq cm and the corner piece cut away covers 3 × 2 = 6 sq cm, so the L-shaped tile left over covers 40 − 6 = 34 sq cm.

y.D: 40 is 8 × 5, the whole rectangle before the corner was cut away. The piece cut out still comes off: 40 − 6 = 34 sq cm.
y.A: 46 adds the corner piece instead of removing it; 40 − 6 = 34.
y.B: 38 takes away 2 rather than 6, and the piece cut out is 3 × 2.

ma.q: Two rectangles each have an area of 36 square units. One measures 6 by 6 and the other measures 12 by 3. How much greater is the perimeter of the 12-by-3 rectangle than the perimeter of the 6-by-6 rectangle?
ma.e: The perimeters are 2 × (12 + 3) = 30 and 2 × (6 + 6) = 24, and 30 − 24 = 6 units.

y.A: 0 says the two perimeters are the same. The areas are — both 36 — but the perimeters are 30 and 24.
y.B: 3 is 6 − 3, one side from each rectangle. The question compares the whole way round both.
y.D: 9 is 6 + 3, one side of each. Going all the way round gives 30 and 24, a gap of 6.

ma.q: A circular tabletop has a radius of 13 inches. What is its diameter?
ma.e: A diameter is twice the radius, so 2 × 13 = 26 in.

y.B: 13 is the radius you started with — the centre to the edge, half the way across.
y.C: 6.5 is 13 ÷ 2. That halves the radius; a diameter doubles it.
y.D: 52 is 26 × 2, the diameter doubled again. One doubling is enough.

ma.q: Point P is located at (7, 5) on a coordinate grid. The point is moved 4 units left and 2 units down. What are the coordinates of its new position?
ma.e: Moving left subtracts from x and moving down subtracts from y: (7 − 4, 5 − 2) = (3, 3).

y.A: (3, 7) goes 4 left but 2 up instead of 2 down. Down makes the second number smaller: 5 − 2 = 3, so the point lands on (3, 3).
y.B: (11, 3) adds the 4 instead of taking it off, which is 4 units right. Left makes the first number smaller: 7 − 4 = 3, giving (3, 3).
y.D: (11, 7) goes right and up — both moves the opposite way round. Left and down both take away: 7 − 4 = 3 and 5 − 2 = 3.

ma.q: A rectangle on a coordinate grid has vertices at (2, 1), (8, 1), (8, 5), and (2, 5). What is the area of the rectangle, in square units?
ma.e: The rectangle is 8 − 2 = 6 units wide and 5 − 1 = 4 units tall, so the area is 6 × 4 = 24 square units.

y.A: 10 is 2 + 8, two of the across numbers added. The rectangle is 8 − 2 = 6 wide and 5 − 1 = 4 tall, so 6 × 4 = 24.
y.C: 20 is 5 × 4, using a corner number instead of a side. The sides are 6 and 4: 6 × 4 = 24.
y.D: 48 is 24 × 2, the rectangle counted twice. 6 × 4 = 24.

ma.q: The point (2, 5) is reflected across the vertical line x = 6. What are the coordinates of its image?
ma.e: The point is 4 units left of x = 6, so its image is 4 units right of it, at (6 + 4, 5) = (10, 5).

y.A: (8, 5) is 6 + 2, using the point's own 2 as its distance from the mirror line. It is really 6 − 2 = 4 away, so its image is at 6 + 4 = 10.
y.B: (2, 7) mirrors the up-and-down number instead: 5 sits 1 below 6, so it moves to 6 + 1 = 7. A mirror on the vertical line x = 6 moves the across number, so the 5 stays put and the 2 travels to 10.
y.D: (6, 5) stops on the mirror line itself. A reflection carries the point the same distance out the far side: 4 units past 6 is 10, so (10, 5).

ma.q: A rectangular room measures 12 feet by 9 feet. Carpet costs $3 for each square foot. What is the total cost to carpet the room?
ma.e: The floor area is 12 × 9 = 108 square feet, and 108 × $3 = $324.

y.A: 108 is 12 × 9, the floor area in square feet, not the cost of covering it. Each square foot costs $3: 108 × 3 = 324.
y.C: 126 is not 108 × $3, which comes to $324.
y.D: 216 is 108 × 2, and the carpet is $3 a square foot.

ma.q: A figure is made of a rectangle with a triangle sitting on top of it. The rectangle is 10 cm wide and 6 cm tall. The bottom edge of the triangle is the whole top edge of the rectangle, so the triangle's base is 10 cm, and the triangle is 4 cm tall. What is the total area of the figure?
ma.e: The rectangle covers 10 × 6 = 60 sq cm and the triangle covers 1/2 × 10 × 4 = 20 sq cm, so the whole figure covers 60 + 20 = 80 sq cm.

y.A: 100 is 60 + 40, with the triangle counted as a whole 10-by-4 rectangle. A triangle covers half of that: 1/2 × 10 × 4 = 20, so 60 + 20 = 80.
y.B: 64 is 60 + 4, the rectangle plus the triangle's height instead of its area. The triangle's area is 1/2 × 10 × 4 = 20, so the figure is 60 + 20 = 80.
y.C: 70 is 60 + 10, the rectangle plus the triangle's base instead of its area. For the triangle, multiply then halve: 10 × 4 = 40 and 40 ÷ 2 = 20, so 60 + 20 = 80.

ma.q: A square and a rectangle each have a perimeter of 40 cm. The rectangle is 14 cm long. How much greater is the area of the square than the area of the rectangle?
ma.e: The square has side 10 cm and area 100 sq cm; the rectangle is 14 cm by 6 cm with area 84 sq cm, and 100 − 84 = 16 sq cm.

y.A: 26 is 40 − 14, what is left of the perimeter after one 14-cm side — a length, not an area. The square's side is 40 ÷ 4 = 10, so it covers 100 sq cm, and the 14-by-6 rectangle covers 84: 100 − 84 = 16 sq cm.
y.B: 44 is not 100 − 84; the square is 10 by 10 and the rectangle 14 by 6.
y.C: 4 is 14 − 10, the gap between the rectangle's length and the square's side, not between their areas.

ma.q: A rectangular sandbox measures 7 feet by 5 feet. Edging costs $4 for each foot. How much will it cost to put edging all the way around the sandbox?
ma.e: The distance around is 2 × (7 + 5) = 24 feet, and 24 × $4 = $96.

y.B: 24 is 96 ÷ 4, the distance all the way round in feet, not the cost of edging it. Each foot costs $4: 24 × 4 = $96.
y.D: $48 is 96 ÷ 2, half of the full cost — edging for one long side and one short side, not all four. The whole way round is 24 feet, and 24 × $4 = $96.
y.A: 140 is 35 × $4, using the area 7 × 5 instead of the distance around.

ma.q: In a triangle, the second angle measures 20° more than the first angle, and the third angle measures 40°. What is the measure of the largest angle?
ma.e: The first two angles share 180° − 40° = 140°, so the first is (140 − 20) ÷ 2 = 60° and the second is 80°, the largest.

y.A: 60° is 80 − 20, the first angle — the smaller of the pair, not the largest one. The second angle is 20° bigger: 60 + 20 = 80°.
y.B: 100° is 20 + 80, the 20° difference added on to the largest angle instead of to the first one. Adding the 20° to the first angle is what gives the largest: 60 + 20 = 80°.
y.D: 70 is half of 140, which would be right only if the first two angles were equal; one is 20° larger.

ma.q: Two angles together form a straight line. One of the angles is 3 times as large as the other. What is the measure of the smaller angle?
ma.e: The two angles total 180°, which is 4 equal parts here, so the smaller angle is 180° ÷ 4 = 45°.

y.D: 135° is 3 × 45, the larger of the two angles — three times the smaller one. The question asks for the smaller: 180 ÷ 4 = 45°.
y.B: 60 would pair with 120, which is twice it rather than three times.
y.C: 30 would pair with 150, and 150 is five times 30.

ma.q: A circular garden has a radius of 11 feet. A straight path runs across the garden through its center, from one edge to the other. How long is the path?
ma.e: A path through the center is a diameter, which is 2 × 11 = 22 ft.

y.A: 44 is 22 × 2, the path doubled again. Across the middle is 2 × 11 = 22.
y.C: 11 is the radius — the centre to the edge, which is half the path.
y.D: 5.5 is 11 ÷ 2. A path across the middle doubles the radius, it does not halve it.

ma.q: The diameter of a large circle is 24 cm. A small circle has a radius that is one third as long as the radius of the large circle. What is the diameter of the small circle?
ma.e: The large radius is 12 cm, so the small radius is 12 ÷ 3 = 4 cm and its diameter is 2 × 4 = 8 cm.

y.A: 12 cm is 24 ÷ 2, the radius of the large circle — the first step, not the answer. A third of it gives the small radius, 4 cm, and doubling that gives the diameter: 2 × 4 = 8 cm.
y.B: 4 cm is 8 ÷ 2, the radius of the small circle — right, but the question asks for its diameter. Double it: 2 × 4 = 8 cm.
y.D: 6 is not the small diameter; the small radius is 4 cm, so its diameter is 8.

ma.q: On a city map, the library is at point (2, 3) and the school is at point (2, 11). Each unit on the map is one block. How many blocks apart are the library and the school?
ma.e: Both points have x = 2, so count along the vertical line: 11 − 3 = 8 blocks.

y.B: 6 is 2 × 3, the library’s two numbers multiplied. Count along the line instead: 11 − 3 = 8.
y.C: 14 is 3 + 11, the two up-numbers added. Distance subtracts them: 11 − 3 = 8.
y.D: 11 is the school’s up-number on its own. The distance between them is 11 − 3 = 8.

ma.q: A playground is drawn on a grid with corners at (1, 2), (9, 2), (9, 7), and (1, 7). A fence is built all the way around it. Each grid unit represents 10 meters. How many meters of fence are needed?
ma.e: The playground is 8 units by 5 units, so the distance around is 2 × (8 + 5) = 26 units, and 26 × 10 = 260 m.

y.C: 130 m is 260 ÷ 2, half of the way round — one long side and one short side, not all four. All the way round is 2 × (8 + 5) = 26 units, and 26 × 10 = 260 m.
y.D: 26 m is 260 ÷ 10, the way round counted in grid squares rather than in meters. Each square stands for 10 meters: 26 × 10 = 260 m.
y.A: 400 is 40 × 10, using the area of 8 by 5 rather than the distance around it.

ma.q: Triangle ABC has vertices A(2, 1), B(6, 1), and C(2, 4). The whole triangle slides 5 units right and 3 units up. What are the coordinates of point C after the slide?
ma.e: A slide adds to both coordinates: (2 + 5, 4 + 3) = (7, 7).

y.B: (7, 4) slides across but not up — the 4 never got its 3. Up adds to the second number: 4 + 3 = 7, so point C lands on (7, 7).
y.C: (5, 3) is the size of the slide, not where point C ends up. Start at point C and add the slide on: 2 + 5 = 7 and 4 + 3 = 7.
y.D: (2, 7) slides up but not across, leaving the 2 where it was. Right adds to the first number: 2 + 5 = 7, so (7, 7).

ma.q: Mr. Diaz has 24 meters of fencing to enclose a rectangular pen. Both side lengths must be whole numbers of meters. What is the greatest area he can enclose?
ma.e: The length and width must add to 12, and 6 × 6 = 36 sq m beats every other pair, such as 5 × 7 = 35 sq m.

y.D: 48 sq m is 24 × 2, the fencing doubled — but fencing measures the way round the pen, not the space inside it. The two side lengths add to 12, and the biggest area they make is 6 × 6 = 36 sq m.
y.A: 35 is 5 × 7, the best of the uneven pairs; 6 × 6 = 36 beats it.
y.C: 32 is 4 × 8, another pair adding to 12 but further from square.

ma.q: Kira's four quiz scores are 78, 85, 91, and 86. What is her mean score?

y.B: 340 is 85 × 4, the four scores added together — the total, not the mean. Share it between the four quizzes: 340 ÷ 4 = 85.
y.A: 84 would need the four scores to total 336, and they total 340.
y.D: 86 is one of the four scores, and it would need a total of 344.

ma.q: A bar graph of raffle tickets sold shows Ana 25, Ben 40, Cara 35, and Dan 20. How many tickets did the four students sell in all?
ma.e: 25 + 40 + 35 + 20 = 120 tickets in all.

y.D: 100 is 120 − 20, the tickets with Dan's 20 left out. All four students count: 25 + 40 + 35 + 20 = 120.
y.C: 110 is ten short of the four totals.

ma.q: What is the median of 26, 15, 31, 19, 12, and 22?
ma.e: In order the values are 12, 15, 19, 22, 26, 31, so the median is the mean of the two middle values: (19 + 22) ÷ 2 = 20.5.

y.D: 19 is 31 − 12, the largest value take away the smallest — the spread of the numbers, not the middle of them. In order they run 12, 15, 19, 22, 26, 31, and with six values the median sits between the middle two: (19 + 22) ÷ 2 = 20.5.
y.A: 21 is not the average of the two middle values; (19 + 22) ÷ 2 = 20.5.
y.C: 22 is the fourth value in order; it pairs with 19, and their average is 20.5.

ma.q: A puppy weighs 3 pounds 5 ounces. How many ounces does the puppy weigh? (1 pound = 16 ounces)
ma.e: 3 pounds is 3 × 16 = 48 ounces, and 48 + 5 = 53 ounces.

y.A: 56 is 3 + 53, the weight in ounces with the 3 pounds counted a second time. Those 3 pounds are already in there as 48 ounces: 48 + 5 = 53.
y.D: 48 is 3 × 16, the 3 pounds turned into ounces, without the 5 ounces that come with them. Add them on: 48 + 5 = 53.
y.C: 35 writes the 3 pounds and 5 ounces side by side; 3 pounds is 48 ounces.

ma.q: A spinner has 8 equal sections numbered 1 through 8. What is the probability that one spin lands on a number greater than 5?
ma.e: Three of the eight sections (6, 7, and 8) are greater than 5, so the probability is 3/8.

y.A: 1/4 is 2 out of 8, one section short of the count. Greater than 5 leaves 6, 7 and 8, so three of the eight sections win: 3/8.
y.B: 5/8 is the chance of landing on 5 or less — the other way round. Above 5 there are only 6, 7 and 8, which is 3/8.
y.C: 1/2 is 4 out of 8, which counts the 5 itself. Greater than 5 starts at 6, leaving 6, 7 and 8: 3/8.

ma.q: A table shows books read: Monday 4, Tuesday 7, Wednesday 3, Thursday 8, Friday 6. How many more books were read on Tuesday and Thursday together than on Monday and Wednesday together?
ma.e: Tuesday and Thursday give 7 + 8 = 15 books, Monday and Wednesday give 4 + 3 = 7 books, and 15 − 7 = 8.

y.A: 5 is 8 − 3, Thursday take away Wednesday. Add each pair first: 7 + 8 = 15 and 4 + 3 = 7.
y.B: 7 is 4 + 3, Monday and Wednesday together. That is one pair; the other is 15, so the gap is 8.
y.D: 15 is 7 + 8, Tuesday and Thursday together. The question asks how many more, so take the other pair off: 15 − 7 = 8.

ma.q: The mean of five numbers is 26. Four of the numbers are 18, 22, 29, and 34. What is the fifth number?
ma.e: The five numbers must total 5 × 26 = 130, and 18 + 22 + 29 + 34 = 103, so the fifth number is 130 − 103 = 27.

y.A: 26 is the mean itself rather than the missing number. The five must total 5 × 26 = 130, and the four given come to 103, so the fifth is 130 − 103 = 27.
y.B: 25 is 26 − 1, a step below the mean where it needs to be a step above. The four given come to 103, one short of 4 × 26 = 104, so the fifth makes it up: 27.
y.D: 33 comes from taking off the 100 and then putting the 3 back on. The 3 comes off too: 130 − 100 = 30, and 30 − 3 = 27.

ma.q: A soup recipe calls for 2 quarts of broth. How many cups of broth is that? (1 quart = 4 cups)
ma.e: Each quart is 4 cups, so 2 quarts is 2 × 4 = 8 cups.

y.A: 6 is 2 + 4. Each quart is 4 cups, so the quarts multiply: 2 × 4 = 8.
y.C: 16 is 4 × 4, four quarts’ worth. There are two: 2 × 4 = 8.
y.D: 4 is the cups in one quart. The recipe asks for two: 2 × 4 = 8.

ma.q: A lunch special comes with one of 3 sandwiches, one of 4 sides, and one of 2 drinks. How many different lunch specials are possible?
ma.e: Each of the 3 sandwiches can go with any of the 4 sides and any of the 2 drinks, so there are 3 × 4 × 2 = 24 different lunch specials.

y.D: 12 is 3 × 4, the sandwiches paired with the sides — right, but the drinks are not in it yet. Each of those 12 can go with either drink: 12 × 2 = 24.
y.B: 18 is 3 × 6, which adds the sides and drinks instead of multiplying all three lists.
y.C: 9 is 3 + 4 + 2, adding the three lists; each stage multiplies.

ma.q: A line plot shows the number of pets owned by nine students: 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 5. How many students own more pets than the mode?
ma.e: The mode is 1 because it appears three times, and the students with 2, 2, 3, and 5 pets — 4 students in all — own more than 1.

y.A: 3 is a number of pets in the list, not a number of students. The mode is 1, and four students own more than one.
y.C: 6 is 2 × 3. Count the students above the mode instead: the two with 2, the one with 3 and the one with 5.
y.D: 5 is the largest number of pets anyone owns, not how many students. Four own more than the mode.

ma.q: A movie starts at 1:45 p.m. and lasts 2 hours 40 minutes. At what time does the movie end?
ma.e: 1:45 plus 2 hours is 3:45, and 3:45 plus 40 more minutes is 4:25 p.m.

y.A: 2:25 p.m. is 1:45 with the 40 minutes added and the 2 hours left off. Both parts of the length go on: 1:45 and 2 hours is 3:45, and 40 minutes more makes 4:25 p.m.
y.B: 3:25 counts only 1 hour of the 2 hours 40 minutes. The full two hours carry 1:45 to 3:45, and 40 minutes more makes 4:25 p.m.
y.C: 3:45 p.m. adds the 2 hours and stops there, leaving the 40 minutes unused. They still have to go on: 3:45 plus 40 minutes is 4:25 p.m.

ma.q: A bag holds 5 green counters, 3 yellow counters, and 4 purple counters. What is the probability of drawing a counter that is NOT yellow?
ma.e: There are 5 + 3 + 4 = 12 counters and 9 of them are not yellow, and 9/12 simplifies to 3/4.

y.A: 2/3 is 8 out of 12, the 4 purple counters taken away instead of the 3 yellow ones. Take the yellow out and 9 are left: 9/12 = 3/4.
y.B: 1/4 is 3 out of 12, the chance of drawing a yellow one — the opposite of what was asked. The other 9 counters are not yellow: 9/12 = 3/4.
y.C: 9/4 comes from 9/12 with only the bottom number divided by 3. Both numbers take the same step: 9 ÷ 3 = 3 and 12 ÷ 3 = 4, so 3/4.

ma.q: Jamal's first three test scores are 82, 91, and 87. What score does he need on his fourth test so that his mean for the four tests is exactly 88?
ma.e: Four tests averaging 88 must total 4 × 88 = 352, and 82 + 91 + 87 = 260, so he needs 352 − 260 = 92.

y.A: 90 is 88 + 2, from counting the 87 as 1 above the 88 instead of 1 below. The three are 6 below, 3 above and 1 below, so 4 has to be made up: 88 + 4 = 92.
y.C: 88 is the mean he is aiming for, not the score that gets him there. Four tests averaging 88 must total 4 × 88 = 352, and his three come to 260, so he needs 92.
y.D: 94 is 88 + 6, making up the 6 points the 82 fell short by and stopping there. The 91 is 3 above and the 87 is 1 below, so only 4 need making up: 88 + 4 = 92.

ma.q: A table shows tickets sold over three weeks. Ana sold 12, then 18, then 14. Ben sold 15, then 9, then 22. Who sold more tickets in all, and by how many?
ma.e: Ana sold 12 + 18 + 14 = 44 and Ben sold 15 + 9 + 22 = 46, so Ben sold 46 − 44 = 2 more.

y.A: 6 is 15 − 9, two of Ben’s weeks. Add all three for each: Ana 44 and Ben 46.
y.B: 4 is 18 − 14, two of Ana’s weeks. The totals are Ana 44 and Ben 46, so Ben is ahead.
y.C: 2 is the right gap with the wrong name on it: Ana sold 44 and Ben sold 46.

ma.q: A soccer practice lasts 1 hour 50 minutes and ends at 6:05 p.m. At what time does the practice start?
ma.e: Going back 1 hour from 6:05 gives 5:05, and going back 50 more minutes gives 4:15 p.m.

y.A: 4:55 p.m. borrows 100 minutes rather than 60: 105 − 50 = 55. An hour is 60 minutes, so the minutes are 65 − 50 = 15, and the start is 4:15 p.m.
y.C: 4:35 p.m. reads 1 hour 50 minutes as one and a half hours and takes off 90 minutes: 6:05 back 1 hour 30 is 4:35. Fifty minutes is ten short of an hour, not half of one — back an hour to 5:05, then 50 more to 4:15 p.m.
y.D: 5:15 p.m. takes off the 50 minutes but never the hour. Go back one hour to 5:05, then 50 minutes further back to 4:15 p.m.

ma.q: A jar holds 8 red marbles, 4 blue marbles, and 3 green marbles. One red marble is taken out and not put back. What is the probability that the next marble drawn is red?
ma.e: After one red is removed, 7 of the 14 marbles left are red, and 7/14 = 1/2.

y.A: 8/15 is the chance on the very first draw, before a red marble was taken out. Once it has gone, 7 reds are left among 14 marbles: 7/14 = 1/2.
y.B: 1/3 counts the three colors instead of the marbles, and the colors are not shared out evenly. Once the red has gone, 7 of the 14 left are red: 7/14 = 1/2.
y.D: 7/15 takes the red marble off the top of the fraction but not off the bottom. The jar lost a marble too, so it is 7 out of 14, which is 1/2.

ma.q: In a class of 20 students, the mean number of books read over the summer was 7. How many books did the class read in all?
ma.e: The total equals the mean times the number of students: 7 × 20 = 140 books.

y.A: 27 is 20 + 7, the class and the mean added. A mean is shared out, so it multiplies back: 7 × 20 = 140.
y.B: 70 is 140 ÷ 2, half the books. Every one of the 20 read 7 on average: 7 × 20 = 140.
y.C: 280 is 140 × 2, the total counted twice. 7 × 20 = 140.

ma.q: A cooler holds 3 gallons of lemonade. If 1 gallon = 4 quarts and 1 quart = 4 cups, how many cups of lemonade does the cooler hold?
ma.e: 3 gallons is 3 × 4 = 12 quarts, and 12 quarts is 12 × 4 = 48 cups.

y.B: 24 is 48 ÷ 2, half of the cups the cooler holds. There are two steps, both of them × 4: 3 × 4 = 12 quarts, then 12 × 4 = 48 cups.
y.C: 12 is 3 × 4, the cooler measured in quarts — right, but the question asks for cups. Each quart holds 4 cups: 12 × 4 = 48.
y.A: 64 is 4 × 4 × 4, which uses four gallons; the cooler holds 3.

ma.q: In a pictograph, each car symbol stands for 6 cars washed. The Saturday row shows 4 and a half symbols. How many cars were washed on Saturday?
ma.e: Four full symbols stand for 4 × 6 = 24 cars and the half symbol stands for 3 more, so 24 + 3 = 27 cars.

y.C: 24 is 6 × 4, the four full symbols — right, but the half symbol is still to come. It stands for 3 more cars: 24 + 3 = 27.
y.D: 21 is 27 − 6, one whole symbol short — three full symbols and the half, rather than four and the half. The four full symbols come to 24, and the half adds 3: 24 + 3 = 27.
y.A: 30 is 5 × 6, counting five full symbols; the row shows four and a half.

ma.q: A box holds only blue pens and black pens. The probability of picking a blue pen at random is 1/4, and there are 5 blue pens in the box. How many pens are in the box in all?
ma.e: The blue pens are 1/4 of all the pens, so the 5 blue pens are one of four equal groups, giving 4 × 5 = 20 pens in all.

y.B: 15 is 20 − 5, the black pens. The question asks how many pens there are altogether: 4 × 5 = 20.
y.C: 9 is 4 + 5. The 5 blue pens are one of four equal parts, so the parts multiply: 4 × 5 = 20.
y.D: 25 is 5 × 5, five parts of five. A quarter means four parts: 4 × 5 = 20.

ma.q: A rectangular photo frame measures 30 centimeters on one side and 0.5 meter on the other. What is the distance all the way around the frame, in centimeters?
ma.e: 0.5 meter is 50 centimeters, so the distance around is 30 + 50 + 30 + 50 = 160 centimeters.

y.B: 80 is 160 ÷ 2, half of the way round — one short side and one long side, 30 and 50. All four sides count: 30 + 50 + 30 + 50 = 160.
y.C: 130 is 160 − 30, the way round with one of the 30-centimeter sides missed out — three sides instead of four. A rectangle has two of each: 30 + 50 + 30 + 50 = 160.
y.D: 1,500 is 30 × 50, the area in square centimeters rather than the distance around.

ma.q: A bar graph shows the minutes Ella practiced piano: Monday 30, Tuesday 45, Wednesday 0, Thursday 60, and Friday 45. What was her mean practice time per day for those five days?
ma.e: The total is 30 + 45 + 0 + 60 + 45 = 180 minutes, and 180 ÷ 5 = 36 minutes per day.

y.C: 45 is the practice on Tuesday, and on Friday too — one day's minutes rather than the average of the five. The five days come to 180 minutes, and 180 ÷ 5 = 36.
y.D: 30 is Monday's practice on its own, one day out of the five rather than the average. The five days come to 180 minutes altogether, and 180 ÷ 5 = 36.
y.A: 44 would need the five days to total 220, and they total 180.

ma.q: Of the 60 students in a survey, 1/4 chose soccer and 1/3 chose basketball. The rest chose swimming. How many students chose swimming?
ma.e: 1/4 of 60 is 15 and 1/3 of 60 is 20, so 60 − 15 − 20 = 25 students chose swimming.

y.B: 20 is the basketball group, a third of the sixty. Swimming is what is left over: 60 − 15 − 20 = 25.
y.C: 30 is 60 ÷ 2, half the students. The two named sports take 15 and 20, leaving 25.
y.D: 35 is 15 + 20, the two named groups together. The rest is the answer: 60 − 35 = 25.

ma.q: A train leaves the station at 9:40 a.m. and arrives at 1:15 p.m. the same day. How long is the trip?
ma.e: From 9:40 a.m. to 12:40 p.m. is 3 hours, and from 12:40 p.m. to 1:15 p.m. is 35 more minutes, for 3 hours 35 minutes.

y.A: 3 hours 25 minutes counts the three hours up to 12:40 and then takes the minutes the wrong way round, 40 − 15 = 25. From 12:40 to 1:15 is 35 minutes forwards, so 3 hours 35 minutes.
y.B: 2 hours 35 minutes is an hour short. From 9:40 a.m. to 12:40 p.m. is three whole hours on its own, and then 35 minutes more reaches 1:15.
y.D: 4 hours 35 minutes is an hour too many: 9:40 plus 4 hours would already be 1:40, past the arrival. Three hours reach 12:40, then 35 minutes more.

ma.q: If 7x = 91, what is the value of x?
ma.e: Divide both sides by 7: x = 91 ÷ 7 = 13.

y.C: 14 is 7 × 2, the 7 doubled — and 7 × 14 = 98, not 91. Dividing is what undoes a × 7: 91 ÷ 7 = 13.

ma.q: On a number line, which number is 9 units to the right of −4?
ma.e: Moving 9 units to the right means adding: −4 + 9 = 5.

y.A: 13 is 9 + 4, as if the start were 4 rather than −4. Going right from −4 adds: −4 + 9 = 5.
y.B: −5 is 5 with a minus sign on it — the right size, the wrong direction. Moving right from −4 lands on 5.
y.C: −13 is −4 − 9, the nine counted to the left instead of to the right. Right means adding: −4 + 9 = 5.

ma.q: If 5n − 8 = 47, what is the value of n?
ma.e: Add 8 to both sides to get 5n = 55, then divide by 5 to get n = 11.

y.C: 55 is 8 + 47, the 5n with the 8 put back on — right, but that is five n's, not one. Share it out: 55 ÷ 5 = 11.
y.D: 39 is 47 − 8, the 8 taken off 47 rather than put back on. Undoing a subtraction means adding: 47 + 8 = 55, and 55 ÷ 5 = 11.

ma.q: What is the value of 48 ÷ (4 + 2) × 3?
ma.e: Parentheses first: 4 + 2 = 6. Then work left to right: 48 ÷ 6 = 8 and 8 × 3 = 24.

y.A: 2 is 4 − 2, the bracket subtracted instead of added. Inside first: 4 + 2 = 6, then 48 ÷ 6 = 8 and 8 × 3 = 24.
y.C: 12 is 48 ÷ 4, dividing before the bracket is done. The bracket is 6, so 48 ÷ 6 = 8 and 8 × 3 = 24.
y.D: 8 is 48 ÷ 6, the division done and the × 3 still to come: 8 × 3 = 24.

ma.q: If a = 6 and b = 4, what is the value of 3a − 2b?

y.A: 2 is 6 − 4, a take away b with the 3 and the 2 left out. Each letter is multiplied first: 3 × 6 = 18 and 2 × 4 = 8, so 18 − 8 = 10.
y.B: 26 is 18 + 8, adding where the expression subtracts.
y.C: 14 is 18 − 4, using b rather than 2b, and 2 × 4 = 8.

ma.q: Which of these numbers is both a multiple of 4 and a factor of 48?
ma.e: 12 is a multiple of 4 because 4 × 3 = 12, and it is a factor of 48 because 48 ÷ 12 = 4.

y.A: 20 is a multiple of 4, but 48 does not divide by it evenly, so it is not a factor of 48. Both tests have to pass, and 12 passes: 4 × 3 = 12 and 48 ÷ 12 = 4.
y.B: 32 is a multiple of 4, but it goes into 48 once with 16 left over, so it is not a factor. 12 goes in exactly: 48 ÷ 12 = 4.
y.C: 18 is even, and being even is not the same as being a multiple of 4 — the fours run 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and skip 18. 12 is a multiple of 4 and a factor of 48.

ma.q: If n ÷ 6 + 4 = 11, what is the value of n?
ma.e: Subtract 4 from both sides to get n ÷ 6 = 7, then multiply both sides by 6 to get n = 42.

y.B: 7 is 11 − 4, which is n after the dividing by 6, not n itself. Multiply it back: 7 × 6 = 42.
y.A: 30 is 5 × 6, which would follow if n ÷ 6 came to 5; it comes to 7.
y.D: 90 is 15 × 6, adding the 4 to 11 before multiplying instead of taking it away.

ma.q: What is the value of 5 + 3 × (12 − 8) ÷ 2?
ma.e: Parentheses first: 12 − 8 = 4. Then 3 × 4 = 12 and 12 ÷ 2 = 6, so 5 + 6 = 11.

y.A: 20 is 5 × 4, adding the 5 in before the multiplying is done. Times and divide come first: 3 × 4 ÷ 2 = 6, then 5 + 6 = 11.
y.B: 8 is 5 + 3, adding left to right. The bracket and the × ÷ go first: 12 − 8 = 4, 3 × 4 = 12, 12 ÷ 2 = 6, so 11.
y.D: 16 is 8 × 2, using the 8 from inside the bracket after it has been used. The bracket is 4, and the answer is 5 + 6 = 11.

ma.q: Which equation says “seven less than a number n is 23”?
ma.e: “Seven less than n” means start with n and subtract 7, so the equation is n − 7 = 23.

y.A: n + 7 = 23 adds the seven on instead of taking it off, which would be seven MORE than n. Seven less means the 7 comes off the number: n − 7 = 23.
y.B: 7n = 23 says seven times the number. “Seven less than n” takes 7 away from n rather than multiplying it, so it is n − 7 = 23.
y.C: 7 − n = 23 takes the number away from seven, the other way round. “Seven less than n” starts at n and takes the 7 off it: n − 7 = 23.

ma.q: Which list of numbers is ordered from least to greatest?
ma.e: On a number line −8 is farthest to the left, then −3, then 0, then 2.

y.A: 2, 0, −3, −8 is the right order backwards — that is greatest to least. Least first means starting at the far left of the number line: −8, −3, 0, 2.
y.C: −3, −8, 0, 2 sorts the two negatives by their digits, as if −3 came first because 3 is less than 8. With a minus in front the bigger digit sits further left, so −8 is the least.
y.D: 0, 2, −3, −8 puts the negatives after the positives. Anything with a minus in front is less than 0, so −8 and −3 belong at the start.

ma.q: A number pattern follows the rule “multiply by 3, then subtract 2.” If the first term is 4, what is the third term?
ma.e: The second term is 4 × 3 − 2 = 10, and the third term is 10 × 3 − 2 = 28.

y.A: 30 is 2 + 28, the answer with the 2 added on instead of taken off. The rule multiplies and then subtracts: the second term is 4 × 3 − 2 = 10, and the third is 10 × 3 − 2 = 28.
y.B: 34 is 12 × 3 − 2, which would follow from a second term of 12; the second term is 10.
y.D: 10 is the second term, and the question asks for the third.

ma.q: If 4(n + 3) = 32, what is the value of n?
ma.e: Divide both sides by 4 to get n + 3 = 8, so n = 8 − 3 = 5.

y.B: 7 is 4 + 3, the two numbers on the left added. Undo the 4 first: 32 ÷ 4 = 8, then 8 − 3 = 5.
y.C: 8 is 32 ÷ 4, which is n + 3 rather than n. Take the 3 off: 8 − 3 = 5.
y.D: 20 is 4 × 5, the answer multiplied back by the 4. n itself is 5.

ma.q: A taxi ride costs a flat fee of $3 plus $2 for each mile. Rosa's ride cost $23 in all. How many miles was her ride?
ma.e: Subtract the flat fee: 23 − 3 = 20 dollars for the miles, and 20 ÷ 2 = 10 miles.

y.C: 13 is 3 + 10, the $3 fee and the 10 miles added together — dollars and miles are not the same thing. The fee comes off the total first: 23 − 3 = 20, and 20 ÷ 2 = 10 miles.
y.A: 8 miles would cost 3 + 2 × 8 = $19, not $23.
y.B: 11 miles would cost $25.

ma.q: In a class of 25 students, 60% ride the bus to school. How many students do NOT ride the bus?
ma.e: 60% of 25 is 15 students who ride, so 25 − 15 = 10 students do not.

y.A: 5 is 10 ÷ 2. Sixty percent of 25 is 15 who do ride, so 25 − 15 = 10 who do not.
y.B: 15 is the number who DO ride the bus. The question asks for the rest: 25 − 15 = 10.
y.D: 40 is 10 × 4. The class is 25, and 15 of them ride, so 10 do not.

ma.q: Marcus read 2/5 of a 120-page book on Monday and 1/3 of the book on Tuesday. How many pages does he have left to read?
ma.e: 2/5 of 120 is 48 pages and 1/3 of 120 is 40 pages, so 120 − 48 − 40 = 32 pages are left.

y.C: 40 is 120 ÷ 3, Tuesday's pages — a third of the book, but only one of the two days. Monday's 48 pages count too: 120 − 48 − 40 = 32.
y.D: 88 is 120 − 32, the pages already read — Monday's 48 and Tuesday's 40 together. The question asks for the ones still left: 120 − 88 = 32.
y.A: 28 is not 120 − 48 − 40, which comes to 32.

ma.q: On a park map, a straight path runs from the fountain at (2, 5) to the gate at (12, 5). A bench is placed on the path exactly halfway between the fountain and the gate. What are the coordinates of the bench?
ma.e: The path is 12 − 2 = 10 units long, so the bench sits 5 units past the fountain at x = 2 + 5 = 7, and every point of the path has y = 5.

y.B: (7, 10) adds the two heights together, 5 + 5 = 10, instead of keeping the one height the path runs along. Every point of the path has y = 5, so the bench is (7, 5).
y.C: (14, 10) adds the ends together, 2 + 12 = 14 and 5 + 5 = 10, but never halves them. Halfway means the middle: 14 ÷ 2 = 7, and the height stays 5.
y.D: (6, 5) is 12 ÷ 2, half of the gate's number rather than the middle of the path. The path runs from 2 to 12, so the middle is 5 past the fountain: 2 + 5 = 7.

ma.q: What is the value of 3 × (14 − 6) + 20 ÷ 4?
ma.e: Parentheses first: 14 − 6 = 8. Then 3 × 8 = 24 and 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so 24 + 5 = 29.

y.A: 11 is 14 − 3, the 14 with the 3 taken off it — but the 3 multiplies the bracket, and it is the 6 that comes off the 14. Brackets first: 14 − 6 = 8, then 3 × 8 = 24 and 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so 24 + 5 = 29.
y.B: 26 is 6 + 20, two of the numbers in the sum added straight together — but the 6 belongs inside the brackets and the 20 gets divided by 4. In order: 14 − 6 = 8, 3 × 8 = 24, 20 ÷ 4 = 5, and 24 + 5 = 29.
y.D: 44 is 3 × 8 + 20, which divides nothing; 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so it is 24 + 5.

ma.q: A rectangular rug is 9 feet long and 4 feet wide. A square rug has the same area as the rectangular rug. What is the side length of the square rug?
ma.e: The rectangle's area is 9 × 4 = 36 square feet, and 6 × 6 = 36, so each side of the square rug is 6 feet.

y.B: 36 is 9 × 4, the area of the rectangular rug in square feet — right, but the question asks for the side of the square. The side is the number that makes 36 when multiplied by itself: 6 × 6 = 36.
y.D: 18 is 9 × 2, the 9-foot side doubled — neither the area nor the side of the square. The area is 9 × 4 = 36, and the square's side is 6 because 6 × 6 = 36.
y.A: 9 is the rug's length, not the side of a square with the same area; 6 × 6 = 36.

ma.q: Five plants have heights of 12, 20, 8, 15, and 15 centimeters. Which is greater, the mean height or the median height, and by how much?
ma.e: The mean is (12 + 20 + 8 + 15 + 15) ÷ 5 = 70 ÷ 5 = 14, and the median of 8, 12, 15, 15, 20 is 15, so the median is greater by 1.

y.B: The mean, by 1 has the gap right and the two the wrong way round. The mean comes to 70 ÷ 5 = 14 and the median is 15, so the median is the greater one.
y.C: The median, by 2 names the right one but doubles the gap. The mean comes to 70 ÷ 5 = 14 and the median is 15, so the gap is 15 − 14 = 1.
y.A: They are not equal: the mean is 70 ÷ 5 = 14 and the median of 8, 12, 15, 15, 20 is 15.

ma.q: A club has 187 stickers to share equally among 12 members. If each member gets the same whole number of stickers, how many stickers are left over?
ma.e: 12 × 15 = 180 stickers are handed out, and 187 − 180 = 7 stickers are left over.

y.C: 5 is 12 − 7, the twelve members take away the seven left over. What the question wants is the left-over itself: 12 × 15 = 180, and 187 − 180 = 7.
y.A: 15 is how many stickers each member gets, not what is left over.
y.B: 9 is two more than the remainder; 12 × 15 = 180, and 187 − 180 = 7.

ma.q: One angle of a triangle measures 90°, and the other two angles are equal to each other. What is the measure, in degrees, of each of those two equal angles?
ma.e: The three angles total 180°, so the two equal angles share 180 − 90 = 90°, and 90 ÷ 2 = 45° each.

y.C: 90 is 45 × 2, the two equal angles put together rather than one of them on its own. The three angles come to 180, so the two equal ones share 180 − 90 = 90, and 90 ÷ 2 = 45 degrees each.
y.A: 60 each would make the three angles total 210; the two equal ones share 90.
y.D: 30 each would total 150 rather than 180.

ma.q: A jug holds 3.6 liters of water. The water is poured equally into 4 bottles. How many liters of water are in each bottle?
ma.e: Because 36 ÷ 4 = 9, we get 3.6 ÷ 4 = 0.9 liter in each bottle, and 0.9 × 4 = 3.6 checks it.

y.A: 14.4 is 3.6 × 4, the jug multiplied by the number of bottles instead of shared between them. Pouring equally means dividing: 3.6 ÷ 4 = 0.9 in each bottle.
y.C: 1.2 is 3.6 ÷ 3, sharing between three bottles; there are 4.
y.D: 0.09 is a tenth of the answer; 36 ÷ 4 = 9, so 3.6 ÷ 4 = 0.9.

ma.q: A box is 5 inches long, 4 inches wide, and 3 inches tall, and it is completely filled with 1-inch cubes. If 45 of the cubes are taken out, how many cubes are still in the box?
ma.e: The box holds 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 cubes, and 60 − 45 = 15 cubes are still in it.

y.B: 20 is 5 × 4, one layer of the box. All three layers hold 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.
y.C: 12 is 4 × 3, one face of the box. It holds 5 × 4 × 3 = 60, and 60 − 45 = 15.
y.D: 45 is the number taken out, not the number left behind: 60 − 45 = 15.

ma.q: Each letter of the word PENCIL is written on its own card, making 6 cards. The cards are turned face down and mixed, and one card is picked at random. What is the probability that the card picked shows a vowel?
ma.e: Two of the six letters in PENCIL are vowels, so the probability is 2/6, which simplifies to 1/3.

y.B: 2/3 comes from 2/6 with only the bottom number halved. Both numbers take the same step: 2 ÷ 2 = 1 and 6 ÷ 2 = 3, so 2/6 is 1/3.
y.C: 1/2 is 2 out of 4, the two vowels set against the four consonants. A chance counts them against every card there is: 2 out of 6, which is 1/3.
y.D: 1/6 is one card out of the six, but PENCIL has two vowels, E and I. Two cards out of six is 1/3.

rc.q: What is the passage mainly about?
c: A garden changed an unused lot into a source of food and community connection.
Tall buildings and poor city soil make growing vegetables impossible.
Collecting rainwater in barrels is what makes any city garden succeed.
The garden's greatest value was the vegetables it grew through the summer.
rc.e: The food, shared tools, recipes, and lessons support both practical and social benefits. Strategy: choose the choice that covers the whole passage, not one example.

y.B: Some residents did doubt it at the start, but by midsummer the tomatoes were climbing and the bees were visiting the flowers, so the passage shows the doubt was wrong.
y.C: The barrels under the roof drains are really there, but they are one thing the volunteers set up, and the question asks what the whole passage is about.
y.D: The garden did produce food, but the passage says its larger success was social - people who had barely nodded to one another began trading recipes and sharing tools.

rc.q: Which action is stated in the passage?
rc.e: The second sentence group directly says volunteers built raised beds. Strategy: point to the exact sentence before choosing.

y.A: The work in the passage is done by neighbors and volunteers, and nobody is hired.
y.B: Children are in the passage, but as the ones the Saturday lessons were planned for, not as the people who did the planting.
y.C: The tall buildings are mentioned as what the garden grew beside, and nothing in the passage says they were taken down.

rc.q: What can the reader reasonably infer about the neighbors by midsummer?
c: They had decided to sell the lot.
They knew one another better than before.
They no longer needed a garden.
rc.e: Trading recipes, sharing tools, and planning lessons show closer relationships. Strategy: infer only the conclusion that the listed facts make likely.

y.A: The passage never says what the neighbors ate - and the people in it end up trading recipes, which points the other way.
y.B: Nothing in the passage is about selling the lot - by midsummer the neighbors are sharing tools and planning Saturday lessons for children.
y.D: The passage ends with the lot as a place where neighbors had a reason to work together, which is the opposite of not needing it.

rc.q: As used in the passage, *vacant* most nearly means
rc.e: Litter had collected on a lot that later became a garden, so it was empty/unused. Strategy: replace the word in its sentence with each choice.

y.A: This is the opposite of what the lot was - it had sat collecting litter for years before anyone used it.
y.B: Testing the soil and building the beds came later, once the volunteers got to work; the word describes the lot as it was before any of that.
y.C: The passage calls it a city lot, beside tall buildings - so it is not somewhere far from town.

rc.q: Why does the author mention tomatoes and bees before describing recipes and lessons?
c: To show that the garden's visible growth led into its wider social effects.
To prove that a garden beside tall buildings can feed a whole city block.
To compare the crops of a city garden with those grown on a large farm.
To show that the residents who doubted the garden had been right all along.
rc.e: The paragraph moves from physical success to community success. Strategy: track what each part adds to the author's developing point.

y.B: The garden did produce food, but the passage never says how many people it fed.
y.C: No large farm appears anywhere in the passage, so there is nothing for the garden's crops to be compared with.
y.D: The doubters are in the passage, but the climbing tomatoes and the visiting bees show they turned out to be wrong.

rc.q: The phrase “not simply become greener” emphasizes that the lot
rc.e: The contrast introduces the garden's social value. Strategy: notice contrasts such as “not simply” for an author's deeper point.

y.A: Greener here points to the plants that grew, not to paint - and the phrase goes on past the greenness to something more.
y.B: The passage never says anything about the lot's size, and the tomatoes did grow there.
y.C: The flowers are described as bright, with bees visiting them, so nothing was lost.

rc.q: What is the passage mainly about?
c: Ships used lamps at night because flags were useless in daylight.
Codes were invented mainly to stop fog from interrupting messages.
Satellite communication has replaced the need for agreed-upon codes.
Old and modern communication both depend on shared signal systems.
rc.e: The final sentence connects older codes to modern communication. Strategy: use the conclusion to test the main idea.

y.A: The passage says a flag could carry a message during daylight; lamps were what extended signaling on into the dark.
y.B: Fog is named as a problem, but the passage says the crews learned codes to reduce confusion about what a signal meant.
y.C: The last sentence says satellite communication depends on the same basic rule, so the need for an agreed system did not go away.

rc.q: Which condition could interrupt ship-to-ship communication?
rc.e: Fog is named with rain and distance as an obstacle. Strategy: distinguish a stated obstacle from a stated solution.

y.B: A shared code is the passage's fix for confusion, not one of the things that got in the way.
y.C: Daylight is when a flag could carry a message, so it helped rather than interrupted.
y.D: Careful observation is listed among the things ships relied on, which makes it a help and not an obstacle.

rc.q: Why could a captain act quickly after seeing a known lamp pattern?
c: Lamps could be seen through every storm.
The code gave the pattern an agreed-upon meaning.
Captains never needed to make decisions.
rc.e: Agreement in advance removes the need to guess. Strategy: connect cause (shared code) to result (quick understanding).

y.A: The passage names fog and heavy rain as things that could interrupt communication, so a lamp was not always visible.
y.C: The passage says the captain did not need to guess what the pattern meant, which is not the same as having nothing to decide.
y.D: Both ships had agreed in advance what the pattern meant, so a pattern that changed daily would undo the whole point.

rc.q: In the passage, *interrupt* most nearly means
rc.e: Weather and distance can stop/disturb communication. Strategy: use the surrounding list of obstacles to define the word.

y.A: The sentence lists fog, heavy rain and long distances - troubles for a message, and not anything to celebrate.
y.B: Nothing in the sentence is being copied; the weather and the distance are keeping the message from getting through.
y.C: This is the opposite: the sentence names fog, rain and distance as things that got in the way.

rc.q: The final sentence mainly serves to
c: add one more example of the weather that could interrupt a signal.
explain the steps engineers follow when they build a satellite system.
compare an older practice with a modern one to state a general principle.
argue that ships today would be safer if they went back to flags.
rc.e: It links ships' codes and satellites through the shared-system principle. Strategy: ask how the ending changes or broadens the earlier information.

y.A: The weather that could interrupt a signal comes earlier in the passage; by the last sentence it has moved on to satellites.
y.B: Satellites are mentioned, but the sentence gives no steps for building one - it states a rule about a sender and a receiver.
y.D: The passage never says today's ships should change anything; it says the old way and the new one rest on the same rule.

rc.q: The author's tone is best described as
c: amused and gently teasing about old sea signals.
worried and critical of modern satellite systems.
informative and appreciative of careful planning.
regretful that ships no longer use flags and lamps.
rc.e: The explanation is calm and respects crews' efforts to reduce confusion. Strategy: judge tone from word choice and purpose, not topic alone.

y.A: The flags, bells and lamps are described plainly, and nothing in the passage makes fun of them.
y.B: Satellite communication is called much faster, and the passage raises no worry about it at all.
y.D: The passage notices the change without wishing the old way back; what interests it is the rule that stayed the same.

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: Gravity does more of a lock's work than a pump does.
A lock raises the water, and the boat rises with it.
Heavy gates hold back the water at each end of a lock.
A canal cannot be built across ground that rises.
rc.e: The closing sentences say plainly that the chamber raises the water and lets the floating boat rise with it, and every earlier step - the gates, the valves, the rising level - exists to make that happen. Gravity and the gates are true details inside that explanation, and the idea that hilly canals are impossible is the very thing the passage sets out to answer. Strategy: choose the choice that covers the whole passage, not one step of it.

y.A: The passage does say gravity does the lifting, but that is one step inside the explanation rather than the point the whole passage builds toward.
y.C: Gates are mentioned at both ends, yet the passage is explaining how the boat gets higher, not which part holds water back.
y.D: The passage opens by saying this only sounds impossible, and then spends the rest of its length showing how it is done.

rc.q: According to the passage, where does the water that fills the chamber come from?
c: From the lower stretch behind the boat.
From a pump built beside the gates.
From the higher stretch of the canal.
From the chamber the boat is waiting in.
rc.e: The sentence about the valves names the source exactly: water from the higher stretch of canal, running downhill. The pump choice is contradicted two sentences later, the lower stretch is where the boat started rather than where the water begins, and the chamber is the destination named in that same sentence. Strategy: find the sentence that answers the question word - here, 'where' - and read it whole.

y.A: That is the side the boat came from, but water runs downhill into the chamber, so it has to arrive from the higher side.
y.B: The passage says the opposite - gravity does the lifting, so most locks need no pump to do it.
y.D: The chamber is where the water arrives, not where it starts; the sentence about the valves says the water runs into the chamber from somewhere else.

rc.q: The passage suggests that how heavy a boat is does not matter much inside a lock because
c: the gates are heavy enough to hold the boat steady.
a boat weighs less once it has entered the chamber.
most locks need no pump to do the lifting.
the boat floats, and the water beneath it rises.
rc.e: The passage says a lock solves the problem without lifting the boat at all, and that the boat rises only because it is floating on water that is rising. Since no part of the lock ever takes the boat's weight, how heavy the boat is never becomes the lock's problem. Strategy: join two nearby statements rather than making a leap past them, and check that a true statement actually answers the question asked.

y.A: The gates are described as holding back water, and the passage never gives them any job of supporting the boat.
y.B: Nothing in the passage changes the boat at all - what changes is the level of the water underneath it.
y.C: The passage does say this, but a missing pump is an answer to how the water moves, not to why the boat's weight stops mattering.

rc.q: In the passage, *stretch* most nearly means
c: the act of pulling a rope tight.
an exercise that loosens the arms.
a period of time that feels long.
rc.e: The phrase is 'the higher stretch of canal', and only a part of something long and continuous can be higher than another part, so the word names a section of the waterway. The pulling and exercising senses are the familiar ones, which is exactly why they are offered. Strategy: put each meaning back into the actual sentence and see which one still makes sense.

y.B: This is the everyday meaning of the word, but nothing in the sentence is being pulled - the phrase names the place the water comes from.
y.C: A real meaning of the word, and the wrong one here, since an exercise cannot be higher than another exercise.
y.D: The word can describe time, but this stretch is described as higher than another one, which only makes sense for a piece of the waterway.

rc.q: How does the passage arrange its description of a boat passing through a lock?
c: It compares a lock with an older way of climbing a hill.
It follows the lock's steps in the order they happen.
It lists the parts of a lock from smallest to largest.
It gives reasons why canals are built across hills.
rc.e: Enters, close, then open, as the water rises, when the level matches - each sentence picks up where the last one stopped, so the description is a sequence of steps in time. The parts are indeed named, but their order is the order of the journey, not an order of size. Strategy: watch the time words ('then', 'as', 'when') to name how a passage is arranged.

y.A: Only one method is ever described, and no earlier method is brought in to compare it with.
y.C: The chamber, gates and valves are all named, but they appear in the order they are used rather than by size.
y.D: The passage explains how a boat gets up the hill, and never takes up the question of why the canal is there.

rc.q: The final sentence, "It raises the water, and lets the boat do what a boat already does," is meant to
c: show how simple the lock's trick really is.
suggest that the boat does most of the real work.
credit the canal's builders for a clever idea.
warn that a lock can go wrong without warning.
rc.e: Saying the boat does only what a boat already does is a quiet, pleased way of showing that the clever part was never complicated: raise the water, and floating handles the rest. Reading it as praise for the boat turns the sentence around, since floating costs the boat no effort at all, and reading it as praise for the builders credits people the passage never mentions. Strategy: ask what a closing sentence is admiring, not just what it mentions.

y.B: The only thing the boat does is float, which it would do anyway - the passage gives the lifting to gravity and the water.
y.C: The sentence admires the arrangement itself, and the passage never mentions the people who designed or built a lock.
y.D: The passage describes a lock working smoothly from start to finish and never raises the idea of failure.

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: The gas in dough comes from yeast feeding on sugar.
Trapped gas from living yeast gives a loaf its shape.
Kneading matters more than any other step in baking.
The yeast in a loaf keeps working after it is baked.
rc.e: Every part of the passage follows one chain: living yeast makes gas, the dough traps it, and the holes left behind are the proof. The closing line says the holes are a record of what the yeast was doing, which is the whole point in one sentence. Strategy: choose the choice that covers the whole passage, not one step of it.

y.A: This is true, but the passage does not stop at the gas being made; it follows that gas into the bubbles and into the holes left behind.
y.C: Kneading is one step the passage explains, but nothing in it ranks the steps against one another.
y.D: The passage says the yeast stops working in the oven, so this goes against what you read.

rc.q: According to the passage, what holds the bubbles inside the dough?
rc.e: The passage states directly that stretchy strands of protein form as the dough is kneaded and hold the bubbles in place. Strategy: point to the exact sentence before choosing.

y.B: The carbon dioxide is what the bubbles are made of, not what keeps them from escaping.
y.C: The sugars are the yeast's food, and the passage gives them no job of holding anything.
y.D: Heat makes the trapped gas expand later on; by then the bubbles are already being held.

rc.q: Based on the passage, what would most likely happen to dough that was never kneaded?
c: It would rise faster with nothing to hold it.
The yeast in it would stop making gas.
It would need a cooler oven to finish baking.
It would hold its gas poorly and swell less.
rc.e: The passage ties the strands to kneading and the swelling to the strands, so dough with no kneading would have weaker strands, less help trapping its gas, and less swelling. Strategy: when a passage gives a cause, ask what follows if that cause is removed.

y.A: Holding the gas is what makes the lump swell, so losing that help would not speed the rising up.
y.B: The yeast feeds on the sugars in the dough whether or not anyone kneads it.
y.C: The passage never links kneading to the temperature the loaf is baked at.

rc.q: As used in the passage, *record* most nearly means
c: a lasting sign of past action.
the best result anyone has reached.
a written list kept on paper.
a copy saved in case it is needed.
rc.e: The holes stay in the bread after the yeast has stopped, so they are a lasting sign of what happened earlier. Strategy: put each meaning back into the sentence and keep the one that still makes sense there.

y.B: That is the everyday meaning from races and contests, and nothing here is being compared or beaten.
y.C: Nothing is written down in this passage; the holes themselves are what remain.
y.D: A copy and a record both keep something, but nothing in the passage is copied — the holes are the original thing the yeast left behind.

rc.q: Why does the author describe the protein strands after describing the gas?
c: To show that the strands make the gas.
To show that kneading comes after baking.
To show what holds the gas already made.
To show that the strands stop the swelling.
rc.e: Gas has to exist before anything can hold it, so the passage releases the carbon dioxide first and then brings in the strands as the thing that keeps it inside the dough. Strategy: when two parts of a process are described in order, ask whether the second one depends on the first.

y.A: The yeast is what releases the carbon dioxide; the strands only hold the bubbles that gas forms.
y.B: Kneading comes before the oven in the passage, and heat is the last stage described.
y.D: Holding the bubbles in place is exactly what lets the whole lump swell, not what prevents it.

rc.q: Saying the holes are “not decoration” shows that the author treats them as
c: a pattern the baker chose to add.
part of how the loaf was made.
a flaw a careful baker avoids.
proof the yeast is still alive.
rc.e: By ruling out decoration, the author says the holes are not there to be looked at — they were left behind by the yeast's work, so they belong to the story of how the loaf came to be. The sentence right after ties them back to what the yeast was doing. Strategy: when an author says what something is not, the point is usually whatever is put in its place.

y.A: Calling the holes not decoration rules out the idea that anyone designed them to look a certain way.
y.C: The passage never treats the holes as a mistake; it explains where they came from with interest, not complaint.
y.D: The passage says the yeast stops working in the oven, so the holes cannot show it is still at work.

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea?
c: Owls hunt in darkness, while falcons prefer to hunt in bright daylight.
Special feathers help owls fly quietly, though the feature has a limit.
Velvety feathers are found on the wings of nearly every bird that hunts.
The owl's soft fringes make it the swiftest hunting bird in the air.
rc.e: Feather structure, quiet-flight benefits, and the speed tradeoff are the whole passage. Strategy: include both the central mechanism and the author's qualification.

y.A: The passage never says when either bird hunts - the falcon comes in only as the fast flier the owl's feathers are not built for.
y.C: The velvety surface is described on the owl alone, and the passage says nothing about the wings of other hunting birds.
y.D: This turns the passage around: the very feathers that make the owl quiet are the ones not designed for high speed.

rc.q: What do the fringes on an owl's feathers do?
c: Break moving air into smaller currents.
