y.B: 28 is twice 14 and stops there; 5 fewer makes 23.
y.C: 33 is 28 + 5, adding the 5 instead of taking it away.
y.D: 18 is not 2 × 14 − 5; doubling 14 gives 28, and 28 − 5 = 23.

QR.q: Which is the best estimate of 398 × 21?

y.A: 10,000 rounds 398 up to 500; it is far closer to 400.
y.C: 6,000 would need 398 to be near 300; 400 × 20 is 8,000.

QR.q: In a club, 18 members play chess, 12 play checkers, and 5 play both. How many play at least one of the games?
QR.e: The overlap was counted twice, so 18 + 12 − 5 = 25.

y.A: 20 subtracts the overlap twice, 18 + 12 − 5 − 5; it comes off once.
y.B: 30 is 18 + 12, counting the 5 who play both twice.
y.D: 35 is 18 + 12 + 5, adding the overlap instead of removing it.

QR.q: A tank is 2/5 full. After 18 liters are added, it is 7/10 full. What is the tank's capacity?
QR.e: The increase is 7/10 − 2/5 = 3/10 of capacity; if 3/10 is 18, the whole is 60 liters.

y.A: 36 would make 3/10 of the tank 10.8 liters, not 18.
y.C: 90 would make 3/10 equal 27 liters.
y.D: 45 would make 3/10 equal 13.5 liters.

QR.q: Which example shows that “all multiples of 4 are multiples of 8” is false?
QR.e: 12 is a multiple of 4 but not of 8, so it is a counterexample.

y.A: 16 is a multiple of both 4 and 8, so it agrees with the claim rather than breaking it.
y.C: 8 is a multiple of both as well, so it cannot be the counterexample.
y.D: 24 is a multiple of 4 and of 8, so it fits the claim too.

QR.q: A basket has three 2-pound bags and two 5-pound bags. What is the mean weight of the five bags?
QR.e: Total weight is 3 × 2 + 2 × 5 = 16 pounds; 16 ÷ 5 = 3.2 pounds.

y.A: 3.5 is the mean of 2 and 5, not of the five bags; three weigh 2 pounds and two weigh 5.
y.B: 2.8 would need the bags to total 14 pounds; they total 3 × 2 + 2 × 5 = 16.
y.C: 3.0 would need a total of 15 pounds; it is 16, and 16 ÷ 5 = 3.2.

QR.q: A rectangular box has volume 168 cubic units, length 7, and width 4. What is its height?

y.C: 7 repeats the length; 168 ÷ 28 = 6.

QR.q: A $45 game is discounted by 20%. What is the sale price?
QR.e: The discount is 0.20 × 45 = $9, so the price is $45 − $9 = $36.

y.A: 40 takes off 5 rather than 20% of 45, which is 9.
y.B: 25 is not 45 less a fifth of itself; 20% of 45 is 9, leaving 36.
y.C: 9 is the discount itself, not the price after it.

QR.q: Which expression always has the same value as 6(n + 3)?
QR.e: Distribute 6 to both terms: 6n + 6 × 3 = 6n + 18.

y.A: 18n multiplies the n by 18; only the 3 gets multiplied by 6.
y.B: 9n adds the 6 and the 3 and hangs an n on the result; the two terms stay apart.
y.D: 6n + 3 distributes the 6 to the n but not to the 3, and 6 × 3 = 18.

QR.q: Two angles form a straight line. One angle is 68°. What is the other angle?
QR.e: Angles on a straight line total 180°, and 180 − 68 = 112°.

y.B: 122 subtracts 58 from 180; the angle given is 68.
y.D: 102 falls ten short of 180 − 68.

QR.q: A cyclist travels 7 1/2 miles in 1/2 hour. At the same rate, how far will the cyclist travel in 1 1/5 hours?
QR.e: The rate is 7.5 ÷ 0.5 = 15 miles per hour; 15 × 1.2 = 18 miles.

y.B: 12 is not 15 × 1.2; the rate is 7.5 ÷ 0.5 = 15 miles an hour.
y.C: 16 falls two short of 15 × 1.2.
y.D: 15 is one hour's distance; the ride lasts 1 1/5 hours.

RC.q: What is the passage mainly about?
c: Household glue sold in stores is made from barnacle cement.
Barnacles damage every ship hull they fasten themselves to.
Barnacle cement inspired a new adhesive for wet surfaces.
Doctors now close most wounds without using any stitches.
RC.e: The passage centers on observing how barnacles bond underwater and adapting that principle into a new adhesive; the other choices exaggerate or contradict details.

y.A: The team designed a new material copying what barnacle proteins do; it did not collect barnacle cement, and nothing here is sold in shops.
y.B: Barnacles fasten to ship hulls, which is how engineers came to study them. Damage is never mentioned.
y.D: A future version might help doctors use fewer stitches. That is a possibility ahead, not something happening now.

RC.q: According to the passage, what does barnacle cement do just before its bond forms?
c: It pushes water away with an oily substance.
It is identical to ordinary glue sold in stores.
It changes salt water into fresh water.
It becomes hard only in bright afternoon sunlight.
RC.e: The passage says the cement first releases an oily substance that pushes water away from the surface, and then the proteins form the bond.

y.B: Identical to ordinary glue is the opposite of the point: ordinary glue performs poorly in moving salt water.
y.C: Changing salt water into fresh water is not something the passage says; the cement moves water aside, it does not change it.
y.D: Bright afternoon sunlight appears nowhere in the passage; the bond forms underwater.

RC.q: Why would an adhesive that works on wet surfaces interest doctors?
c: It would make hospital rooms look cleaner and neater.
It might hold moist body tissue together.
It would dry a wound completely before sealing it.
It would prevent injuries from happening at all.
RC.e: The wound example and wet-surface focus support the inference that the adhesive could bond moist tissue.

y.A: How a room looks has nothing to do with an adhesive that works while wet.
y.C: The whole value is bonding without drying the surface first; drying it would remove the advantage.
y.D: An adhesive closes a wound that already exists. Preventing injury is a different job.

RC.q: In the final sentence, “underlying” most nearly means:
RC.e: The underlying principle is the basic idea beneath the visible feature, not something literally underground.

y.A: Nothing in the sentence is about measurement being difficult.
y.C: This is the literal sense. The principle lies beneath the visible feature as the idea behind it, not under the ground.
y.D: The principle has just been described, but the word says where it sits in the explanation, not when it was found.

RC.q: How is the passage mainly organized?
c: It presents a problem, a natural feature, and a possible use.
It lists many kinds of sea animals from smallest to largest.
It argues that nature is always wiser than human technology.
It gives step-by-step directions for making glue at home.
RC.e: The author moves from underwater bonding, to the barnacle feature, to engineered and medical applications.

y.B: Only one animal appears, the barnacle, and nothing is ordered by size.
y.C: The passage adapts one useful feature. It never claims nature beats human technology in general.
y.D: No instructions are given; the tests are described, not taught.

RC.q: Why does Nia almost stay silent?
c: She thinks a helper is not supposed to speak up.
She is afraid the customer will scold her.
She wants the clock to stay broken a while longer.
She does not notice anything unusual in the case.
RC.e: The sentence “after all, she was only the helper” reveals her doubt about speaking beyond her assigned role.

y.B: The customer is not in the room when Nia hesitates, and no scolding is mentioned anywhere.
y.C: She points out the scratch, which is the opposite of wanting the clock left broken.
y.D: She had already noticed the lever brushing the wheel. Noticing is exactly what she does.

RC.q: What clue does Nia point out?
c: A crack across the clock face
A bright scratch on a lever
A loose bell inside the wooden case
A missing screw under the table
RC.e: The passage explicitly identifies a bright scratch where the lever brushed the wheel.

y.A: No crack appears. What Nia sees is a mark on the lever inside the case.
y.C: The clock chimes thirteen times rather than sounding wrong, and no bell is described as loose.
y.D: Nia is allowed to sort screws, but no screw is missing.

RC.q: Which trait most helps Nia solve the problem?
RC.e: Nia notices the lever and scratch, so attentiveness is the trait supported by the text.

y.A: Nothing she does needs strength; she watches and points.
y.C: The last sentence says the opposite — guessing quickly would not keep her the new task.
y.D: She almost stays silent rather than rushing in, and her reward is a task that asks her to describe before touching.

RC.q: Which statement best expresses a theme of the passage?
c: Adults should repair broken objects without any help.
Difficult work should be completed as quickly as possible.
A job is worth doing only when it is exciting and new.
Careful observation can earn trust and responsibility.
RC.e: Nia's observation solves the problem and earns a more demanding learning task; the ending warns against quick guessing.

y.A: Her uncle takes her help and then gives her more responsibility for it.
y.B: Speed is what the ending warns against: guessing quickly would not keep the task.
y.C: Nia had been sorting screws and polishing cases, and the passage treats that patience as what earned her the next step.

RC.q: Why does the author mention that “guessing quickly would not keep” the new task?
c: To explain why the alarm clock on the bench is broken
To show that keeping trust depends on thoughtful work
To suggest that her uncle dislikes being asked questions
To show that Nia plans to leave the repair shop soon
RC.e: The final contrast shows Nia knows she must continue observing and reasoning carefully to keep earning responsibility.

y.A: The alarm clock is broken so that she has something to study; the sentence is about her, not about it.
y.C: Her uncle asks her to describe what each part might do, which invites questions rather than refusing them.
y.D: Nothing suggests she is leaving; she has just been given more to do.

RC.q: What is the passage mainly explaining?
c: Why copying a book by hand always introduced errors
How to repair stains in valuable old books
How marks in old books reveal readers' responses
Why readers today should write notes in every book
RC.e: The passage describes several kinds of marginal evidence and explains their value and limits for historians.

y.A: A reader correcting a copying error is one example among several, not what the passage is about.
y.B: A stain is treated as evidence of frequent use. Repairing it is never discussed.
y.D: The passage explains what old notes tell historians. It gives no advice to readers now.

RC.q: According to the passage, what might a reader write in a margin?
c: The price of every book in the library
Instructions for making paper by hand
A definition of an unfamiliar word
A list of books that were never written
RC.e: Defining unfamiliar words is one of the explicit examples given.

y.A: Prices never appear. The examples are corrections, definitions and arguments with the author.
y.B: Paper-making is not mentioned; copying by hand is.
y.D: Books that were never written could not be read or annotated.

RC.q: As used in the passage, “encounters” most nearly means:
RC.e: Individual encounters with words are readers' experiences of meeting and reacting to the text.

y.A: Arguing with an author is one kind of note, but the word covers all the reactions described, the calm ones included.
y.B: Nothing about these meetings is sudden; the conversation is called slow.
y.C: It means a reader meeting the words, not something unlucky happening.

RC.q: Why does the author say the evidence must be interpreted cautiously?
c: Margin notes were always added by the book's author.
Historians are rarely permitted to handle old books.
All old books contain false information.
A mark's writer and meaning may be uncertain.
RC.e: The passage directly notes that writers may be unknown and marks may have multiple explanations.

y.A: The passage says a note's writer may be unknown, which is the opposite of always knowing it was the author.
y.B: Historians are described as valuing and interpreting these notes, so they clearly reach them.
y.C: The caution is about reading the marks, not about the books being untrue.

RC.q: The phrase “a slow conversation across years” refers to:
c: later readers replying to earlier readers' notes
scribes talking about how to copy a page
historians reading old books aloud to one another
authors meeting their readers in person years later
RC.e: The surrounding sentences describe readers leaving notes and later readers replying, which resembles a delayed conversation.

y.B: The conversation is between readers in the margins, not between the people copying the text.
y.C: Historians interpret the notes later; they are not the ones talking.
y.D: The exchange happens on the page across years, which is why it is called slow.

RC.q: Why can a dark roof become especially hot?
c: It produces electricity during the hot afternoon.
It blocks all of the moving air above the street.
It absorbs much of the sunlight that hits it.
It is always built from dark heat-absorbing pavement.
RC.e: The first two sentences state that dark roofs absorb sunlight and release the energy as heat.

y.A: No electricity appears. The roof absorbs sunlight and later gives that energy off as heat.
y.B: Ventilation is one of the other methods mentioned, but a dark roof is never described as blocking air.
y.D: Pavement is named separately, as something parks could replace.

RC.q: What happened in the trial of coated buildings?
c: Their roofs never required maintenance afterward.
They became warmer than the buildings around them.
Their winter heating needs disappeared completely.
They used less air-conditioning in the hottest hours.
RC.e: The passage explicitly reports reduced air-conditioning use during hot hours.

y.A: Maintenance is listed among the things that affect whether a coating is useful, not something the trial removed.
y.B: Pale coatings reflect more sunlight, so the coated buildings were cooler rather than warmer.
y.C: Winter heating needs are raised as a reason a coating may not suit a place; they do not vanish.

RC.q: Which statement best describes the author's view of cool roofs?
c: They are useless in every climate and on every roof.
They solve the urban heat island problem by themselves.
They can help, but only as part of a local, mixed plan.
They should replace shade trees and neighborhood parks.
RC.e: The author presents a benefit, several limitations, and a combined local approach.

y.A: One trial found coated buildings needed less air-conditioning, so the author grants a real benefit.
y.B: The passage says plainly that cool roofs are not a complete solution.
y.D: Trees and parks are offered alongside coatings, as part of the mix.

RC.q: In the last sentence, “universal” most nearly means:
RC.e: A universal answer would apply everywhere; the passage argues that local conditions matter.

y.A: Cost is never discussed.
y.B: The author is in favor of local measurement, so being based on science is not what is being warned against.
y.D: How long a coating lasts is a maintenance question; the word here is about where it works.

RC.q: How does the author develop the discussion?
c: By presenting a problem, one response, and then its limits
By giving step-by-step instructions for painting a roof
By listing roof colors in order of their popularity
By comparing two cities and declaring one the winner
RC.e: The sequence is heat-island cause, cool-roof evidence, then limits and complementary methods.

y.B: Nothing here tells you how to paint anything.
y.C: Only dark and pale roofs come up, and not in any order of popularity.
y.D: Some cities are mentioned together, but no two are compared and no winner is named.

RC.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
c: Audiences prefer music that contains no rests at all.
Conductors should tap the beat during every performance.
Loud passages are always harder to play than quiet ones.
Musicians must count and practice silence in a piece.
RC.e: The rehearsal problem and solution both show that measured silence requires active, shared counting.

y.A: The passage argues a rest does real work — building expectation, separating ideas, giving a melody room.
y.B: Tapping is a rehearsal method; the audience would hear no tapping.
y.C: The loudest section was not the problem. Three beats of silence were.

RC.q: What caused the players to enter at different times?
c: Some players stopped counting during the rest.
The melody was written too high for the players.
The conductor changed the speed of the music.
The audience began tapping along with the beat.
RC.e: The passage directly states that several players treated the rest as a chance to stop counting.

y.B: The pitch of the melody is never raised as a difficulty.
y.C: The tempo does not change; the players stop counting through a rest.
y.D: The students tap in rehearsal, where there is no audience.

RC.q: Why will the audience not hear the students tapping?
c: The tapping is far too soft for anyone to hear.
The orchestra will remove the silent measure.
The audience will arrive after that section ends.
Tapping is a rehearsal method, not a performance step.
RC.e: The conductor uses tapping to teach internal counting; the final lines say listeners hear its result, not the tapping itself.

y.A: Loudness is not the reason. The tapping simply is not part of the performance.
y.B: The silent measure is the part they practice most carefully; it stays.
y.C: Nothing is said about when the audience arrives.

RC.q: What does “give a melody room to breathe” suggest?
c: A melody is a living creature that must breathe air.
A rest creates space that makes musical ideas clearer.
Musicians should breathe only during silent measures.
The concert hall needs more fresh air for the players.
RC.e: The phrase figuratively describes how a pause separates or highlights musical ideas.

y.A: This reads the phrase literally; it is a figure of speech about space between ideas.
y.C: Wind players breathe throughout. The phrase is about the music, not the players' lungs.
y.D: The air in the hall is not the subject.

RC.q: Which broader lesson is best supported by the passage?
c: An unnoticed part of a process may need careful work.
Large groups learn best when no one is guiding them.
Speed matters far more than accuracy in group work.
Only actions that can be seen contribute to success.
RC.e: The silent, unheard counting work is essential to the successful entrance, supporting the broader lesson.

y.B: The conductor is the one who asks them to tap, and that guidance is what fixes it.
y.C: The fast passages were already fine. What needed work was getting the quiet measure exactly right.
y.D: The counting is unheard and unseen, and it is what makes the entrance work — the passage says the reverse.

MA.e: Add by place value: 3,684 + 2,957 = 6,641.

y.A: 6,741 is 100 more than the sum; the tens column makes 8 + 5 + 1 = 14, which carries one hundred, not two.
y.B: 6,631 is 10 short; the units make 4 + 7 = 11, so a ten carries into the tens column and its digit is 4, not 3.
y.D: 6,531 loses both carries — the ten out of 4 + 7 and the hundred out of 8 + 5 + 1 — which costs 110.

MA.e: Regroup across the zeros; 8,000 − 3,476 = 4,524.

y.B: 5,476 takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column — 6, 7, 4 — instead of regrouping across the three zeros.
y.C: 5,524 has the last three digits right but keeps 8 − 3 in the thousands; the regrouping already spent one thousand, so it is 7 − 3.
y.D: 4,624 is 100 too many; after the regrouping the hundreds column is 9 − 4 = 5, not 10 − 4.

MA.q: What is 47 × 26?

y.A: 1,272 is 50 more than 47 × 26; work the partial products separately, 47 × 20 = 940 and 47 × 6 = 282.
y.C: 1,122 adds 47 × 20 = 940 to 7 × 26 = 182, taking one partial product from splitting 26 and the other from splitting 47.
y.D: 1,302 is 80 more than 47 × 26; the other split checks it — 40 × 26 = 1,040 plus 7 × 26 = 182.

MA.q: What is 1,764 ÷ 21?

y.B: 78 is too small: 21 × 78 = 1,638, which is 126 under 1,764.
y.C: 74 is smaller still: 21 × 74 = 1,554. Multiplying your answer back by 21 catches this.
y.D: 86 overshoots: 21 × 86 = 1,806, which is 42 over 1,764.

MA.q: What is 5/12 + 1/3?

y.A: 7/12 is two twelfths short; 1/3 is 4/12, so 5/12 + 4/12 = 9/12.
y.B: 2/5 adds tops and bottoms separately, 6/15; the denominators have to match before anything is added.
y.C: 1/2 is 6/12, which treats 1/3 as 1/12; it is 4/12.

MA.q: What is 7/8 − 5/12?
MA.e: 7/8 = 21/24 and 5/12 = 10/24; the difference is 11/24.

y.A: 13/24 is two twenty-fourths too big; 7/8 is 21/24 and 5/12 is 10/24, leaving 11/24.
y.B: 2/5 is not a twenty-fourth at all; put both fractions over 24 first, where 7/8 is 21/24 and 5/12 is 10/24.
y.D: 1/3 is 8/24, three twenty-fourths under the difference.

MA.q: What is 4/9 × 3/8?
MA.e: Multiply and simplify: 12/72 = 1/6.

y.B: 1/3 is double the product; 4/9 × 3/8 is 12/72, which simplifies to 1/6.
y.C: 7/17 adds instead of multiplying, 4 + 3 over 9 + 8.
y.D: 3/8 is one of the two fractions left untouched; 4/9 of 3/8 is smaller than either of them.

MA.q: What is 1 1/2 ÷ 3/5?

y.B: 9/10 multiplies instead of dividing, 3/2 × 3/5; dividing by 3/5 means multiplying by 5/3.
y.C: 1 9/10 is 19/10, short of the 5/2 the division gives; turn 1 1/2 into 3/2 first.

MA.e: Align decimal points: 12.680 + 4.907 = 17.587.

y.A: 17.577 falls 0.01 short; lined up as 12.680 + 4.907, the hundredths are 8 + 0 = 8.
y.C: 16.587 keeps 12 + 4 = 16 and misses the carry out of the tenths: 6 + 9 = 15, so one whole carries and the answer starts 17.
y.D: 17.487 falls 0.1 short; the tenths are 6 + 9 = 15, leaving 5 once the whole has carried.

MA.q: What is 3.6 × 1.25?
MA.e: 1.25 × 36 = 45, then place one decimal digit: 4.5.

y.A: 4.05 falls 0.45 short; 1.25 × 36 = 45, and 3.6 carries one decimal place, so 4.5.
y.C: 45 is 1.25 × 36 with the decimal point never put back; 3.6 is a tenth of 36, so the product is a tenth of 45.
y.D: 3.75 is 3 × 1.25, which drops the 0.6; all of 3.6 has to be multiplied.

MA.q: What is 9.24 ÷ 0.7?
MA.e: Multiply both numbers by 10: 92.4 ÷ 7 = 13.2.

y.B: 1.32 is a tenth of the quotient; multiplying both numbers by 10 gives 92.4 ÷ 7 = 13.2.
y.C: 13.02 has a stray zero in the tenths: 7 goes into 92.4 thirteen times with 1.4 left, and 1.4 ÷ 7 = 0.2.
y.D: 132 is ten times too big — 0.7 × 13 is already 9.1, nearly the whole 9.24.

MA.q: What is 35% of 240?
MA.e: 30% of 240 is 72 and 5% is 12; together they equal 84.

y.A: 72 is 30% of 240 and stops there; the remaining 5% is 12 more.
y.C: 96 is 40% of 240, one step too far.
y.D: 80 is a third of 240, and 35% is a little more than a third.

MA.e: Parentheses first: 5 + 1 = 6; then 2 × 6 = 12; 18 − 12 = 6.

y.A: 8 is 18 − 2 × 5, which leaves the + 1 inside the brackets out; 5 + 1 = 6 happens first.
y.B: 10 is 18 − 2 − 6, subtracting the 2 and the bracket separately instead of multiplying them together.
y.C: 4 is 16 − 12: the 2 comes off the 18 first and is then used again in 2 × 6, so it counts twice.

MA.q: What is 3^4?

y.A: 27 is 3 × 3 × 3, only three threes; 3^4 uses four of them.
y.B: 12 is 3 × 4, multiplying the base by the exponent instead of using 3 as a factor four times.
y.D: 64 is 4 × 4 × 4 — the base and the exponent swapped. Here 3 is the factor and 4 is how many times.

MA.q: What is the greatest common factor of 42 and 70?
MA.e: Factors common to both include 1, 2, 7, and 14; the greatest is 14.

y.A: 2 is a common factor but not the greatest; 7 divides both as well, and 2 × 7 = 14.
y.B: 21 divides 42 but not 70, so it is not a common factor at all.
y.C: 28 divides neither 42 nor 70; the factors the two share are 1, 2, 7 and 14.

MA.q: What is the least common multiple of 9 and 12?
MA.e: Multiples first shared are 36, 72, ...; the least is 36.

y.A: 18 is a multiple of 9 but not of 12, which goes 12, 24, 36.
y.B: 108 is 9 × 12, a common multiple but not the least; 36 comes first.
y.C: 24 is a multiple of 12 but not of 9, which goes 9, 18, 27, 36.

MA.q: If y/6 = 11, what is y?
MA.e: Multiply both sides by 6: y = 11 × 6 = 66.

y.A: 77 is 11 × 7, not 11 × 6; the 6 under the y is what has to be undone.
y.B: 17 is 11 + 6, adding the 6 instead of multiplying by it.
y.D: 55 is 11 × 5. Multiplying both sides by 6 gives 66.

MA.q: Solve 5x − 8 = 37.
MA.e: Add 8 to get 5x = 45, then divide by 5: x = 9.

y.A: 11 does not check: 5 × 11 − 8 = 47, not 37.
y.C: 7 does not check either: 5 × 7 − 8 = 27, ten short of 37.
y.D: 5.8 comes from subtracting the 8 instead of adding it, 29 ÷ 5; moving the − 8 across makes 5x = 45.

MA.q: What is 2a^2 + 3 when a = 4?

y.A: 11 is 2 × 4 + 3, multiplying before squaring; the exponent belongs to the a alone.
y.B: 67 squares the 2a together, (2 × 4)² + 3 = 64 + 3; only the a is squared.
y.C: 19 comes from taking 4² as 8 — doubling instead of squaring. 4² is 16, so 2 × 16 + 3 = 35.

MA.q: What is the reflection of (−5, 2) across the x-axis?
MA.e: Reflection across the x-axis keeps x and changes the sign of y.

y.B: (5, −2) flips both signs; reflecting across the x-axis leaves x at −5 and changes only the y.
y.C: (−2, 5) swaps the two coordinates; a reflection across the x-axis keeps x where it is.
y.D: (5, 2) changes the sign of x and leaves y alone, which is a reflection across the y-axis.

MA.q: A rectangle is 13 meters long and 7 meters wide. What is its area?
MA.e: Area = length × width = 13 × 7 = 91 square meters.

y.A: 40 is 2 × (13 + 7), the perimeter; area multiplies the two sides together.
y.C: 182 is 13 × 7 × 2, the area counted twice.
y.D: 78 is 13 × 6; the width is 7 meters, so it is 13 × 7.

MA.q: A triangle has base 15 cm and height 8 cm. What is its area?
MA.e: Area = 1/2 × 15 × 8 = 60 square centimeters.

y.B: 120 is 15 × 8, the whole rectangle around the triangle; a triangle is half of it.
y.C: 23 is 15 + 8, adding the base and height instead of multiplying and halving.
y.D: 46 is 2 × (15 + 8), a perimeter; area needs 1/2 × 15 × 8.

MA.q: The perimeter of a square photo frame is 56 cm. What is the length of one side?
MA.e: A square has four equal sides, so each side is 56 ÷ 4 = 14 cm.

y.A: 28 is 56 ÷ 2, which counts only two sides; a square has four.
y.C: 16 divides the 40 and then appends the leftover 6 (10 + 6); the whole 56 goes into the division, giving 14.
y.D: 52 subtracts 4 instead of dividing by 4.

MA.q: What is the volume of a rectangular prism measuring 9 cm by 5 cm by 4 cm?
MA.e: Volume = 9 × 5 × 4 = 180 cubic centimeters.

y.B: 200 is not 9 × 5 × 4; multiplying the three out gives 180.
y.C: 160 is 8 × 5 × 4, with the 9 taken as 8.
y.D: 90 is half the volume — 9 × 5 = 45 and then 45 × 2 rather than 45 × 4.

MA.q: A triangle has angles of 37° and 68°. What is the third angle?
MA.e: Triangle angles total 180°; 180 − 37 − 68 = 75°.

y.B: 85 is ten over; the two known angles add to 105, not 95.
y.C: 70 subtracts 110 from 180; 37 + 68 is 105, which leaves 75.

MA.q: How many centimeters are in 2.35 meters?
MA.e: One meter is 100 centimeters, so 2.35 × 100 = 235.

y.A: 23.5 multiplies by 10; a meter holds 100 centimeters.
y.B: 2,350 multiplies by 1,000, which turns meters into millimeters.
y.D: 0.0235 divides by 100 instead of multiplying; centimeters are smaller than meters, so the number gets bigger.

MA.q: How much time passes from 9:38 a.m. to 11:05 a.m.?
MA.e: From 9:38 to 10:38 is 1 hour, then to 11:05 is 27 minutes.

y.B: 1 hour 33 minutes subtracts the minutes the wrong way round, 38 − 5; borrowing an hour gives 65 − 38 = 27.
y.C: 1 hour 17 minutes falls ten short; 10:38 to 11:05 is 27 minutes.
y.D: 2 hours 27 minutes counts an extra hour; 9:38 to 11:05 passes 10:38 only once.

MA.q: What is the mean of 14, 19, 21, and 26?
MA.e: The total is 80, and 80 ÷ 4 = 20.

y.A: 19 is one of the four numbers, not their average; they total 80, and 80 ÷ 4 = 20.
y.C: 18 would need a total of 72; 14 + 19 + 21 + 26 is 80.
y.D: 21 is one of the four numbers again, and 21 × 4 = 84, more than the 80 they total.

MA.q: A fair spinner has 10 equal sections numbered 1 through 10. What is the probability of landing on a multiple of 3?
MA.e: The multiples of 3 are 3, 6, and 9, so 3 of 10 outcomes are favorable.

y.A: 1/2 is 5/10, which counts five favorable numbers; the multiples of 3 up to 10 are 3, 6 and 9.
y.B: 1/5 is 2/10, counting only two multiples of 3; there are three.
y.D: 2/5 is 4/10, which counts a fourth multiple of 3; the next one after 9 is 12, past the spinner.

MA.q: What is the range of 23, 31, 18, 27, and 35?
MA.e: Range = greatest − least = 35 − 18 = 17.

y.A: 53 is 35 + 18, adding the greatest and least instead of subtracting.
y.B: 12 is not the spread from 18 to 35; the range is 35 − 18 = 17.
y.D: 13 is 31 − 18, using 31 rather than the greatest value, 35.

VR.e: To devour is to eat something quickly and hungrily, the way a starving dog finishes its dinner in seconds. Eat is the plain word for it.

y.A: Chew is one step of eating—grinding food with the teeth—so it names a part of the act, not the whole hungry rush of devouring.
y.C: Swallow is the other step of eating, getting the food down; it is a piece of devouring, not its meaning.
y.D: Taste is to try a small amount of something, close to the opposite of gulping all of it down.

VR.e: To hoist is to raise something up, often with a rope or a pulley: a crew hoists a sail, a scout hoists the flag.

y.A: Haul means to pull or drag something heavy along, usually across the ground; it moves a load, but not upward.
y.C: Lower is the opposite motion: a flag is hoisted up the pole in the morning and lowered at night.
y.D: Tie comes from the rope: ropes are what you hoist with, but tying fastens something in place; it does not raise it.

VR.e: To conquer is to defeat an enemy and take control of its people or land by force.

y.B: Defend is to protect a place against an attack—the other side of the battle from conquering it.
y.C: Invade means to enter a place by force; an army can invade a country and still fail to conquer it.
y.D: Surrender is to give up, which is what the conquered side does, not the conqueror.

VR.e: Dense means closely packed, with little space between the parts: a dense forest has trees growing thickly together, and dense fog is hard to see through.

y.A: Dark describes how little light there is; a dense forest is often dark, but that is a result of the crowding, not the meaning of the word.
y.B: Deep measures how far down or how far in something goes, not how tightly it is packed.
y.D: Wide measures how far across something stretches, not how crowded it is.

VR.e: A triumph is a great victory or success—the kind that is celebrated.

y.A: Battle is the fight itself, which can end in a triumph or in a defeat.
y.B: Contest is the competition; a triumph is how one ends, not the event.
y.C: Prize is what a winner is handed afterward, not the winning itself.

VR.e: Frigid means extremely cold, as in a frigid January morning; the word is a cousin of refrigerator.

y.B: Damp means slightly wet; winter air can be frigid and perfectly dry.
y.C: Foggy is about mist hanging in the air, a different kind of weather altogether.
y.D: Windy describes moving air; wind can make a day feel colder, but frigid names the cold itself.

VR.e: Tart means sharply sour, like a lemon or an apple picked too early.

y.A: Salty is a different taste, the one that comes from salt, not the sharp bite of a lemon.
y.C: Spicy is the hot burn of pepper, not the sharpness of unripe fruit.
y.D: Sweet is the opposite taste—and the pastry called a tart is sweet, which is the trap in this word.

VR.e: Seldom means not often—hardly ever. Snow seldom falls in the desert.

y.A: Always is the far opposite end of how often something happens.
y.B: Never goes one step too far: something that seldom happens still happens once in a while.
y.C: Often is the opposite of seldom.

VR.e: Valiant means showing great courage, as in a valiant rescue or a valiant effort.

y.B: Noble means of high character or high rank; knights were called noble, so the words travel together, but noble is not about courage.
y.C: Proud is how a person feels about themselves; a valiant act may make someone proud, but pride is not the meaning.
y.D: Violent looks and sounds a little like valiant, and both can describe a fight, but violent means using force to hurt, not brave.

VR.e: A mishap is an unlucky accident, usually a small one—a dropped tray, a bus missed by a minute.

y.B: Mess is what a mishap may leave behind on the floor, not the unlucky event itself.
y.C: Mistake is a wrong action or wrong answer that a person makes; a mishap is a stroke of bad luck that nobody chose.
y.D: Surprise is anything unexpected, good or bad; a mishap is unlucky by definition.

VR.e: To summon is to call someone to come, usually with authority: a judge summons a witness, and the bell summons students to class.

y.B: Dismiss is the opposite—to send people away once they are no longer needed.
y.C: Greet is what happens after someone arrives; summoning is the call that brings them.
y.D: Send moves someone away from you; to summon is to bring someone to you.

VR.e: To thrive is to grow or develop well—to flourish, as a plant thrives in rich soil or a business thrives in a busy town.

y.A: Fail is the opposite of thriving.
y.B: Struggle means to have a hard time; a plant that struggles is the reverse of one that thrives.
y.D: Survive means only to stay alive; a plant can survive a drought without thriving, so the word stops short.

VR.e: Adequate means enough to meet a need—satisfactory, and no more than that.

y.B: Extra means more than what is needed, where adequate means just what is needed.
y.C: Perfect means without a single fault; adequate is lower praise—it means good enough.
y.D: Plenty means a large, generous amount, more than enough.

VR.e: An ailment is an illness, especially a mild or lingering one—a cold, a cough, an aching back. The word comes from ail, to be unwell.

y.A: Cure is what ends an ailment—the other side of it.
y.C: Injury is harm from an outside cause, such as a fall or a cut; an ailment is a sickness within the body itself.
y.D: Medicine is what treats an ailment, not the ailment.

VR.e: An omen is a sign of something to come, good or bad—a red sky at dawn that sailors took as a warning of storms.

y.A: Curse is a wish for harm to fall on someone; an omen does not cause anything, it only hints at what is coming.
y.B: Dream is something seen in sleep; people once searched their dreams for omens, but the dream is not the omen.
y.D: Wish is what a person hopes will happen; an omen is a hint of what will happen whether anyone hopes for it or not.

VR.e: To coax is to persuade someone gently and patiently, with kind words or small rewards—coaxing a shy kitten out from under the bed.

y.A: Comfort is to ease the sadness of someone who is upset—the same gentle tone as coaxing, but no one is being talked into anything.
y.B: Command means to order someone to do something; coaxing is the opposite in manner—soft where a command is firm.
y.D: Tease means to make fun of someone or pester them playfully; coaxing is gentle, and teasing is a poke.

VR.e: Chiefly means mainly or mostly—for the most part. The chief part of something is its main part.

y.A: Bravely comes from picturing a chief as a bold leader; the adverb has nothing to do with courage.
y.B: Finally means at last—it is about time, not about amount.
y.D: Nearly means almost; something that is chiefly true is mostly true, not almost true.

VR.q: Since the old wooden bridge was built to carry only people on foot, a sign at each end ____ cars and trucks.
VR.e: Since gives the reason: a bridge meant only for walkers cannot take vehicles, so the sign must keep cars and trucks off—it forbids them.

y.A: Allows turns the clue around: if the bridge carries only people on foot, the sign cannot be letting vehicles on.
y.C: Slows is what a speed-limit sign does; it treats the bridge as safe for careful driving when the sentence says it is for walkers only.
y.D: Welcomes is the reverse of what a foot-traffic-only bridge needs its sign to do.

VR.q: Although the final rehearsal of the school play had been full of mistakes, the opening-night performance was ____.
VR.e: Although sets up a reversal: a rehearsal full of mistakes leads us to expect a bad performance, so the night itself must have been the opposite—flawless.

y.B: Lively is a pleasant thing to say about a performance, but a lively show can still be full of mistakes, so it does not answer the although.
y.C: Loud describes the volume of the night, which has nothing to do with whether the mistakes were gone.
y.D: Sloppy carries the mistakes of the rehearsal straight into the performance, which is what although tells us did not happen.

VR.q: Although the sea appears motionless from the beach, strong ____ beneath its surface can pull a swimmer far from shore.
VR.e: Although contrasts the still-looking surface with something moving underneath it; the only thing that flows beneath the surface and pulls a swimmer along is a current.

y.B: Ripples are tiny movements on top of the water, far too small to pull anyone anywhere, and they would show on the surface the sentence calls motionless.
y.C: Waves rise on the surface where they can be seen, so they cannot be the hidden force beneath a sea that looks motionless.
y.D: Winds blow through the air above the water, not beneath its surface.

VR.q: The climbers set out before dawn so that they could stand on the ____ of the mountain before the afternoon storms arrived.
VR.e: So that gives the purpose of the early start: the one place that takes all morning to reach is the top of the mountain, its summit.

y.A: Base is the bottom of the mountain, where the climbers already were when they set out; it takes no early start to stand there.
y.B: Slope is the side of the mountain, which the climbers are on from the first step; nothing about it explains leaving before dawn.
y.D: Trail is the path they walk, under their feet the whole way, not a goal to reach before the storms.

VR.q: Frogs spend the first part of their lives in water and the rest mostly on land, which is why scientists classify them as ____.
VR.e: The sentence defines the word before it names it: an animal that lives first in water and then on land is an amphibian, from a Greek word meaning both kinds of life.

y.B: Insects have six legs and a hard outer shell; nothing in the sentence points to them, and a frog is not one.
y.C: Mammals are warm-blooded animals with fur that feed their young milk, and they do not begin life in water the way frogs do.
y.D: Reptiles is the usual mix-up, because snakes and lizards also have scaly-looking skin, but reptiles hatch on land and stay there; the water-then-land life is what makes a frog an amphibian.

VR.q: Bats, owls, and raccoons are ____ animals: they rest during the day and become active after dark.
VR.e: The colon introduces the definition: animals that sleep by day and move about at night are nocturnal, from the Latin word for night.

y.A: Furry fits bats and raccoons but not owls, and it describes their coats, not the day-and-night habit the colon spells out.
y.B: Migratory animals travel long distances with the seasons; that is a different habit from resting by day and waking at night.
y.D: Playful describes a mood, not a schedule; the sentence is about when these animals are active.

VR.q: The traveling exhibit filled the library’s hall with ____ from many lands: a clay vase, a carved wooden mask, a woven blanket.
VR.e: The examples after the colon decide it: a vase, a mask, and a blanket are handmade objects from past cultures, which is what artifacts means.

y.B: Fossils are the remains of ancient plants and animals preserved in rock; a vase, a mask, and a blanket were made by people.
y.C: Maps show places; none of the three examples is a map.
y.D: Paintings is what an exhibit usually brings to mind, but a vase, a mask, and a blanket are not paintings—they are objects.

VR.q: While a steel bolt sinks the moment it touches water, a cork is ____ enough to float.
VR.e: While sets the sinking bolt against the floating cork, so the blank must name the quality that lets something float: buoyant.

y.B: Firm means not easily bent or pressed; a steel bolt is firmer than a cork and sinks anyway, so firmness is not what floats.
y.C: Rough describes the texture of the surface, which has nothing to do with sinking or floating.
y.D: Solid means not hollow or not liquid; the bolt is solid too, and it sinks, so solid cannot be what keeps the cork up.

VR.q: Because the castle’s outer wall was several feet thick, attackers found it nearly impossible to ____.
VR.e: Because links the thickness of the wall to what it prevented: a wall several feet thick cannot be broken through, so the attackers could not penetrate it.

y.A: Climb is defeated by a wall that is tall, not one that is thick; the sentence gives the thickness as the reason.
y.B: Defend is what the people inside the castle do; attackers are not trying to defend the wall.
y.D: Surround depends on how far around the wall runs, and a thick wall is no harder to circle than a thin one.

VR.q: After the storm, Wren walked the beach picking up the ____ that the waves had left behind—broken boards, tangled rope, and pieces of a wooden dock.
VR.e: The list after the dash gives the meaning: broken boards, rope, and pieces of a dock are scattered wreckage, which is what debris means.

y.B: Footprints cannot be picked up, and boards and rope are not footprints.
y.C: Puddles are pools of water left on the sand; the sentence lists solid things she is picking up.
y.D: Seaweed is what the sea usually leaves on a beach, but the list names broken pieces of things people built, not plants.

VR.q: The town council moved its meeting to the school gym because the usual room could not ____ such a large crowd.
VR.e: Because gives the reason for moving: the usual room did not have space for everyone, so it could not accommodate the crowd—hold it comfortably.

y.B: Attract means to draw people in; the crowd had already come—too many of them—so attracting was not the room’s problem.
y.C: Control is about managing how a crowd behaves, which a room cannot do; the sentence is about how many people fit.
y.D: Impress means to make people admire something, and nobody moves a meeting because a room is not impressive enough.

VR.q: Unlike the ____ letters of a printed page, handwriting changes from one person to the next.
VR.e: Unlike demands the opposite of changing from person to person: printed letters are all the same, which is what uniform means when it describes things rather than clothing.

y.A: Curly describes the shape of some lettering, but curly letters could still differ from one page to the next, so it draws no contrast with changing handwriting.
y.B: Fancy letters can vary as much as plain ones; the sentence needs the quality of always being the same.
y.C: Slanted is how italic letters lean, and handwriting slants too, so it is not what sets print apart.

VR.q: Unlike the oak, which drops its leaves every autumn, the pine ____.
VR.e: Unlike sets up an opposite: the oak loses its leaves each year, so the pine must do the reverse and keep its needles, staying green all year.

y.A: Has rough bark describes the pine without answering unlike; oaks have rough bark too.
y.B: Grows in sandy soil is a fact about where a pine lives, not the opposite of dropping leaves, which is what unlike asks for.
y.C: Is home to many birds could be said of the oak just as well, so it draws no contrast between the two trees.

VR.q: Because sailors long ago had no instruments to show where their ship was, they ____.
VR.e: Because promises a result of having no instruments: with nothing to show their position, sailors found it from the sky, steering by the stars.

y.B: Built their ships of oak is about what the ship was made from, which has nothing to do with knowing where the ship was.
y.C: Traded goods at every port is something sailors did whether or not they had instruments; it is not a result of lacking them.
y.D: Painted their ships bright colors would help other people see the ship, not help the sailors know where they were.

VR.q: The sculptor usually worked in marble, but for the garden fountain she ____.
c: carved a figure of a heron
worked on it for several months
VR.e: But signals a change from her usual marble, so the ending must name something different—a figure made of bronze instead of stone.

y.A: Carved a figure of a heron names a subject she could carve in marble as easily as anything else, so it changes nothing the but could point to.
y.C: Polished every surface by hand is finishing work she would do on marble as well; there is no contrast in it.
y.D: Worked on it for several months tells how long the job took, not what was different about it; marble takes months too.

VR.q: Many people long ago never traveled more than a few miles from home, while others ____.
c: stayed in one house all their lives
crossed oceans to settle in new lands
farmed the land their parents had farmed
married neighbors they had known as children
VR.e: While sets the others against the people who never traveled, so the ending must describe the opposite—going far away, across oceans to new lands.

y.A: Stayed in one house all their lives describes the same stay-at-home people, so it repeats the first half of the sentence instead of contrasting with it.
y.C: Farmed the land their parents had farmed also keeps people where they were born; it is the same side of the contrast.
y.D: Married neighbors they had known as children is one more picture of a life spent close to home.

VR.q: Although the recipe said the cake would need an hour in the oven, Jonah ____.
c: set a timer for one full hour
took it out after forty minutes
greased the pan before pouring the batter
VR.e: Although means Jonah did not follow the hour the recipe gave, so the ending must go against it—taking the cake out after only forty minutes.

y.A: Measured the flour carefully is a step that has nothing to do with the baking time the although points at.
y.B: Set a timer for one full hour follows the recipe’s hour exactly, which is agreement, and although needs disagreement.
y.D: Greased the pan before pouring the batter is ordinary preparation, not a break from the recipe’s hour.

QR.q: Dev buys 3 packs of pencils with 8 pencils in each pack, then gives 5 pencils to his cousin. Which number sentence shows how many pencils Dev has left?
QR.e: Three packs of 8 pencils is 3 × 8 pencils, and giving 5 away takes 5 off, so the sentence is 3 × 8 − 5.

y.A: 3 + 8 − 5 adds the number of packs to the pencils in one pack; 3 packs of 8 pencils means 3 × 8.
y.C: 3 × 8 + 5 adds the 5 pencils Dev gave away instead of taking them off.
y.D: 3 × (8 − 5) takes 5 pencils out of every pack, but Dev gave away 5 pencils in all.

QR.sk: data and probability—reading a bar graph
QR.q: The graph shows the favorite pet of each student in Ms. Okafor's class. How many students chose a pet other than a dog?
QR.e: The cat, fish, and bird bars reach 7, 4, and 2, and 7 + 4 + 2 = 13.

y.A: 6 is 4 + 2, the fish and bird bars; the 7 students who chose a cat are left out.
y.B: 9 is the height of the dog bar, the one group the question leaves out.
y.C: 11 is 7 + 4, the cat and fish bars; the 2 students who chose a bird are left out.

QR.q: Ravi writes a four-digit number. It has a 4 in the thousands place and a 7 in the tens place. Which could be Ravi's number?
QR.e: The thousands place is the first digit and the tens place is the second digit from the right, so the number looks like 4 _ 7 _. Only 4,571 fits.

y.A: 4,517 puts the 7 in the ones place, the last digit, not the tens place.
y.C: 4,715 puts the 7 in the hundreds place; the tens place is the second digit from the right.
y.D: 7,418 swaps the two digits, putting the 7 in the thousands place and the 4 in the hundreds place.

QR.q: The figure is drawn on a grid of unit squares. What is the area of the figure, in square units?
QR.e: Count the squares inside the figure: the bottom part has 5 × 2 = 10 squares and the upper part has 2 × 2 = 4 squares, and 10 + 4 = 14.

y.A: 10 counts only the squares in the bottom part, 5 across and 2 up, and misses the 4 squares in the upper part.
y.C: 18 is the number of unit lengths around the outside of the figure — its perimeter — not the squares inside it.
y.D: 20 is 5 × 4, every square in the rectangle around the figure, including the 6 empty squares at the top right.

QR.sk: algebra—missing number in a number sentence
QR.q: Felix wrote the number sentence 9 × □ = 72. What number belongs in the box?
QR.e: The box holds the number of 9s that make 72. Since 9 × 8 = 72, the box holds 8.

y.A: 7 comes from a times-table slip: 9 × 7 is 63, not 72.
y.C: 63 is 72 − 9, subtracting instead of asking how many 9s make 72.
y.D: 81 is 72 + 9, adding the two numbers instead of dividing.

QR.q: Which unit is the best choice for measuring the length of a school bus?
QR.e: A school bus is about 12 meters long, so meters give a handy number. Smaller units give numbers in the thousands and kilometers are for distances between places.

y.A: centimeters would give a number over a thousand for a bus; they suit something the size of a book.
y.B: kilometers measure the distance between towns; a whole bus is only a tiny part of one kilometer.
y.D: millimeters are for tiny things, like the thickness of a coin.

QR.q: A theater has 28 rows of seats with 31 seats in each row. Which is the best estimate of the total number of seats?
QR.e: 28 is close to 30 and 31 is close to 30, and 30 × 30 = 900.

y.A: 60 is about 28 + 31; the rows and the seats in each row should be multiplied, not added.
y.B: 600 is 20 × 30, rounding 28 down to 20; 28 is much closer to 30.
y.D: 9,000 is 30 × 300 — one zero too many; 30 × 30 is 900.

QR.q: The pictograph shows the cans each class collected for a food drive. How many cans did Room 12 collect?
QR.e: Room 12 has 3 whole symbols and a half symbol. Each whole symbol is 10 cans and the half is 5, so 30 + 5 = 35.

y.A: 3 is the number of whole symbols in the row, not the number of cans they stand for.
y.B: 30 counts the three whole symbols as 10 cans each and leaves out the half symbol.
y.D: 40 counts the half symbol as a whole symbol worth 10 cans; a half symbol stands for 5.

QR.sk: numbers and operations—money from a price list
QR.q: The table shows the prices at a school snack stand. Oscar buys two pretzels and one juice. How much does he spend in all?
QR.e: Two pretzels cost 2 × $1.25 = $2.50, and the juice adds $1.50, so he spends $4.00.

y.A: $2.75 is one pretzel and one juice, $1.25 + $1.50; the second pretzel is not counted.
y.C: $4.25 is two juices and one pretzel, $3.00 + $1.25 — the items are switched.
y.D: $5.50 doubles both items, 2 × ($1.25 + $1.50), as if Oscar bought two juices as well.

QR.sk: algebra—finding the rule of an input/output table
QR.q: The table shows the inputs and outputs of a number machine. Which rule does the machine use?
QR.e: Test each rule on every row. Only "multiply by 3, then add 2" works for all of them: 3 × 3 + 2 = 11, 5 × 3 + 2 = 17, 8 × 3 + 2 = 26, and 10 × 3 + 2 = 32.

y.A: Add 8 fits only the first row: 5 + 8 is 13, but the table shows 17.
y.B: Multiply by 2, then add 5 fits the first row only: 5 × 2 + 5 is 15, not 17.
y.D: Multiply by 4, then subtract 1 fits the first row only: 5 × 4 − 1 is 19, not 17.

QR.sk: numbers and operations—fraction of a shaded figure
QR.q: The figure shows a community garden divided into equal plots. The shaded plots are planted with tomatoes. What fraction of the garden is planted with tomatoes?
QR.e: There are 12 plots and 4 of them are shaded, so the fraction is 4/12, which is 1/3.

y.A: 1/4 writes 1 over the number of shaded plots, 4; a fraction compares the 4 shaded plots with all 12.
y.C: 1/2 compares the 4 shaded plots with the 8 unshaded ones instead of with the whole garden.
y.D: 2/3 is the part of the garden that is not shaded, 8 of the 12 plots.

QR.q: The clock shows the time Jonah's soccer practice ended one afternoon. Practice lasted 1 hour 15 minutes. At what time did it start?
QR.e: The clock shows 4:40. Going back 1 hour gives 3:40, and going back 15 more minutes gives 3:25.

y.B: 3:55 p.m. takes off the hour but adds the 15 minutes instead of taking them off too.
y.C: 4:25 p.m. takes off only the 15 minutes and forgets the hour.
y.D: 5:55 p.m. adds 1 hour 15 minutes to the clock time instead of going back from it.

QR.q: The figure shows a stack built from identical small cubes, with no gaps or hidden holes. How many cubes are in the stack?
QR.e: The stack is 3 cubes wide, 2 cubes deep, and 2 cubes tall, so it holds 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 cubes.

y.A: 6 is 3 × 2, the cubes on the front face only; there is a second layer of cubes behind them.
y.B: 7 is 3 + 2 + 2, the three edge lengths added instead of multiplied.
y.C: 10 counts only the cubes that show a face in the drawing; two cubes at the back of the bottom layer are hidden but still there.

QR.sk: numbers and operations—matching a question to an operation
QR.q: Which question can be answered by finding 36 ÷ 4?
c: Greta has 36 grapes and eats 4. How many grapes are left?
Greta has 36 grapes and picks 4 more. How many grapes does she have now?
Greta puts 36 grapes equally into 4 cups. How many grapes are in each cup?
Greta fills 36 cups with 4 grapes in each cup. How many grapes does she use?
QR.e: Dividing shares a total equally into groups. Putting 36 grapes equally into 4 cups asks how many are in each cup, which is 36 ÷ 4.

y.A: 36 grapes with 4 eaten asks what is left, which is 36 − 4, a subtraction.
y.B: 36 grapes and 4 more asks for a total, which is 36 + 4, an addition.
y.D: 36 cups with 4 grapes in each asks for a total of 36 × 4 grapes, a multiplication.

QR.sk: data and probability—reading a Venn diagram
QR.q: The Venn diagram shows the pets of the students in Mr. Lindqvist's class. How many students have a dog?
QR.e: Everyone inside the dog circle has a dog: the 6 who have only a dog and the 4 who have both, so 6 + 4 = 10.

y.A: 4 is only the students in the overlap, who have both a cat and a dog.
y.B: 6 is the students who have a dog but no cat; the 4 who have both have a dog too.
y.C: 7 is the students who have only a cat — the other circle.

QR.sk: numbers and operations—rounding to the nearest hundred
QR.q: Keiko is thinking of a number. Rounded to the nearest hundred, it is 600. Which could be Keiko's number?
QR.e: A number rounds to 600 when it is from 550 up to 649. Only 562 is in that range.

y.A: 549 rounds down to 500 because its tens digit is 4; it is closer to 500 than to 600.
y.C: 651 rounds up to 700: its tens digit is 5, which says to round up, even though it starts with 6.
y.D: 695 is in the six hundreds but is only 5 away from 700, so it rounds to 700.

QR.q: The table shows how many tiles are in each stage of a pattern. If the pattern continues the same way, how many tiles will Stage 7 have?
QR.e: Each stage has 3 more tiles than the one before. Continuing from Stage 4: Stage 5 has 16, Stage 6 has 19, and Stage 7 has 22.

y.A: 16 is the number of tiles in Stage 5, two stages short of Stage 7.
y.B: 19 is the number of tiles in Stage 6; the count stops one stage early.
y.D: 28 is 4 × 7, as if every stage had 4 tiles for each stage number; the pattern adds 3 tiles each stage.

QR.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 20 centimeters. Which could be its length and width?
QR.e: The perimeter is the distance around all four sides: length + width + length + width. With 4 cm and 6 cm, that is 4 + 6 + 4 + 6 = 20 cm.

y.A: 2 cm and 10 cm multiply to 20, which would be the area; the perimeter would be 2 + 10 + 2 + 10, which is 24 cm.
y.B: 4 cm and 5 cm multiply to 20, the area, not the distance around; the perimeter would be 18 cm.
y.D: 10 cm and 10 cm add to 20, but that counts only two of the four sides; the perimeter would be 40 cm.

QR.sk: numbers and operations—fraction on a number line
QR.q: The number line shows the course of a 12-kilometer race. Point P marks where Hana is now. What fraction of the race has she finished?
QR.e: P is one tick past 8, at 9 kilometers. She has run 9 of the 12 kilometers, and 9/12 is 3/4.

y.A: 1/4 is the part of the race still ahead of her, 3 of the 12 kilometers.
y.B: 1/3 compares the 3 kilometers left with the 9 she has run, instead of with the whole 12.
y.C: 2/3 reads P as 8, the last labeled mark, but P is one tick past 8, at 9.

QR.sk: data and probability—probability from a spinner
QR.q: The spinner is divided into the three sections shown. If the arrow is spun once, what is the probability that it lands on blue?
QR.e: The blue section is one quarter of the spinner — the red section is half and blue and green are a quarter each. So the chance of blue is 1/4.

y.B: 1/3 counts three sections with one of them blue, as if the sections were equal; the red section is twice as big as the others.
y.C: 1/2 is the chance of red, the section that takes up half the spinner.
y.D: 3/4 is the chance of not landing on blue — red and green together.

QR.q: Lucia has a ribbon 3 meters long. She cuts it into pieces that are each 25 centimeters long. How many pieces does she get?
QR.e: 3 meters is 300 centimeters, and 300 ÷ 25 = 12 pieces.

y.A: 4 is 100 ÷ 25, the pieces that come from just 1 meter of the 3.
y.C: 75 is 3 × 25, multiplying the two numbers in the question instead of changing meters to centimeters and dividing.
y.D: 120 is 3000 ÷ 25, as if a meter had 1,000 centimeters; a meter has 100.

QR.q: Simone is 3 years older than twice her brother's age. Her brother is b years old. Which expression shows Simone's age?
QR.e: Twice her brother's age is 2b, and 3 years older than that is 2b + 3.

y.A: 2b − 3 would make Simone 3 years younger than twice her brother's age, not older.
y.C: 3b + 2 switches the two numbers: it triples the brother's age and adds 2.
y.D: 2(b + 3) adds the 3 years to the brother's age first and then doubles, so the extra years get doubled too.

QR.sk: numbers and operations—percent of a shaded whole
QR.q: The bar in the figure is divided into equal parts. What percent of the bar is shaded?
QR.e: The bar has 5 equal parts, so each part is 100% ÷ 5 = 20%. Two parts are shaded, and 2 × 20% = 40%.

y.A: 2% is the number of shaded parts with a percent sign on it; each part is worth 20%, not 1%.
y.B: 20% is one part of the five, not the two parts that are shaded.
y.D: 60% is the part of the bar that is not shaded, 3 of the 5 parts.

QR.q: Three vertices of a rectangle are plotted on the grid. What are the coordinates of the fourth vertex?
QR.e: The fourth corner sits directly above J, at 1 across, and level with L, at 4 up, so it is at (1, 4).

y.B: (1, 6) uses the 6 from point K as the height, but the top side of the rectangle is at 4 up, level with point L.
y.C: (4, 1) swaps the two coordinates: 4 across and 1 up is on the bottom side, not at the top left corner.
y.D: (4, 6) reverses the coordinates of point L, (6, 4), instead of finding the corner above J.

QR.sk: data and probability—median of a data set
QR.q: The graph shows the goals a soccer team scored in each of five games. What is the median number of goals?
QR.e: Read the bars and put the numbers in order: 2, 2, 3, 5, 8. The median is the middle number, 3.

y.B: 4 is the mean: the 20 goals shared equally over the 5 games.
y.C: 6 is the range, the difference between the most goals in a game, 8, and the fewest, 2.
y.D: 8 is the middle bar as the games are drawn, Game 3; the median is the middle value after the numbers are put in order.

QR.sk: numbers and operations—breaking a product apart
QR.q: Which expression has the same value as 6 × 23?
QR.e: 23 is 20 + 3, so 6 groups of 23 are 6 groups of 20 and 6 groups of 3: 6 × 20 + 6 × 3.

y.A: 6 × 20 + 3 multiplies only the 20 by 6; the 3 ones must be multiplied by 6 as well.
y.B: 6 × 20 × 3 multiplies the 20 and the 3 together instead of adding the two products; 20 × 3 is not 23.

QR.q: The table shows the schedule for a class field trip. How long were the students at the museum before lunch?
QR.e: They arrived at 10:15 and ate lunch at 12:45. From 10:15 to 12:15 is 2 hours, and 12:15 to 12:45 is 30 more minutes.

y.B: 2 hours 45 minutes counts from 10 o'clock to 12:45 and drops the 15 minutes after 10 that passed before the class arrived.
y.C: 3 hours counts the hour numbers 10, 11, and 12 as three whole hours, but the visit began a quarter past 10 and ended before 1.
y.D: 3 hours 15 minutes is the time from leaving school at 9:30 until lunch, not the time spent at the museum.

QR.sk: algebra—finding an unknown from two number sentences
QR.q: In these number sentences, the same shape always stands for the same number. △ + △ = 14 and △ + □ = 11. What number does □ stand for?
QR.e: Two triangles make 14, so one triangle is 7. Then 7 + □ = 11, so the square is 4.

y.B: 7 is the value of the triangle, half of 14; the question asks about the square.
y.C: 11 is the triangle and the square together, the total in the second number sentence, not the square alone.
y.D: 25 is 14 + 11, the two totals added together.

QR.q: The figure shows the outline of a patio with four of its six sides labeled. Every side meets the next at a right angle. What is the perimeter of the patio?
QR.e: The two unlabeled sides can be worked out: the short vertical side is 6 − 3 = 3 cm and the short horizontal side is 8 − 4 = 4 cm. So the perimeter is 8 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 28 cm, the same as the 8 by 6 rectangle around the patio.

y.A: 14 cm is 8 + 6, the two longest sides only; the perimeter goes all the way around.
y.B: 21 cm is the four labeled sides added, 8 + 3 + 4 + 6; the two unlabeled sides add 3 + 4 = 7 cm more.
y.D: 36 cm is 8 × 3 + 4 × 3, the area in square centimeters, not the distance around.

QR.q: A ferry can carry 8 cars on each trip. There are 50 cars waiting to cross. What is the least number of trips the ferry must make to carry all of them?
QR.e: 6 trips carry 6 × 8 = 48 cars, and 2 cars are still waiting, so a seventh trip is needed: 7 trips.

y.A: 2 is the remainder when 50 is divided by 8 — the cars left for the last trip, not the number of trips.
y.B: 6 trips carry only 48 cars; the 2 cars left over need a seventh trip.
y.D: 48 is 6 × 8, the cars carried in six full trips, not the number of trips.

QR.sk: data and probability—probability of a simple event
QR.q: A box holds 12 crayons. Without looking, Anya picks one crayon. The probability that it is blue is 1 out of 3. How many blue crayons are in the box?
QR.e: 1 out of 3 means that 1 in every 3 crayons is blue. 12 crayons make 4 groups of 3, so 4 crayons are blue.

y.A: 1 is the top number of the probability, not a count of crayons; 1 out of 3 means 1 in every 3 crayons is blue.
y.B: 3 is the bottom number of the probability; with 12 crayons, 1 out of 3 means 12 ÷ 3 of them are blue.
y.D: 8 is the number of crayons that are not blue, 12 − 4.

QR.q: Which of these is closest to 1 meter long?
QR.e: A meter is about the distance from the floor to a doorknob. A baseball bat is close to that; the others are far shorter or far longer.

y.A: a car is about 4 or 5 meters long — several meter sticks end to end.
y.B: a paper clip is about 3 centimeters long, only a small part of a meter.
y.C: a soccer field is about 100 meters long.

QR.q: Three identical boxes of books and one 3-kilogram bag of magazines weigh 24 kilograms altogether. How much does one box of books weigh?
QR.e: Take off the bag first: 24 − 3 = 21 kilograms for the three boxes. Then share it among the three: 21 ÷ 3 = 7 kilograms each.

y.B: 8 kg is 24 ÷ 3, as if the bag weighed nothing; the bag's 3 kilograms must come off first.
y.C: 9 kg is 27 ÷ 3, from adding the bag's 3 kilograms instead of taking them away.
y.D: 21 kg is the weight of the three boxes together, 24 − 3, before it is shared among the three boxes.

QR.sk: numbers and operations—fractions of a set
QR.q: Mateo has 24 marbles. He gives 1/4 of them to his sister and 1/8 of them to a friend. How many marbles does he give away in all?
QR.e: 1/4 of 24 is 6 and 1/8 of 24 is 3, so he gives away 6 + 3 = 9 marbles.

y.A: 2 comes from adding the denominators 4 and 8 to make 1/12, and 1/12 of 24 is 2.
y.B: 4 comes from adding tops and bottoms, 1/4 + 1/8 as 2/12, and 2/12 of 24 is 4.
y.C: 6 is only the sister's share, 1/4 of 24; the friend's 3 marbles must be added on.

QR.q: How many lines of symmetry does the figure have?
QR.e: A line of symmetry is a fold that makes the two halves match exactly. Folding this slanted parallelogram along a diagonal or through its middle always leaves a corner sticking out, so it has no lines of symmetry.

y.B: 1 counts a diagonal as a fold line, but folding along a diagonal does not land one half exactly on the other.
y.C: 2 counts both diagonals as lines of symmetry; they cut the figure into matching triangles, but the halves do not fold onto each other.
y.D: 4 treats the figure like a square, with two midlines and two diagonals; a slanted parallelogram has none of these.

QR.sk: data and probability—drawing a conclusion from a line graph
QR.q: The graph shows the temperature outside a school at five times during one day. Which statement is true?
c: It was cooler at 6 p.m. than at 6 a.m.
It rose more from 9 a.m. to noon than from noon to 3 p.m.
It rose by the same amount from 6 a.m. to 9 a.m. as from noon to 3 p.m.
QR.e: From 9 a.m. to noon the line climbs from 55°F to 70°F, a rise of 15 degrees; from noon to 3 p.m. it climbs only from 70°F to 75°F, a rise of 5 degrees.

y.A: Warmest at noon reads the wrong peak: the highest point on the graph is 75°F at 3 p.m., not the 70°F at noon.
y.B: At 6 p.m. it was 65°F, which is warmer than the 45°F at 6 a.m., not cooler.
y.D: From 6 a.m. to 9 a.m. it rose 10 degrees, from 45°F to 55°F, but from noon to 3 p.m. it rose only 5 degrees, from 70°F to 75°F.

QR.sk: algebra—continuing a pattern from a graph
QR.q: The graph shows what it costs to rent a kayak for 1, 2, 3, or 4 hours. If the pattern continues, how much will it cost to rent the kayak for 6 hours?
QR.e: Each extra hour adds $4: the points rise from $8 to $12 to $16 to $20. Two more hours after the $20 for 4 hours gives $24 for 5 hours and $28 for 6 hours.

y.A: $24 is the cost for 5 hours — one more step of $4 — but the question asks about 6 hours.
y.C: $32 is 2 × $16, doubling the 3-hour cost; the cost does not double when the hours double, because the first hour costs more than the others.
y.D: $48 is 6 × $8, using the first hour's price as the price of every hour; each extra hour adds only $4.

QR.q: The rectangle in the figure is made of two identical squares. Its perimeter is 36 cm. What is the side length of one square?
QR.e: Going around the rectangle you pass 6 sides of a square: 2 along the top, 2 along the bottom, and 1 at each end. Six sides make 36 cm, so one side is 36 ÷ 6 = 6 cm.

y.B: 9 cm is 36 ÷ 4, as if the whole rectangle were one square with four equal sides.
y.C: 12 cm is the long side of the rectangle, two squares end to end, not the side of one square.
y.D: 18 cm is 36 ÷ 2, the length and the width added together.

RC.q: According to the passage, where do monarchs from the West spend the winter?
c: on the branches of oyamel firs
RC.e: Lines 15–17 say that monarchs from the West spend the winter on the California coast, resting in groves of pine, cypress, and eucalyptus trees.

y.A: Fields in Canada are where the butterflies arrive at the end of the trip north (line 33), the opposite end of the journey from their winter home.
y.C: The mountains of Mexico are where the monarchs from the eastern part of the continent gather (lines 10–11); the question asks about the western ones.
y.D: Oyamel firs are the trees the eastern monarchs cluster on in Mexico (lines 11–13), not the pines and cypresses of the California coast.

RC.q: In line 8, “cover” most nearly means
RC.e: The sentence says the butterflies can cover 50 to 100 miles in a single day, so here cover means to travel across a distance.

y.A: Hide is one meaning of cover, to put something out of sight, but the sentence counts miles in a day, a distance and not a hiding place.
y.B: Protect is what a cover does for a plant or a pot, but the sentence is about how many miles the butterflies fly in a day, not about shelter.
y.D: Wrap comes from picturing a cover as a blanket laid over something; the sentence is measuring how far the butterflies travel in a day.

RC.q: Which best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: A monarch born in early summer lives for just a few weeks.
Monarch caterpillars depend on milkweed plants for their food.
Scientists are not sure how monarchs know when it is time to leave.
Monarchs make a long yearly journey that no single butterfly completes.
RC.e: Every paragraph is about the journey: how far the monarchs fly, where they spend the winter, how long the traveling generation lives, and how three or four generations bring them north again.

y.A: A monarch born in early summer living a few weeks is one fact from the third paragraph (lines 20–21), there to explain why the migrating generation is unusual, not the subject of the whole passage.
y.B: Caterpillars depending on milkweed is a detail from the last paragraph (lines 29–30) about the trip north; it says nothing about the flight south or the winter in Mexico.
y.C: Scientists being not sure comes from reading “Scientists think” (line 24) as doubt; the sentence gives their explanation, and it is one detail about timing, not what the passage is about.

RC.q: The last paragraph (lines 27–36) is mainly about
c: how several generations share the trip north
how monarchs survive the cold winter in Mexico
why the fall generation lives for so much longer
where the monarchs from the West spend the winter
RC.e: Lines 27–36 follow the monarchs north from Mexico: each generation flies a little farther and lays eggs, and three or four generations are needed to reach Canada.

y.B: Surviving the cold winter in Mexico comes from the second paragraph (lines 11–14), where the butterflies cluster on cool mountain trees; the last paragraph has already left Mexico.
y.C: The fall generation living longer is what the third paragraph (lines 19–24) explains; the last paragraph is about the generations that follow it.
y.D: The monarchs from the West wintering in California is a detail at the end of the second paragraph (lines 15–18), not the subject of the last one.

RC.q: It can be inferred from the passage that the monarchs arriving in Mexico each fall
c: will live for just a few more weeks
were born in Mexico the spring before
are making their first trip to the south
are the same butterflies that left in spring
RC.e: A summer monarch lives only a few weeks and no single butterfly makes the round trip (lines 20–21 and 27), so the butterflies reaching Mexico were born in the North that year and have never flown south before.

y.A: A few more weeks is the lifespan of a summer monarch (lines 20–21); the ones that reach Mexico are the long-lived generation that can last nine months (line 22).
y.B: Born in Mexico the spring before comes from reading “the monarchs leave Mexico” (line 28) as if they had hatched there; those butterflies were born in the North the summer before, and it is their descendants that fly south in the fall.
y.D: The same butterflies that left in spring is ruled out by line 27, “No single butterfly makes the whole round trip.”

RC.q: The passage suggests that for Mary's family, collecting fossils was mainly
c: a way to earn a living
a hobby that was in fashion
a way to become famous scientists
a path into the Geological Society
RC.e: The family was poor and in debt after Richard died, Mary's mother encouraged her to keep selling what she found, and scientists bought her fossils (lines 11–13 and 29–30).

y.B: A hobby in fashion is what fossil collecting was for the people who paid for curiosities (lines 9–10); for the Annings, who sold to them, it paid the family's debts.
y.C: Becoming famous scientists stretches “treated as true experts” (lines 22–23); the passage says the scientists who wrote about her fossils left her name out (lines 29–31).
y.D: A path into the Geological Society is the opposite of what happened: it did not allow women to join until 1908 (lines 31–32), long after Mary died.

RC.q: According to the passage, who found the fossil skull in 1811?
RC.e: Lines 14–15 say that in the autumn of 1811 her brother Joseph found a strange fossil skull; Mary found the rest of the animal about a year later.

y.A: Her father is the one who taught Mary to find fossils (lines 6–8), but he died in 1810 (line 11), the year before the skull was found.
y.C: Mary herself found the rest of the animal and dug out the skeleton about a year later (lines 15–17); the skull came first, and Joseph found it.
y.D: A French scientist appears later, doubting a drawing of the plesiosaur (lines 20–21); he found nothing on the beach.

RC.q: The passage is primarily about
c: how a poor girl became an expert on fossils
the first flying reptile found outside Germany
the history of the Geological Society of London
how fossils formed in the cliffs beside Lyme Regis
RC.e: The passage follows Mary from a childhood selling fossils to pay her family's debts, through her great finds, to the respect she earned even when she was not given credit.

y.B: The first flying reptile found outside Germany is one of Mary's discoveries (lines 23–25), a single detail in a passage about her whole life.
y.C: The Geological Society of London appears in one sentence (lines 31–32), as an example of how women were kept out; the passage is about Mary, not the Society.
y.D: How fossils formed in the cliffs is not explained anywhere; the first paragraph says only that the cliffs are packed with fossils, to set the scene for Mary's story.

RC.q: In line 22, “genuine” most nearly means
RC.e: The French scientist first doubted that the skeleton was real; once he realized it was genuine, he accepted it, so genuine means real, not fake.

y.A: Ancient fits a fossil in general, but the scientist's doubt was about whether the skeleton was real, and genuine is the word that answers that doubt.
y.B: Complete comes from “the first complete skeleton” three lines earlier (line 19); the question in line 21 is whether the find was real, not whether it was whole.
y.D: Valuable comes from the fossils being sold (lines 8–10); the sentence is settling a doubt about whether the skeleton was real.

RC.q: According to the passage, the Geological Society of London
c: put up a statue of Mary in 2022
sent scientists to study Lyme Regis
did not allow women to join until 1908
RC.e: Lines 31–32 say the Geological Society of London did not allow women to join until 1908.

y.A: Buying her fossils was done by individual scientists who then wrote about them (lines 29–30); the passage does not say the Society bought anything.
y.B: The statue in 2022 came after a campaign led by an eleven-year-old girl (lines 33–35), not from the Society.
y.C: Sending scientists is not in the passage; the French scientist studied a drawing (lines 20–21), and the visitor who wrote in her diary (lines 27–29) is not said to have been sent by anyone.

RC.q: The passage is mainly about
c: a visit to a very messy garage
a girl who learns to make a footstep
how the sounds in movies are made by hand
the many uses of celery and coconut shells
RC.e: The passage shows a class learning how a sound artist makes the everyday sounds in a film, from footsteps in snow to a horse, by hand in a studio.

y.A: A messy garage is only what the studio looked like (line 8); the visit was about the sounds made inside it.
y.B: A girl learning to make a footstep is how the passage ends (lines 31–33), one example of what the students tried, not the subject of the whole visit.
y.D: Celery and coconut shells are two of the objects used for sounds (lines 21–22 and 25–26); the passage is about the sounds, not the objects.

RC.q: When Ms. Castellano says, “Your ears believe whatever your eyes tell them” (lines 22–23), she means that
c: people hear better when they can also see
pictures matter more than sounds in a film
a sound seems real when it matches the picture
the students should watch the screen while they work
RC.e: She says it right after a bag of cornstarch sounded like snow and celery sounded like a branch: when a sound fits what the viewer sees, the viewer accepts it as real.

y.A: Hearing better reads the sentence as being about how sharp our ears are; it is about being fooled, since cornstarch passed for snow once the picture showed snow.
y.B: Pictures mattering more takes the sentence as ranking the two; it is about how the two work together, with the picture making the sound believable.
y.D: Watching the screen is what Mina does later (lines 32–33); the sentence is about an audience's ears and eyes, not instructions for the students.

RC.q: According to the passage, Ms. Castellano made the sound of footsteps in snow by
c: walking in place on a plank
galloping two coconut shells in a tray
squeezing a bag of cornstarch in her fists
RC.e: Lines 18–20 say that for the footsteps in snow she squeezed a bag of cornstarch in her fists, and the crunch sounded real.

y.A: Snapping celery was for the branch the woman broke from the tree (lines 21–22), not for her footsteps.
y.B: Walking in place on a plank is how Mina finally made a footstep on wood at the end (lines 31–33), not how the snow was done.
y.C: Galloping two coconut shells in a tray was a boy's way of making a horse (lines 25–26).

RC.q: In line 33, “fixed” most nearly means
RC.e: Mina kept her eyes on the screen without looking away while she stepped, so her eyes were fixed on it, held steady in one place.

y.A: Closed is the opposite of what Mina was doing; she had to watch the woman's steps on the screen to match them.
y.B: Open describes eyes that are simply awake; fixed says more, that they stayed on one spot, the screen, without moving away.
y.C: Repaired is the everyday meaning of fixed, as in fixing a bike, but eyes are not broken; here fixed means held steady on something.

RC.q: Several students glanced down at their own feet (lines 20–21) most likely because
c: they were choosing shoes from the rack
the crunch seemed to come from under them
they were about to try the sound themselves
Ms. Castellano had told them to watch their steps
RC.e: The crunch was “so real” (line 20) that for a moment the students checked whether the sound of snow had come from their own shoes.

y.A: Choosing shoes from the rack mixes in the rack of shoes in every size from the description of the studio (lines 9–10); nobody is said to pick out shoes.
y.C: Trying the sound themselves comes next, in the fourth paragraph (line 24); at this moment they were still watching the artist.
y.D: Watching their steps is advice Ms. Castellano gives later about how real people walk (lines 29–31), after the students had tried footsteps.

RC.q: The passage provides information to answer which question?
c: Who started the first bike bus?
How long does the ride to school take?
How many riders came on the first morning?
What time does the bike bus reach the school?
RC.e: Lines 15–17 say that on the first morning only four riders showed up; the passage never says who started the first bike bus, how long the ride takes, or when it reaches the school.

y.A: Who started the first bike bus is tempting because a parent leads this one (line 5), but the passage never names a founder or says where the idea began.
y.B: How long the ride takes is not given; the passage says the bus rolls slowly (lines 29–30) but gives no time for the trip.
y.D: What time it reaches the school is not stated; a quarter to eight (line 1) is when the bus pulls up at one corner, not when it arrives at school.

RC.q: According to the second paragraph (lines 6–14), the speaker on the leader's bike plays music so that
c: the riders keep a steady pace
the riders know when to make a turn
